Breaking: 6 ways to use AI to shop smarter—without giving it access to your wallet

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1332 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thanksgiving is fast approaching, which means Black Friday is too.
  • Recent findings suggest that thanksgiving is fast approaching, which means Black Friday is too.
  • Recent findings suggest that personally, I’m not a Black Friday shopper.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanksgiving is fast approaching, which means Black Friday is too. In the era of AI-assisted shopping, tech companies offer tools that allow you to shop directly on their platforms, or through integrations with online retailers and payment providers. Personally, I’m not a Black Friday shopper. I also don’t feel comfortable giving an AI model my credit card information (or letting it invest for me or make other financial transactions on my behalf). But I do feel comfortable sharing low-stakes information about my needs and interests and stretching a model’s search capability to its limit. Treating my chatbot like a research assistant has saved me time and money, and helped me avoid the annoyance of navigating online stores. Below are a few tips for using artificial intelligence to shop more efficiently, without handing over your credit card information to a bot. Use AI to find exactly what you need, faster Shopping online can be a nightmare, especially if you need something really specific. Say you need to find a bookshelf that fits in a space with very specific dimensions. Why waste time sifting through myriad websites—and endless advertisements—when AI can search for a product that meets your exact needs? The same goes for everything from household repair items to bridesmaid dresses of a certain hue: AI saves you time by searching for exactly what you need, whether that’s a certain size, color, or operating system. And it’s less mentally taxing than going through an endless number of websites. Tell AI where you have a subscription—and where you don’t Many of us have subscriptions to services we prefer, and platforms we prefer to avoid. Telling AI where you already have memberships, and where you might even be collecting points, can help you shop more efficiently. If you’re part of a loyalty program and have a credit card from Lowe’s, there’s little reason for AI to recommend products from Kmart or Walmart. Tell your AI where you like to shop and have it tailor its results accordingly. This might involve telling AI that you want links only from Costco, not Amazon, or that you prefer to read suggestions from Fast Firm, where you have a login (ahem). This advice also applies to frequent flyer miles and credit card rewards. Have AI search for coupons and other cost-saving measures Use AI to find coupon codes and other money-saving opportunities. This isn’t any special application of AI, but simply involves exploiting the powerful search capabilities of large language models to benefit your wallet. About to buy an expensive product? Ask a model where else you can buy it, and whether it’s available for less. You might even ask it to investigate whether a purchase qualifies for reimbursement through a Flexible Spending Account, and what documentation you’d need. Develop a shopping plan with AI Sometimes you really want to see something in person before you buy it. AI can help you come up with an itinerary of stores to check out in person, and direct you to the best neighborhoods for window shopping. It can also help you prioritize your time and travel, drawing up efficient routes and suggesting the best time of day to head out. Ask AI for suggestions Perhaps there’s a product that will make your life better and you just don’t know it yet. AI might have some good ideas, though. It can also help you find reviews that speak to specific concerns you might have about a product, searching the web more thoroughly. This might mean investigating whether anyone has complained about safety problems with, say, a robotic cat litter box, or searching for resort reviews written by parents who can speak to how well a place works for families. Help understand warranties and refunds Sometimes a purchase that seemed perfect turns out to be anything but. AI can help you navigate complicated warranty and refund policies—and potentially get your money back. Have it review the terms of your purchase, identify the strongest grounds for a refund, and even draft a persuasive request on your behalf.

Industry News: Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1178 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors.
  • Industry observers note that the approach has already revealed upcoming candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications.
  • Industry observers note that one of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors. Developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), the method makes it much easier to identify promising materials for quantum technology, potentially opening the door to advances across many areas of science.

Industry observers note that the approach has already revealed upcoming candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications. The findings were recently published in ACS Central Science and have attracted attention from other researchers in the field.

Industry observers note that one of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions. Many candidates require extremely low temperatures to function reliably. Diamond materials stand out because certain quantum properties can remain useful even at room temperature.

This capability could help advance technologies that are notable to national research priorities and the development of next-generation computing. Quantum sensors promise levels of sensitivity and precision beyond those of conventional instruments, while quantum computers could eventually solve certain extraordinarily complex problems much faster than today's most powerful supercomputers.

Why Imperfect Diamonds Could Be the Key to Quantum Computing.

Although diamonds are made of carbon atoms, a flawless diamond crystal is not enough to create a useful quantum computing system. The key lies in tiny irregularities within the crystal structure.

These imperfections, known as defects, can occur when a carbon atom is absent from its normal position, when another element replaces a carbon atom, or when both changes occur together. The atoms surrounding these defects can form qubits, the basic units used to store and process quantum information in quantum computers and sensors.

Finding the most useful defects, however, has been difficult. Accurately modeling their quantum behavior traditionally requires enormous computational resources, making it challenging to evaluate large numbers of possible candidates.

A Simpler Way to Discover Better Diamond Qubits.

Mark Martirez, a staff research scientist at PPPL, developed a way to dramatically reduce the complexity of these calculations. Instead of simulating a much larger diamond structure, he isolates a small region containing just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect.

It has been revealed that by "carving out" this tiny atomic cluster and treating it like a separate molecule, Martirez can use powerful computational methods that chemists have spent decades refining. These established techniques make it possible to analyze the quantum properties of diamond defects much more efficiently without sacrificing the high level of accuracy needed for the calculations.

"Because we're treating the qubits as molecules, the cost of calculating these defects is equivalent to the cost of just modeling a simple molecule," Martirez mentioned. "This method really opened the floodgates" in terms of how qubits can be assessed.

It has been revealed that the new technique allows researchers to calculate how different qubits respond to laser light and microwave pulses far more quickly than before. Using this approach, the team identified promising defects involving boron and oxygen that could serve as new types of qubits.

Newly introduced Diamond Defects Reveal a Spectrum of Quantum Colors.

Industry observers note that light plays an key role in how scientists interact with diamond qubits. Researchers use lasers and microwave pulses to manipulate their quantum states and retrieve stored information.

Much of the previous work in this area has centered on a defect known as the nitrogen-vacancy center. This structure forms when a nitrogen atom takes the place of a carbon atom in a diamond crystal, while an adjacent position that would normally contain another carbon atom remains empty.

Under laser illumination, this type of defect can emit red light when it occupies a particular quantum state.

In a recent development, the newly investigated defects offer different optical properties. Oxygen defects can produce blue light, while those involving boron emit ultraviolet light.

It has been revealed that these differences could make it possible to combine several types of qubits within a single quantum device. Because each type responds differently to light, researchers might be able to interact with one group of qubits without disturbing another.

"One could imagine, then, combining different qubits of different responses, so you can basically probe one qubit but not the other," Martirez said.

Beyond identifying upcoming candidates, the findings suggest a broader change in how researchers approach quantum technology. Diamond qubits have traditionally been studied primarily through physics, but understanding their underlying chemistry could provide additional ways to design them.

Martirez believes that researchers could eventually engineer qubits for particular functions using principles similar to those applied when chemists create specialized molecules, including compounds designed for latest medications.

How Quantum Chemistry Could Transform Future Research.

The potential benefits extend well beyond the development of quantum computers themselves. Martirez sees an intriguing possibility in which advances made possible by quantum chemistry eventually lead to quantum technologies that help improve the field of chemistry.

In other words, quantum chemistry could develop the very tools needed to "enrich itself" in the coming decades.

Industry observers note that A practical quantum system containing multiple qubits could make molecular calculations substantially more accurate. That would allow scientists to study increasingly complex chemical structures, including large biological molecules and proteins, with a level of detail that is difficult to achieve using conventional methods.

Recent findings suggest that "We could describe larger molecules, biomolecules, proteins and everything like that in a more accurate way, and that could improve all the chemical-adjacent industries, such as pharmaceutical science and materials science. Even our fundamental understanding of molecular systems could be enriched.".

Such improvements could have far-reaching implications for pharmaceutical development, materials research, and the fundamental study of how molecules behave.

Recent findings suggest that martirez also hopes the research will encourage more chemists to explore solid-state physics. Although building advanced quantum computers is often viewed as a challenge primarily for physicists, he argues that chemistry offers valuable expertise that could help accelerate progress.

Sources indicate that "At this moment in time, there's a great emphasis on building the first state-of-the-art qubit computer," he said. "But it's not just physicists who should be participating in this research. Chemists have decades of developed intuition about chemical systems that could be easily translated into understanding defects in solids as well.".

By bringing these disciplines together, scientists may be able to develop more effective ways to discover, understand, and eventually engineer the quantum materials needed for future technologies.

The research was funded through PPPL's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program under prime contract number DE-AC02-09CH11466, with additional support from the DOE Office of Science, Office of Fusion Energy Sciences.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you're looking to pick up a brand-newly introduced mouse this Black Friday, look no further than Logitech's MX Master 3S, an accomplished mouse that is still a staple at Tom's Hardware towers. Now, it's just gotten cheaper, and you can pick up the Logitech MX Master 3S for just $75 at Amazon, just in time for Black Friday. With its signature MagSpeed scrolling, this deal is unmissable for anyone who wants to pick up a mouse perfect for working through large spreadsheets, code, and more.

It has been revealed that the 0.31-pound (141g) Logitech MX Master 3S sports a Darkfield laser sensor that can be configured up to 8,000 DPI, offers a total of seven programmable buttons, including the scroll wheel, can be customized via the Logitech app, and also boasts quiet switches that Logitech claims are up to 90% less noisy than the standard MX Master 3. While the MX Master 3S has been supplanted by the newer, shinier MX Master 4, this mouse is still capable and, more importantly for your wallet, cheaper than the latest pointer from the company.

According to recent reports, one of the best productivity mice, the MX Master 3S, has 3 wireless profiles, five customizable buttons, and a side scroll wheel. The scroll wheel can be tight or smooth and has up to an 8,000 DPI resolution.

Back in 2022, we awarded this mouse our Editor's Choice award in our review, noting that the adjustable options on the magnetic scroll wheel felt buttery smooth, offering plenty of support for customization via the Logitech Options+ app, where you can set up the functions for all of the additional keys, DPI, MagSpeed wheel, and more. The mouse also supports up to three profiles and connectivity options, which is excellent for those using multi-device setups and who don't want to switch mice, thanks to both its Logi Bolt wireless support and Bluetooth.

Recent findings suggest that logitech's rated battery life is perhaps one of the most vital reasons to reach for the MX Master 3S. The manufacturer claims that it can reach up to 70 days of battery life and is rechargeable via USB-C, which is a far cry from the higher-spec gaming mice that you typically see have much lower operational runtimes.

Now just $75 at Amazon, the Logitech MX Master 3S is an excellent option for anyone who wants to pick up a premium mouse without having to spend over $100.

#149439. Industry News: What if Trump’s arch became a reflecting pool instead?

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1608 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: What if Trump’s arch became a reflecting pool instead?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1608 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A federal judge on Wednesday extended a temporary block on President Donald Trump’s proposed monumental arch just outside Arlington National Cemetery, and the stopped clock gives the public more time to reflect on Trump’s intends for the land.
  • A federal judge on Wednesday extended a temporary block on President Donald Trump’s proposed monumental arch just outside Arlington National Cemetery, and the stopped clock gives the public more time to reflect on Trump’s intends for the land.
  • There’s a consensus that a 250-foot-tall structure is a misfit for the site.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A federal judge on Wednesday extended a temporary block on President Donald Trump’s proposed monumental arch just outside Arlington National Cemetery, and the stopped clock gives the public more time to reflect on Trump’s intends for the land. There’s a consensus that a 250-foot-tall structure is a misfit for the site. But maybe an alternative project might be better suited to it? A pair of landscape architecture students think it could become a circular reflecting pool. The current site. [Photo: Duane Lempke/Wikimedia Commons.] Memorial Circle, where Trump wants to build the arch, is for now an empty roundabout. It sits between Arlington Cemetery to its southwest and the Lincoln Memorial just across the Potomac to its northeast. Despite its location between popular tourist destinations, it’s not designed for pedestrians to access. [Image: © Jeremy Dvorak and Jake Geitner/courtesy The Cultural Landscape Foundation] The two alternative designs for what to do with the circle, released this week by the Cultural Landscape Foundation, a nonprofit education and advocacy group, imagine the space in upcoming ways. One concept turns the circle into a single, circular reflecting pool, making the Lincoln Memorial a hinge between two reflecting pools; the other imagines it as a larger park configured as pedestrian-friendly, civic space. [Image: © Jeremy Dvorak and Jake Geitner/courtesy The Cultural Landscape Foundation] “We are having right now in Washington a crisis of imagination and also an inability to understand that Washington is a mosaic of spaces that people move through in the public realm,” Charles A. Birnbaum, founding president and CEO of the foundation, tells Fast Tech giant. “The projects that we’ve been seeing from the administration, whether it’s the ballroom or the arch or the Garden of Heroes [a statue park proposed for parkland south of the Lincoln Memorial], they’re all being forced upon the civil and cultural landscape of Washington.” The foundation’s two alternative design provocations were made in collaboration with Jeremy Dvorak and Jake Geitner, landscape architecture students in a class Birnbaum teaches at the Harvard University Graduate School of Design. Both proposals use water to convey monumentality instead of sheer height, as in Trump’s proposal. Trump’s proposed 250-foot arch would tower above D.C.’s maximum 130-foot height limit. The project is being sued by veterans, who say it will block the sight line from the cemetery to the Lincoln Memorial, meant to symbolize national reunification after the Civil War, as well as by Arlington County, the Commonwealth of Virginia, and the District of Columbia, who’ve argued it’s unauthorized. It’s also unpopular. Two-thirds of Americans, including half of Republicans, oppose Trump’s dedicating time and energy to construction projects like the arch, according to a Reuters-Ipsos poll conducted last month. Neither of the students’ proposals rise to a level that would block anyone’s view. [Image: © Jeremy Dvorak and Jake Geitner/courtesy The Cultural Landscape Foundation] The first alternative proposal would turn Memorial Circle into a circular reflecting pool meant to be viewed by passing cars. The pool purposely sits at a low elevation so you can see it at car level, since there’s no safe passage to cross the street as a pedestrian in its current configuration. It’s a minimalist, modest monument for motorists that keeps Memorial Circle’s function intact while simultaneously elevating it as a space for reflection. Words conveying unity and belonging would be inscribed in a granite profile enclosing the reflecting pool. [Image: © Jeremy Dvorak and Jake Geitner/courtesy The Cultural Landscape Foundation] The second alternative proposal would reconfigure the roundabout, turning the Memorial Avenue corridor into a pill-shaped park for pedestrians. Anchored by two fountain pools with high water sprays, the park would have trees and benches ringing the outside, giving tourists and visitors shade and seating. The lack of a single focal point for this idea was purposeful, Birnbaum states. It becomes a processional experience between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington Cemetery. Instead of an arch or other central element that reveals itself, it serves as a midpoint that visually and environmentally ties the cemetery to the National Mall. [Image: © Jeremy Dvorak and Jake Geitner/courtesy The Cultural Landscape Foundation] Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966 requires an assessment of adverse effects of any projects on historic federal properties, and these proposals more closely follow that mandate than a grand arch does, Birnbaum says. “The letter of the law is to avoid, minimize, and mitigate adverse effects,” he says. He also argues they more closely follow Interior Secretary Doug Burgum’s stated rationale for the project, which is “to reinforce the historical and ceremonial role of the Arlington Memorial Bridge and Memorial Avenue corridor as a symbolic gateway between Washington, D.C., and Arlington National Cemetery, while providing a new destination for public interpretation, reflection, and appreciation of the nation’s history.” For the students and foundation, these proposals are just a starting point. “This is about fostering a dialogue, but also addressing what we feel is a lack of imagination,” Birnbaum says.

According to recent reports, GPT OSS is a hugely anticipated open-weights release by OpenAI, designed for powerful reasoning, agentic tasks, and versatile developer use cases. It comprises two models: a significant one with 117B parameters (gpt-oss-120b), and a smaller one with 21B parameters (gpt-oss-20b). Both are mixture-of-experts (MoEs) and use a 4-bit quantization scheme (MXFP4), enabling fast inference (thanks to fewer active parameters, see details below) while keeping resource usage low. The large model fits on a single H100 GPU, while the small one runs within 16GB of memory and is perfect for consumer hardware and on-device applications.

To make it even better and more impactful for the community, the models are licensed under the Apache 2.0 license, along with a minimal usage policy:.

We aim for our tools to be used safely, responsibly, and democratically, while maximizing your control over how you use them. By using gpt-oss, you agree to comply with all applicable law.

In a recent development, according to OpenAI, this release is a meaningful step in their commitment to the open-source ecosystem, in line with their stated mission to make the benefits of AI broadly accessible. Many use cases rely on private and/or local deployments, and we at Hugging Face are super excited to welcome OpenAI to the community. We believe these will be long-lived, inspiring and impactful models.

It has been revealed that openAI GPT OSS models are accessible through Hugging Face’s Inference Providers service, allowing you to send requests to any supported provider using the same JavaScript or Python code. This is the same infrastructure that powers OpenAI’s official demo on gpt-oss.com, and you can use it for your own projects.

Below is an example that uses Python and the super-fast Cerebras provider. For more info and additional snippets, check the inference providers section in the model cards and the dedicated guide we crafted for these models.

Inference Providers also implements an OpenAI-compatible Responses API, the most advanced OpenAI interface for chat models, designed for more flexible and intuitive interactions.Below is an example using the Responses API with the Fireworks AI provider. For more details, check out the open-source responses.js project.

You need to install the latest transformers release (v4.55.1 or later), as well as accelerate and kernels. We also recommend installing triton 3.4 or better, as it unblocks support for mxfp4 quantization on CUDA hardware:.

The model weights are quantized in mxfp4 format, which was originally available on GPUs of the Hopper or Blackwell families, but now works on previous CUDA architectures (including Ada, Ampere, and Tesla). Installing triton 3.4, together with the kernels library, makes it possible to download optimized mxfp4 kernels on first use, achieving large memory savings. With these components in place, you can run the 20B model on GPUs with 16 GB of RAM. This includes many consumer cards (3090, 4090, 5080) as well as Colab and Kaggle!

If the previous libraries are not installed (or you don’t have a compatible GPU), loading the model will fall back to bfloat16, unpacked from the quantized weights.

The following snippet shows simple inference with the 20B model. As explained, it runs on 16 GB GPUs when using mxfp4, or ~48 GB in bfloat16.

Recent findings suggest that the models use attention sinks, a technique the vLLM team made compatible with Flash Attention 3. We have packaged and integrated their optimized kernel in kernels-community/vllm-flash-attn3. At the time of writing, this super-fast kernel has been tested on Hopper cards with PyTorch 2.7 and 2.8. We expect increased coverage in the coming days. If you run the models on Hopper cards (for example, H100 or H200), you need to pip install --upgrade kernels and add the following line to your snippet:.

In a recent development, this snippet will download the optimized, pre-compiled kernel code from kernels-community, as explained in our previous blog post. The transformers team has built, packaged, and tested the code, so it’s totally safe for you to use.

It has been revealed that we recommend you use mxfp4 if your GPU supports it. If you can additionally use Flash Attention 3, then by all means do enable it!

Industry observers note that if your GPU is not compatible with mxfp4, then we recommend you use MegaBlocks MoE kernels for a nice speed bump. To do so, you just need to adjust your inference code like this:.

MegaBlocks optimized MoE kernels require the model to run on bfloat16, so memory consumption will be higher than running on mxfp4. We recommend you use mxfp4 if you can, otherwise opt in to MegaBlocks via use_kernels=True.

MegaBlocks MoE kernel acceleration is already available for OpenAI GPT OSS on AMD Instinct (e.g., MI300-series), enabling better training and inference performance. You can test it with the same inference code shown above.

GPT OSS models are reasoning models: they therefore require a very large generation size (maximum number of upcoming tokens) for evaluations, as their generation will first contain reasoning, then the actual answer. Using too small a generation size risks interrupting the prediction in the middle of reasoning, which will cause false negatives. The reasoning trace should then be removed from the model answer before computing metrics, to avoid parsing errors, especially with math or instruct evaluations.

Here’s an example on how to evaluate the models with lighteval (you need to install from source).

For the 20B model, this should give you 69.5 (+/-1.9) for IFEval (strict prompt), and 63.3 (+/-8.9) for AIME25 (in pass@1), scores within expected range for a reasoning model of this size.

If you want to do your custom evaluation script, note that to filter out the reasoning tags properly, you will need to use skip_special_tokens=False in the tokenizer, in order to get the full trace in the model output (to filter reasoning using the same string pairs as in the example above) - you can discover why below.

Sources indicate that openAI GPT OSS uses the concept of “channels” in its outputs. Most of the time, you will see an “analysis” channel that contains things that are not intended to be sent to the end-user, like chains of thought, and a “final” channel containing messages that are actually intended to be displayed to the user.

Assuming no tools are being used, the structure of the model output looks like this:.

Most of the time, you should ignore everything except the text after <|channel|>final<|message|>. Only this text should be appended to the chat as the assistant message, or displayed to the user. There are two exceptions to this rule, though: You may need to include analysis messages in the history during training or if the model is calling external tools.

Recent findings suggest that when training: If you’re formatting examples for training, you generally want to include the chain of thought in the final message. The right place to do this is in the thinking key.

You can feel free to include thinking keys in previous turns, or when you’re doing inference rather than training, but they will generally be ignored. The chat template will only ever include the most recent chain of thought, and only in training (when add_generation_prompt=False and the final turn is an assistant turn).

The reason why we do it this way is subtle: The OpenAI gpt-oss models were trained on multi-turn data where all but the final chain of thought was dropped. This means that when you want to fine-tune an OpenAI gpt-oss model, you should do the same.

According to recent reports, openAI GPT OSS is unusual because it distinguishes between a “system” message and a “developer” message at the start of the chat, but most other models only use “system”. In GPT OSS, the system message follows a strict format and contains information like the current date, the model identity and the level of reasoning effort to use, and the “developer” message is more freeform, which makes it (very confusingly) similar to the “system” messages of most other models.

Recent findings suggest that to make GPT OSS easier to use with the standard API, the chat template will treat a message with “system” or “developer” role as the developer message. If you want to modify the actual system message, you can pass the specific arguments model_identity or reasoning_effort to the chat template:.

Industry observers note that GPT OSS supports two kinds of tools: The “builtin” tools browser and python, and custom tools supplied by the user. To enable builtin tools, pass their names in a list to the builtin_tools argument of the chat template, as shown below. To pass custom tools, you can pass them either as JSON schema or as Python functions with type hints and docstrings using the tools argument. See the chat template tools documentation for more details, or you can just modify the example below:.

If the model chooses to call a tool (indicated by a message ending in <|call|>), then you should add the tool call to the chat, call the tool, then add the tool result to the chat and generate again:.

In a recent development, this is a genuinely impressive and consequential release. Open-weight models at this scale, with Apache 2.0 licensing and serious attention to inference efficiency, feel like a real inflection point rather than a symbolic gesture. The combination of MoE architecture, MXFP4 quantization, and practical ecosystem support (Transformers, vLLM, llama.cpp, and ROCm) makes this usable today, not just theoretically interesting.

What stands out most is the emphasis on deployment reality: single-H100 feasibility for 120B, 16GB consumer GPUs for 20B, and first-class support for multiple inference backends. That’s exactly what developers and researchers need if these models are going to be experimented with, fine-tuned, and embedded into real products rather than living only in benchmarks.

It’s also refreshing to see clear guidance around reasoning traces, chat templates, and evaluation pitfalls. Too many “reasoning models” gloss over those operational details, which matter a lot once you leave the demo stage.

It has been revealed that as someone working across text, vision, and creative tooling, I also appreciate how releases like this pair well with the broader AI stack. Strong open reasoning models combined with next-gen creative tools—like Experience the future of AI image editing—open up some very compelling hybrid workflows for agents, content pipelines, and local-first applications.

In a recent development, overall, this feels like a long-lived contribution to the open ecosystem, not a short-term headline. Kudos to OpenAI and Hugging Face for shipping something that’s both ambitious and genuinely usable.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that hello and welcome to Modern CEO! I’m Stephanie Mehta, CEO and chief content officer of Mansueto Ventures. Each week this newsletter explores inclusive approaches to leadership drawn from conversations with executives and entrepreneurs, and from the pages of Inc. and Fast Company. If you received this newsletter from a friend, you can sign up to get it yourself every Monday morning. I was in Silicon Valley for part of last week, where many investors, founders, and executives seem to shrug off the midterm elections, in which voter distrust of big tech and AI safety played a role in the blue wave. Their conclusion? Data centers—those massive, resource-heavy computing facilities—simply have a “PR problem.” They maintain that the tech sector needs to launch a charm offensive to remind communities of all the good that will come from these massive computing facilities, such as jobs and support for small businesses. Heck, the tech giants might even send some employees to volunteer at local schools! A growing concern  This interpretation of the election results is naively narrow and largely misses the point. “Data centers are the foil,” says Jim O’Leary, CEO of the global advisory firm Penta. “They’re the face of the AI backlash, but the matter is bigger.” Indeed, a Pew Research Center report published in August found that 52% of Americans stated they are more concerned than excited about the use of artificial intelligence in daily life, up from 37% in 2021. Sentiment analysis from Penta found that negative press coverage of AI safety rose 233% from May to October of this year versus from November 2025 to April 2026. All that translates into lawmakers focusing their attention on AI and the companies that are building and deploying the technology. Nearly half (46%) of policymakers interviewed by Penta in the weeks prior to the midterm elections said safety and responsibility were their top AI concerns—and government interest in AI is only going to grow in the run-up to 2028. “I think AI will be the defining issue of the general election,” O’Leary says. Beyond data centers   Some of the scenarios O’Leary is contemplating make the data center backlash seem almost quaint. Over the next 24 months, he foresees one or more of the following AI-related crises: a safety incident that could involve loss of life, an AI market correction or outright bubble burst, or a cyberattack larger than those we’ve recently seen. If all three scenarios materialize, “it will create an environment that is extraordinarily complicated,” O’Leary says. “A significant portion of the population will push for an AI slowdown. And business leaders will need to ask, ‘How do we continue to drive AI transformation across our business, which we know we have to do?’”  Even business leaders who have a strong conviction to expand AI usage in their companies will bump up against stakeholders such as employees and community leaders who may want to pump the brakes. Leaders will need to engage in conversations with all of these groups to understand objections and, where possible, work together to overcome them. After two years of courting the White House, big businesses will need to build bridges with an emboldened legislative branch. Says O’Leary: “Corporations are now going to have to start prioritizing congressional engagement in a way they didn’t over the past 24 months.”  Modern CEO of the year  Modern CEO is seeking nominations for the 2026 Modern CEO of the Year. If you or a CEO you know has had an exceptional year driving innovation, transforming a business, or future-proofing a company, please share their story via this form. The deadline for submissions is December 4, and the Modern CEO (or CEOs) of the Year will be unveiled on December 28. Even business leaders who have a strong conviction to expand AI usage in their companies will bump up against stakeholders such as employees and community leaders who may want to pump the brakes. Leaders will need to engage in conversations with all of these groups to understand objections and, where possible, work together to overcome them.

After two years of courting the White House, massive businesses will need to build bridges with an emboldened legislative branch. Says O’Leary: “Corporations are now going to have to start prioritizing congressional engagement in a way they didn’t over the past 24 months.”.

Quantum computers are getting too powerful to check. Scientists have a solution

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (985 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that as quantum computers grow more powerful, researchers face a troubling question: How can they know whether the results are correct when conventional computers can no longer verify them?
  • The technique uses experimental measurements to reconstruct how a quantum system behaves, then calculates how uncertainties in that reconstruction affect the results.
  • In a recent development, quantum systems are expected to become capable of solving increasingly complex problems that traditional computers struggle with or cannot handle at all.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that as quantum computers grow more powerful, researchers face a troubling question: How can they know whether the results are correct when conventional computers can no longer verify them? Scientists have now developed a promising new method that could help overcome this challenge by measuring the accuracy of quantum simulations and identifying how much uncertainty their predictions contain.

The technique uses experimental measurements to reconstruct how a quantum system behaves, then calculates how uncertainties in that reconstruction affect the results. Researchers successfully demonstrated the approach using a quantum simulator with up to 51 qubits in Innsbruck, Austria.

In a recent development, quantum systems are expected to become capable of solving increasingly complex problems that traditional computers struggle with or cannot handle at all. However, this progress creates a verification problem. When a simulation is small enough, scientists can compare its results with calculations performed on a conventional computer. As quantum systems grow beyond those limits, that direct comparison becomes impractical, making alternative ways to assess their reliability essential.

A Newly introduced Way to Measure Quantum Computing Accuracy.

It has been revealed that the breakthrough comes from an international research team led by Tristan Kraft at the Technical University of Munich and Peter Zoller at the University of Innsbruck and the Institute for Quantum Optics and Quantum Information of the Austrian Academy of Sciences, working alongside Barbara Kraus of the Technical University of Munich. The researchers developed a method for experimentally determining how a quantum simulator operates and translating uncertainties in its behavior into measurable limits on the accuracy of its results.

According to recent reports, quantum simulators are specialized physical systems designed to reproduce the behavior of other quantum systems. They are especially useful for investigating situations involving large numbers of interacting particles, where the calculations required can swiftly overwhelm even powerful conventional computers.

But quantum experiments are never entirely free from errors. "But no real experiment is perfect," notes Tristan Kraft. "Interactions may turn out differently than expected, the system is influenced by its environment, and measurements are also subject to uncertainties.".

It has been revealed that rather than assuming a quantum simulator behaves exactly as intended, the latest approach examines experimental data to determine what is actually happening inside the system. This allows researchers to identify notable interactions and account for disturbances such as fluctuations and noise.

Industry observers note that "From this data, we determine the relevant interactions as well as key influences from fluctuations and noise. We then calculate how the uncertainties in this model affect the simulation results," explains Tristan Kraft. "The quantum simulator thus provides not just a single value, but a result with error margins that quantify its accuracy.".

Successfully Tested on a 51 Qubit Quantum Simulator.

Recent findings suggest that to evaluate the method, the researchers began with a relatively small quantum system containing ten trapped ions. Because conventional computers can still calculate the behavior of a system of this size, the team could test its reconstructed models and calculated error limits against independent measurements.

Sources indicate that after this initial validation, the researchers expanded their experiments to a chain of 51 trapped ions. The larger demonstration, carried out by a team led by Manoj Joshi and Christian Roos using an ion trap quantum simulator, highlighted that the technique could also work with substantially more complex quantum systems.

This represents an crucial step toward establishing how trustworthy quantum simulation results are, particularly as quantum devices advance into territory where direct verification with traditional computing methods becomes increasingly difficult.

Extending the Breakthrough to More Complex Quantum Systems.

It has been revealed that the next challenge is to bring the technique to two-dimensional quantum simulators. These systems can model more complicated interactions among particles, making them valuable for exploring quantum physics. At the same time, their growing complexity makes their results particularly difficult to confirm using conventional calculations.

"This is particularly key because classical calculations for such systems become significantly more difficult as the number of particles increases," explains quantum computing pioneer Peter Zoller. "This also makes independent verification of the results increasingly complex, making the question of experimentally determined error limits all the more important.".

The researchers are now adapting their method for the newest generation of two-dimensional quantum simulators, which offer improved precision and can investigate systems containing larger numbers of particles.

Looking further ahead, the approach could help scientists establish a more meaningful way to measure quantum advantage, the ability of quantum systems to outperform conventional computers. Instead of comparing machines based only on their processing speed or the size of the problems they can handle, researchers could also examine how accurately each system produces its answers.

Industry observers note that "After all, when a classical computer and a quantum simulator tackle the same problem, it's not just a matter of which one delivers a result faster. What's also crucial is which one can solve the problem with a smaller, verifiable margin of error," notes Peter Zoller.

Recent findings suggest that this shift could change how progress in quantum computing is evaluated. Future breakthroughs may be judged not simply by how many particles a simulator can model or how rapidly it performs calculations, but by its ability to solve increasingly difficult problems with demonstrably reliable results.

In a recent development, the findings were published in Physical Review X. The research received support from the Austrian Science Fund (FWF), the German Ministry of Research, Technology and Space, the European Union, BMW, and other funding organizations.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has released an interim final rule (IFR) [PDF] that will prevent Chinese AI companies from leasing data compute outside of China to access advanced U.S.
  • In a recent development, washington’s previous export controls only focused on high-performance AI chips like Nvidia’s Blackwell and upcoming Vera Rubin chips.
  • The 16nm and 14nm nodes have been around for around 10 years now, and they could even be found inside consumer devices like smartphones and TVs, as well as in automotive applications.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has released an interim final rule (IFR) [PDF] that will prevent Chinese AI companies from leasing data compute outside of China to access advanced U.S. chips like Nvidia Blackwell AI GPUs. However, Nikkei Asia reports that the new regulations have also affected foundries making chips for consumers and the automotive industry, as TSMC has put several shipments to both Chinese and non-Chinese chip designers on hold as it reviews their compliance with the changes to U.S.

In a recent development, washington’s previous export controls only focused on high-performance AI chips like Nvidia’s Blackwell and upcoming Vera Rubin chips. The newly introduced rules expand it to include all chips, with front-end fabricators (chip foundries) or OSATs (outsourced semiconductor assembly and test companies), also known as packaging and testing companies, required to assume that semiconductors with a 16nm or 14nm node are automatically classified as export-controlled advanced computing chips. The ruling even mentioned that even if the designed chip has less than 30 billion transistors and has no HBM, it cannot be assumed that the chips aren’t built for high-performance computing.

The 16nm and 14nm nodes have been around for around 10 years now, and they could even be found inside consumer devices like smartphones and TVs, as well as in automotive applications. This latest rule means that designers making chips using 16nm or newer nodes, even if they’re not specifically built for data centers, must secure documentation from an approved designer certifying the chip’s Total Processing Performance or performance density if they want to avoid additional scrutiny from the fab.

Industry observers note that "The new rule is very strict this time, and the affecting scope is far beyond only chips for data centers but covers smartphone processors, autonomous driving and other types of chips for consumer electronics as well as others if they are using nodes that are 14nm or 16nm or more advanced tech," a source told the publication. "The move would delay shipments to many chip developers worldwide before they can clear compliance and hit many emerging startups in many Asian nations.".

According to recent reports, aside from this, the U.S. also now requires export licenses to ship advanced AI chips to the following countries: Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Brazil, and Thailand. The IFR states that these countries are often used as transshipment points for chips that are being diverted to China, as evidenced by the Supermicro and Megaspeed investigations, which used one of these countries as the destination of the Nvidia servers they ordered, before sending them forward to their final destination in China.

Chip smuggling has long been a simmering issue in the United States, but it seemingly has bubbled over after the revelation of Jensen Huang’s affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, who’s also suspected of being instrumental in diverting $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia chips and passing on information to Chinese intelligence. While his alleged relationship with a direct subordinate was the apparent primary cause of his departure from Nvidia, sources say that the real reason behind his ousting is the mass smuggling of 1.5 million Nvidia AI GPUs that happened right under his nose.

#149433. The conversation you’re avoiding is already costing you

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2014 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fastcompany ↗ Open Full Page

The conversation you’re avoiding is already costing you

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2014 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that it’s 2 a.m., and a capable leader is wide awake.
  • Sources indicate that it’s 2 a.m., and a capable leader is wide awake.
  • The organizational psychologist Liane Davey makes a useful distinction here.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that it’s 2 a.m., and a capable leader is wide awake. In their mind, they’re replaying a difficult conversation that hasn’t happened yet. They’ve been waiting for the “perfect time”: a calmer week, a better mood, the right moment. The irony is that they can approve a major budget without blinking, yet they’ve spent the last few weeks avoiding a five-minute talk. And it’s not because they don’t care. It’s because they care a great deal about the person, the relationship, and the work. The organizational psychologist Liane Davey makes a useful distinction here. Conflict aversion is the natural discomfort most of us feel when a conversation could go badly; conflict avoidance is what happens when we let that discomfort drive our behavior. Avoiding a difficult conversation may buy some relief in the short term but it usually costs far more later on. But something else is going on when leaders avoid difficult conversations. By staying silent, they’re deciding for the other person that they can’t handle it, don’t want to know, or will react badly. What employees actually want Employees do want to know. In a March 2024 survey of 1,500 employees in Canada and the U.S. by the Achievers Workforce Institute, two-thirds said they want to have tough conversations at work. But one-third said they don’t feel safe having them with their manager, and fewer than one-third say they trust their managers. That gap is the real story. People aren’t asking to be protected from hard truths. They’re asking for two things: the truth, and a safe way to hear it. Let’s agree that not every conversation ends in agreement, and it shouldn’t be the goal. Leaders have to make decisions that disappoint people from time to time. It’s part of the job, part of the responsibility to deliver excellence, not the easiest or most popular solution. And the beauty is that people usually accept a no when they’ve been heard and understand how the decision was made. What they struggle with is a no that arrives out of nowhere. Nice isn’t the same as kind I work with leaders and teams to help them get more comfortable with difficult conversations. One of the first things we look at is the difference between being nice and being kind. Protecting everyone from the discomfort of the conversation can feel nice, but it isn’t kind. Kindness means we respect people enough to give them the information they need to make their own choices, even when it costs short-term friction. Imagine an employee who repeatedly misses deadlines and nobody says anything. That’s unkind to the employee who is never given the opportunity to adjust, learn, and protect their reputation. It’s also unkind to their teammates who are watching. Every missed deadline chips away at their trust in their leader, their team, and the organization. And, as their teammate’s poor performance continues, they start asking why they should work hard when good work earns them only the job of doing someone else’s work. Fast-forward eight months. Valuable team members are quitting out of frustration. And the low-performing employee is surprised by a “meets most expectations” performance review, so starts looking for another job. All this happens because no one told one person they were falling short or gave them a chance to adjust. Avoidance happens at the executive level as well. I’ve coached business partners who have come close to losing their company because trust between them slowly eroded. In that case, as in so many, conflict wasn’t the original problem. Conflict was the result of the distrust and frustration that grew because important conversations had been avoided. Build trust before you need it Building trust is the best first step. In the Achievers study, trust in the manager was the key predictor of whether employees felt safe having tough conversations. But safety on its own isn’t the whole answer. Amy Edmondson, the Harvard Business School professor who pioneered research on psychological safety, tells us that psychological safety alone can create a comfort zone. Safety doesn’t mean everyone agrees and it doesn’t protect anyone from disappointment. What safety does mean is that both people believe there’s respect and a purpose worth protecting, and that openness is expected. I find one of the best ways to build trust is for leaders to ask for permission to have difficult conversations long before they are needed. My two favorite moments are during employee onboarding and during team resets. In both situations, you might say, “At some point we will need to have a difficult conversation: a difference of opinion, a mistake, a missed expectation. That’s a usual part of work. I know most of us, me included, are tempted to avoid these moments. Can we agree now that we won’t hide from or avoid those moments, that we’ll reward honesty, respect differing opinions, and respond calmly, and that this goes in every direction, including toward me? I’d like to hear how you feel about that.” Notice that this is a request, not an announcement. It’s a conversation that gives the team a say in how they’ll talk to each other, so when the day comes, you’re not springing a surprise on anyone; you’re keeping an agreement you made together. And you might open with, “We agreed we’d be honest with each other, so I’d like to talk about the client deadline.” Continue earning trust The agreement is only a starting point. From there, everyone needs to keep earning and building trust every day. That means honoring every commitment, protecting confidence, admitting mistakes, and offering help. It also means showing respect, celebrating successes, and recognizing greatness whenever it happens. I can’t promise you’ll never have another anxious 2 a.m. But when trust is in place and expectations are clear, these conversations come with less dread. So what conversation have you been putting off? And what might become possible if you approached it not as conflict, but as an act of respect?

Ukraine revives its grounded fleet of 500+ US-made Puma drones with homegrown anti-jamming tech

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (505 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • delivered more than 500 RQ-20A Puma AE drones to Ukraine in 2023 for use in reconnaissance missions.
  • Russia’s 2022 escalation of the war in Ukraine saw the widespread use of small and medium-sized drones, with both sides deploying countermeasures like GPS jamming and radio interference to defend against these UAVs.
  • The proliferation of drones has also forced militaries across the world to develop cheaper countermeasures against them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The U.S. delivered more than 500 RQ-20A Puma AE drones to Ukraine in 2023 for use in reconnaissance missions. These hand-debuted uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs) are equipped with optical and infrared sensors for surveying the battlefield, but the evolving electromagnetic warfare landscape meant that the entire fleet had to be grounded. Now, Ukrainian defense firm Rise Technologies has upgraded the drones with its Palych communications system, which allows the UAVs to withstand the advanced electronic warfare (EW) environment found on the frontlines in 2026. According to United24 Media, this latest component allows drone operators to select the drone’s operating frequency band to avoid heavily jammed channels and maintain communications during flight. It also increases the range of the Puma to 31 miles (50 kilometers) from its basic range of 10 miles (16 kilometers).

Russia’s 2022 escalation of the war in Ukraine saw the widespread use of small and medium-sized drones, with both sides deploying countermeasures like GPS jamming and radio interference to defend against these UAVs. Because of this, we’ve seen various innovations to counter the countermeasures, like the use of fiber optic drones, which are essentially jam-proof, and the installation of a camera and magnetic compass on Russian drones to counter GPS jamming. Ukraine has also devised a "flying modem" relay system for its drones, allowing its forces to conduct strategic drone strikes even without the use of finicky Starlink connections. The indigenous communications system was also installed on other drones from DJI and Autel, as well as on some attack UAVs, giving Ukrainian drone operators an advantage on the battlefield.

The proliferation of drones has also forced militaries across the world to develop cheaper countermeasures against them. The U.S. has already deployed high-energy lasers to shoot down Mexican cartel drones crossing its southern border, while the Royal Navy is testing the DragonFire laser that can target UAVs traveling at up to 400 mph while only costing $13 per shot. Israel has also deployed its 100,000-watt Iron Beam system, while China has built a man-portable anti-drone laser system that weighs 55 pounds and can hit targets up to 1,600 feet away.

These laser systems are ideal for taking down a few drone units. But for drone swarm threats, microwave systems are a better solution, as they could take down multiple drones in a single shot. Some examples of this include the Leonidas AGV from the U.S. and Turkey’s Aselsan Ejderha, or “Dragon” in English, which uses high-power electromagnetic systems to overwhelm the sensitive electronics found inside most drones.

Enhancement Monday, 9:40 a.m.: Shares of Nvidia Corporation soared more than 30% on Monday after the company’s board of directors announced that founder Jensen Huang would return as CEO. The surprise announcement comes less than two weeks after Huang was ousted over his relationship with an alleged Chinese spy, a scandal that rattled markets as investors pondered the uncertain future of a semiconductor giant at the center of the AI boom. Jensen’s reinstatement is “effective immediately,” Nvidia stated. “The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” Harvey C. Jones, Nvidia’s chairman of the board, said in a statement. The company said its investigation into reports that Huang was “the target of a foreign intelligence” effort would continue. In a remarkable disclosure, Nvidia’s announcement also said the board’s decision was made after receiving input from “senior levels of the United States government” that Huang’s return would not be a threat to national security. News of Jensen’s return added fuel to a market bounce-back on Monday morning, not just for Nvidia but for other so-called Magnificent 7 stocks—most of which were already up in premarket trading after a punishing losing streak the week before. Original story: Last week was one of the worst weeks for stock markets in years. America’s three major indices saw sharp declines as investors turned sour on AI-related stocks. The Dow ended the week down 8%, the S&P 500 down 8.6%, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq, where most AI-adjacent stocks trade, down 10%, placing it in correction territory. But this week, the narrative is looking a little different. In premarket trading today, Dow, S&P, and Nasdaq futures are all bouncing back. Here’s which stocks are moving, why, and what to expect in the holiday week to come. Tech stocks poised for a comeback? Some of the hardest-hit stocks last week were tech stocks, especially companies operating in the AI space. Over the previous five trading days, Nvidia shares plummeted more than 20%, Meta Platforms fell nearly 12%, Microsoft and SpaceX declined over 7.6% each, Google lost 7.8%, and Amazon fell 5.6%. Even Anthropic, which saw its shares jump 17% in its IPO on Thursday, ended the week up just 7% after falling 8.5% on Friday. So far, today is a very different story. In premarket trading, as of the time of this writing, America’s three major stock markets are posting a comeback. At the moment, S&P Futures are up 2.8%, Dow futures are up 2.1%, and Nasdaq futures are up 3.4%. Many of the tech stocks that got hammered so hard last week are leading the charge today, including: Nvidia Corporation (Nasdaq: NVDA): up 7.3% Microsoft Corporation (Nasdaq: MSFT): up 3.3% Tesla, Inc. (Nasdaq: TSLA): up 4.4% Amazon.com, Inc. (Nasdaq: AMZN): up 3.6% Alphabet Inc. (Nasdaq: GOOG): up 5.4% Meta Platforms, Inc. (Nasdaq: META): up 3.6% Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (Nasdaq: SPCX): up 2.8% Micron Technology, Inc. (Nasdaq: MU): up 4.6% Outside of the biggest of big tech, other AI-adjacent companies are also rebounding, including neoclouds: CoreWeave, Inc. (Nasdaq: CRWV): up 6.1% Nebius Group N.V. (Nasdaq: NBIS): up 7.1% IREN Limited (Nasdaq: IREN): up 6.3% All three companies fell by double-digit percentages last week. What’s leading the turnaround? Simply put: This appears to be a case of buying the bounce. Stocks had a horrible week, with some of the biggest tech players seeing exceptionally steep declines; investors are now buying back into those same companies at a steep discount compared to their October highs. That’s good for investors who want to scoop up what they see as heavily discounted shares, but the rebound in these tech stocks—and the broader markets—does nothing to address the fundamental concerns that caused last week’s steep sell-off. Investors have grown fearful that we are in an AI bubble, one that looks dangerously close to popping as Big Tech companies continue their AI-driven capex spending sprees. Those concerns will not be so easy to wave away. Challenges still ahead While today’s early-morning recovery (if it holds) is no doubt music to investors’ ears, major challenges still lie ahead that could determine how long a recovery lasts, or whether markets head further into correction territory. On the tech side, one of the most pressing concerns is who will lead Nvidia after its cofounder and CEO, Jensen Huang, resigned earlier this month in the wake of scandal over his extramarital relationship with an alleged spy. Nvidia is perhaps the single most crucial company in the AI space, and its fate will heavily impact the broader industry. Right now, there is much uncertainty about who will be the company’s next CEO, even as supporters of Huang clamor to get him reinstated. Beyond Nvidia, investors will be closely monitoring hyperscalers’ capex for signs of spending slowdowns that could ripple across smaller players in the AI space. Industry watchers will also be closely tracking how Anthropic’s shares trade in the next several weeks given its much-hyped market debut last week. A healthy appetite for the stock could signal faith in the AI markets, whereas a pullback could have the opposite effect. Of course, less market activity than normal is already expected this week as markets will be closed on Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday. And on Friday, markets have a shortened trading session that ends at 1 pm ET.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, vision Language Models (VLMs) are getting stronger, but aligning them to human preferences still matters. In TRL, we already indicated how to post-train VLMs with Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). This time, we’re going further.

tl;dr Here’s what’s new in TRL:.

These go beyond pairwise DPO, extracting richer signals from preference data and scaling better with modern VLMs.

We’ve also extended existing methods to support VLMs:.

This enables more efficient and scalable multimodal alignment.

Industry observers note that traditionally, you would take a base model, apply SFT to follow instructions, and then apply DPO to align it to preferential data. Previously, we adapted this approach to Vision Language Models (VLMs) and validated it on IDEFICS2, showing improvement in model responses.

DPO works by optimizing preferences between pairs of model responses using a contrastive loss: you have a chosen and a rejected answer and you optimize your preferences based on what you want and don’t want.

Recent findings suggest that but in the last year, fresh multimodal alignment methods have gained popularity, GRPO and MPO, that can push VLM performance even further. At the end of the blog post you can find a table that showcases the differences between model responses.

Sources indicate that aligning multimodal models with SFT to do reasoning tasks falls short due to distribution shift. Meanwhile, models aligned with DPO fail to generate coherent rationales and might generate repetitive responses. To address this, there’s a fresh technique called Mixed Preference Optimization (MPO) specifically made for multimodal models. This method is essentially an extension of DPO with multiple losses: preference loss from DPO (sigmoid), quality loss from Binary Classifier Optimization (BCO), and generation loss from SFT. According to the paper, simply switching to this combined loss results in 6.2 pts improvement in MathVista!

Sources indicate that since this is only modifying the loss, we added combined loss support to TRL's DPOTrainer class. To use it, you can initialize the DPOConfig as follows:.

Then initialize the DPOTrainer:.

Industry observers note that group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) is a cutting-edge alignment method initially introduced in DeepSeek Math paper and later integrated to DeepSeek R1, the groundbreaking LLM. It’s an addition to PPO where the policy updates are done over groups (batches of trajectories that represent how a dialogue rolls out). This feature makes it more robust to reward noise, as the noise averages out within groups. Since the model learns broader sense of a good response rather than singular high reward samples, this method also makes the model highly performant.

In TRL, we now introduce GRPO support for vision language models. We will not provide a full training script example, as you can find it in the notebook. Instead, we'll focus on highlighting the key component and concepts.

To make the training script work effectively, we need to validate that the format of the answer is correct and that the solution itself is close to the completed parts, so we write two reward functions. In order to really see improvements in the latter reward, you would need a rather maximalist setup, where you have relatively larger models, a lot of generations, and a high-quality, diverse dataset.

Then, you can initialize GRPOConfig and GRPOTrainer, pass in the reward functions we defined above and call train() to start training.

Explore the full notebook example here.

Recent findings suggest that group Sequence Policy Optimization (GSPO) is a RL alignment algorithm recently released by Qwen that overcomes some limitations of GRPO. It achieves a more stable training computing importance sampling weights at the sequence level instead of per-token. Its benefits are more relevant in MoE style models.

Industry observers note that latest TRL also introduces support for GSPO and since it’s a variant of GRPO's loss, it comes with multimodal support. To create the trainer, the process is the same as with GRPO, but adding the following extra params (values are extracted from the paper).

In addition to MPO, GRPO, and GSPO, TRL now supports Reinforce Leave One Out (RLOO) and Online Direct Preference Optimization (Online DPO) for Vision Language Models (VLMs), enabling alignment on multimodal datasets.

RLOO now supports common VLMs. You can find a complete training example in the rloo_visual_math.py script.

According to recent reports, previously, SFTTrainer was partially supporting vision language models. This was primarily due to many differences across VLM implementations in transformers API. With the standardization of the transformers API, we have shipped a full support for vision language models. You can simply initialize SFTTrainer with a VLM.

To train a VLM, you need to provide a dataset with an additional images column containing the images to be processed. You can take a look at Dataset Formats — Vision Datasets for more information on how it should look like. A good example is LLaVA Instruct Mix.

We also have a sft_visual_chat.py script that works out of the box for transformers vision language models.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Two cybersecurity companies are coming together in one of the industry’s biggest ever mergers.
  • Two cybersecurity companies are coming together in one of the industry’s biggest ever mergers.
  • On Monday, November 23, CrowdStrike declared that it will purchase Zscaler in an all-stock deal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two cybersecurity companies are coming together in one of the industry’s biggest ever mergers. On Monday, November 23, CrowdStrike announced that it will purchase Zscaler in an all-stock deal. The transaction values Zscaler at a whopping $43.9 billion, with the company’s shareholders getting 1.135 CrowdStrike common shares (Nasdaq: CRWD) for each Zscaler share (Nasdaq: ZS) they own. “Security used to be about keeping the adversary out. Today, safety is required to let AI in,” said George Kurtz, CEO and founder of CrowdStrike. “The network used to connect people to places. Now it connects agents to data.” CrowdStrike stock falls, Zscaler rises In response to the news, CrowdStrike’s shares fell more than 8% in premarket trading, while Zscaler shares rose over 17%. CrowdStrike expects the deal to expand its total addressable market by $185 billion, with the combined company bringing in over $10 billion in annual recurring revenue. Kurtz will stay on as CEO of the joint company, while Jay Chaudhry, founder and CEO of Zscaler, will lead Zscaler’s business and become a member of CrowdStrike’s board. The deal is expected to close in the second half of 2028, subject to regulatory approvals. It comes amid growing concerns over vulnerable tech infrastructure and a future of bot-fueled cyberattacks. “With Zscaler, we’re building cybersecurity’s operating system: a single control plane to deploy AI, control AI, and enable any agentic application to run safely,” Kurtz added. “We see a path to become the largest AI safety and security company the world has ever seen.” Alongside the purchasing announcement, CrowdStrike and Zscaler both shared their quarterly earnings reports. Kurtz called CrowdStrike’s most recent quarter the company’s best yet. CrowdStrike had record-high cash flow from operations with $665 million. Its revenue rose 28% year-over-year (YOY) to $1.58 billion. Similarly, Zscaler’s quarterly revenue rose 25% YOY to $898.2 million.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

KFC Spain has kicked off a new marketing campaign that leans on the recent digital-only Grand Theft Auto VI release. In 2026, gamers have become numb to digital-only releases, piles of early bugs, and multiple layers of DRM. However, as GTA 6 is such a highly anticipated release, folks are still entitled to moan about the physical Blu-ray-style case, which opens to reveal absolutely no physical media at all, just a vacant plastic hub and a redeemable online code. KFC Spain is putting things right, as best as it can, by giving away a free fried chicken disc to those bringing their empty game cases to select outlets in the country.

'The Replacement Disc' campaign is a pretty simple proposition. You can buy and enjoy your GTA 6 release now, but on December 19 and 20 from 4:00 PM to 8:00 PM, take your empty game case down to KFC to get a free KFC disc. Branches where you can get this freebie food are located in major Spanish cities like Madrid, Barcelona, Valencia, Malaga, and Zaragoza.

Recent findings suggest that the KFC disc will be formed from a piece of crunchy coated fried chicken, of course. While it surely will taste better than a platter of polycarbonate with a reflective metal alloy layer, it is only a substitute in spirit. We don't recommend you put greasy food directly in your game's case, even though it is basically useless. Definitely don't put your chicken disc anywhere near your console's optical media slot, if it has one.

GTA 6, released on November 19, is already a barnstorming success. The latest in this seminal series brought in US$3.79 billion in retail sales on its first day, publisher Rockstar Games remarked. That's about 5x the revenue of its predecessor. An incredible 32.5 million units were sold before release, and broke records across all platforms. So, it is canny for KFC to hitch its marketing wagon to this game, in such an unofficial but knowing social media-friendly way.

Industry observers note that KFC has something of a track record of marketing off the back of tech and gaming culture. Its most famous tech adventure is probably the KFC Chicken Bucket Console. But more recently, last year, it teamed up with Asus to release some top-of-the-line burgers made from Wagyu beef with ROG branding.

#149426. Power BI MCP server: how to brief an AI agent to build accurate measures
