#149415. Latest Update: What If Netscape Did SSL the HTTP Way?

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 18m • 📚 Deep Dive (3545 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Billpg ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: What If Netscape Did SSL the HTTP Way?

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3545 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Billpg

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that when you visit a secure website today, your browser connects to port 443 and immediately starts speaking TLS.
  • This is why so many good ideas from HTTP had to be reinvented, years later, inside TLS.
  • Let’s take a trip into a parallel universe where Netscape didn’t take the easy way out.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that when you visit a secure website today, your browser connects to port 443 and immediately starts speaking TLS. Only once the encryption is up and running does it get around to speaking HTTP. That’s two protocols stacked on top of each other, and the one at the bottom doesn’t know or care about anything the one on top has learned over the decades.

This is why so many good ideas from HTTP had to be reinvented, years later, inside TLS. The most notorious is SNI, which is a Host header with extra steps.

It didn’t have to be this way. Let’s take a trip into a parallel universe where Netscape didn’t take the easy way out.

Sources indicate that when Netscape released SSL in 1995, it came with a newly introduced URL scheme (https://) and a new port number (443). Plenty of people grumbled. The web already had a protocol and a port, so why invent new ones? Why not secure the conversation you’re already having?

To be fair to Netscape, in 1995 there wasn’t really a “proper” way to do that. HTTP/1.0 had no mechanism for handing a connection over to another protocol. The Upgrade header didn’t arrive until HTTP/1.1 in 1997, and the Host header, which made it possible to run many websites on one IP address, came with it. Netscape couldn’t have used either of them because neither existed yet.

But this is my parallel universe, so let’s say HTTP grew those headers a couple of years early and Netscape decided to wait for them.

In a recent development, in our universe, a TLS connection begins with a ClientHello and the server replies with its certificate. In the parallel universe, that first exchange is just plain HTTP in the clear.

Industry observers note that the browser wants to buy something from shop.example.com. It connects to port 80, the same as always, and asks for the server’s certificate.

(Yes, /.well-known/ is from 2010. It’s a parallel universe. Let me have this one.).

According to recent reports, the server responds with its certificate, and the certificates of any intermediate CAs, as an ordinary HTTP response. The browser checks the chain against its list of root CAs, exactly as it would in our universe. Is it signed by someone we trust? Is it for shop.example.com? Has it expired?

Sources indicate that if you’re worried about sending the certificate in the clear, don’t be. Every version of SSL and TLS up to 1.2 sent the certificate unencrypted too. A certificate is public by design. An attacker can swap it for a different one, but they can’t make one that’s valid for shop.example.com without a CA’s help, and if they can get one of those, you have bigger problems.

It has been revealed that once the browser is happy, it knows the server’s public key. It invents a random secret, encrypts it with that key and asks to upgrade.

Only the real server, holding the private key, can decrypt that secret. It replies with a random value of its own and switches protocols.

Both sides now derive their encryption keys from the browser’s secret, the server’s random value and a hash of everything that was mentioned in the clear up to this point. Mixing in that hash means that if anyone tampered with the plaintext part, the two sides end up with different keys and the connection fails. From this point on everything on the connection is encrypted, starting with the response to GET /checkout.

I’m describing the 1995 approach, where the browser encrypted a secret with the server’s RSA key. When Diffie-Hellman key exchange came along, it would have been just a different pair of headers: the browser sends its half of the exchange, and the server replies with its half, signed by the key in its certificate. Changing how keys are exchanged becomes header negotiation, which HTTP is already very good at.

Recent findings suggest that browser: Hello, shop.example.com. Who are you?Server: Here’s my certificate.Browser: That checks out. Here’s a secret only you can read. Shall we go somewhere private?Server: 101.Eavesdropper: Aw.

The first thing we get for free is the one that took our universe the longest to sort out.

That very first request for the certificate has a Host header. A server hosting a thousand websites on one IP address knows exactly which certificate to send back, because the browser told it, using a header the server already understands. There’s nothing to retrofit.

Industry observers note that in our universe, the server had to pick a certificate before it knew which website you wanted. For years, every secure website needed its own IP address, which was one of the reasons HTTPS stayed expensive and rare for so long. The fix was SNI, standardized in 2003: an extension that lets the browser mention the website’s name at the very start of the TLS handshake. In other words, a Host header, reinvented inside TLS. The parallel universe never needs it.

And it’s all on one port. Firewalls, proxies and load balancers deal with port 80 and nothing else. A URL is a URL.

So if SNI was standardized in 2003, why couldn’t a website rely on it until the mid-2010s? This is the part I find most interesting.

According to recent reports, in our universe, TLS is a black box. Your application hands a socket to a TLS library, and the library takes care of everything: negotiating versions, swapping certificates, exchanging keys and the encryption itself. The box comes with a large “do not touch” sign, which is good advice. People who write their own cryptography tend to get it wrong.

In a recent development, the trouble is that a black box that does everything can only be improved by whoever owns it. Browsers couldn’t use SNI until their TLS library supported it, and on many platforms that library was part of the operating system. Internet Explorer on Windows XP never got SNI at all. A website couldn’t rely on SNI until XP was finally gone.

In the parallel universe, the black box is much smaller. Finding the certificate, checking it and exchanging keys all happen in HTTP, in code that browsers and web servers already enhancement all the time. What’s left inside the box is the genuinely hard part: given these keys, encrypt and authenticate everything that follows. That still deserves a “do not touch” sign, but it’s a box that rarely needs touching. The bits people keep wanting to change live outside it.

The parallel universe’s first request can do another job, too: it makes life much easier for newly introduced certificate authorities.

In our universe, a server sends one certificate chain to everyone, before it knows anything about who’s asking. In practice, that means a server operator can only use a CA that every browser on Earth already trusts. Nobody will pick a CA with less than 100% support, however good it is, so a fresh CA can’t get started. Even Let’s Encrypt, which had about the most compelling offer imaginable (free certificates, issued automatically), had to launch with a cross-signature from IdenTrust, an established CA, so that older browsers would accept its certificates. When that old IdenTrust root expired in 2021, devices that had never learned to trust Let’s Encrypt directly started failing.

In the parallel universe, the browser simply says which CAs it trusts, in the request:.

It has been revealed that the server can hold certificates from several CAs and pick one the browser will accept. That’s content negotiation, which HTTP has done since the beginning. A new CA can start out with only the newest browsers, and sites can use it alongside their old CA until everyone catches up.

It’s worth noting that a list of trusted CAs, sent in the clear, is one more thing a website could use to fingerprint its visitors. I’d be surprised if it told them much, though. For most people, the list would be whatever came with their browser and operating system, which the User-Agent header already gives away. The exception would be anyone whose employer has added its own root CA to their machine, whose list would announce exactly where they work.

Early implementations in the parallel universe might simply have sent the entire list. As trust stores grew, browsers would probably have evolved more efficient ways to express the same information: compact identifiers, Bloom-filter-style summaries, or a two-stage negotiation where the browser sends a reduced list and the server replies, “I don’t have certificates for any of those authorities, but I do have these.” HTTP has had a status code for exactly that answer since the 1990s: 300 Multiple Choices. At that point the browser can make a second request with a CA it knows is acceptable to both sides.

According to recent reports, our universe is, once again, getting there slowly. TLS 1.3 has an extension that lets a browser list the CAs it trusts, but no browser sends it, partly because a full list is so large. There’s now a proposal called Trust Anchor Identifiers that would let browsers say the same thing in a compact form, so that servers can pick the right certificate. It’s still a draft. And just like SNI, it will only be usable once the TLS library in every browser, operating system and server has caught up.

In a recent development, there’s another secure protocol that was born in 1995: SSH. Look at how it works and it’s already halfway into the parallel universe. An SSH connection opens with both sides exchanging version strings and lists of supported algorithms in the clear, then exchanging keys, and only then switching over to encrypted packets.

In a recent development, so in the parallel universe, someone at the standards meeting would notice that the TLS people and the SSH people are building the same thing. Both have a handshake that ends with “here are our keys”. Both then need the same thing after that: chop the data into records, number them, encrypt them, authenticate them, and notice if anything is replayed, reordered or dropped. Why have two committees writing two versions of the hardest part?

According to recent reports, I think the two groups would merge and settle on a common core. TLS would keep its handshake, with certificates and CAs and an HTTP Upgrade. SSH would keep its own, with host keys you’re asked to trust the first time you connect. Each would finish by handing a set of keys to the same small, heavily-reviewed piece of code. Every improvement to that core, whether a faster cipher or a fix for a subtle attack, would land in both protocols at once.

Remember the small black box from earlier? This is where it ends up. HTTP owns the TLS handshake. SSH owns its own. That doesn’t make the handshake easy. Checking a certificate chain is still code where one wrong line can undo everything, as Apple found in 2014 when a single duplicated line skipped the signature check in its TLS handshake. But the handshake lives alongside the rest of the protocol, where it can be reviewed and updated by the same people, on the same schedule. Something like SNI ships with the next browser upgrade, not the next operating system.

The real “do not touch” sign hangs on the shared core that both protocols hand their keys to. It would still be free software, in the GNU sense: anyone can read it, study it, fork it and change it. But the official version would be maintained by cryptographers, and getting a change accepted into it would mean convincing them. Instead of every secure protocol carrying its own massive black box, there’s one small one, with the strictest gatekeepers, and everyone uses it.

This isn’t as far-fetched as it sounds. QUIC, the protocol underneath HTTP/3, already works this way. It borrows the TLS 1.3 handshake and nothing else: once the handshake produces keys, they are handed to QUIC’s own packet encryption, and TLS’s record layer is never used. The handshake and the core have already come apart. Our universe just took until 2021 to do it.

There’s a warning in our universe too. In 2023, an attack called Terrapin indicated that an attacker could quietly delete messages from the start of the encrypted part of an SSH connection. It worked by slipping extra messages into the plaintext handshake, which threw off the message numbering the encryption relied on, without either side noticing. The handover from “talking in the clear” to “talking securely” is exactly where the parallel universe would need to be most careful. It’s also exactly the sort of thing you’d want one shared core and one set of eyes on, rather than two.

It has been revealed that once the two protocols share a core, the wall between them starts to look a bit thin. In a universe where every secure connection already starts with an HTTP Upgrade, it’s a short step to one more. Sooner or later, someone would modify OpenSSH to accept a shell over HTTP.

That request is sent after the connection has already been upgraded to TLS, so it’s encrypted, and the server knows exactly who’s asking, because the browser (or the SSH client) presented a certificate during the handshake. The server replies 101 Switching Protocols, and what follows is SSH, with its channels, port forwarding and all. TLS has already done the encryption and checked both sides’ identities, so SSH can skip its own key exchange and get straight to the shell. In our universe, WebSocket had to be invented to tunnel things through HTTP. The parallel universe just asks.

In a recent development, port 22 would still have its fans. Plain SSH doesn’t depend on a CA, so nobody else’s mistake can let an attacker pretend to be your server, and nothing breaks because a certificate expired over the weekend. I expect it would live on in the corner of the server room, run by people who know exactly why they want it.

I’d be a poor advocate if I didn’t look at the downsides, and there’s one significant one: stripping.

Recent findings suggest that credit where it’s due: having https:// as a separate URL scheme does give our real universe something genuinely useful. It’s an explicit sign that security is expected, and that the browser shouldn’t proceed without it. When you click on an https:// link, the author of that page is telling your browser “this must be encrypted, and if it isn’t, stop”.

The parallel universe gives that up. Its security is opportunistic: the browser asks whether the server can do encryption and uses it if so. That’s great, right up until someone hides the opportunity before the handshake completes. The negotiation happens in the clear, so an attacker sitting in the middle doesn’t need to break the encryption. They just stop it from ever starting. Anyone who has set up STARTTLS for email will recognize this one.

Recent findings suggest that so what’s a browser to do? You connect to your bank’s website, ask for /.well-known/tls-cert, and get back “404 Not Found”. Maybe the bank really has forgotten to set up its certificate. Maybe someone in the coffee shop is lying to you. The browser can’t tell the difference. Does it keep going without security?

In a recent development, in fairness, our universe has the same problem. When you type bank.example into your browser, it has traditionally tried plain HTTP on port 80 first. The bank’s server replies with a redirect to https://, and an attacker can simply hide that redirect and keep you on the insecure version. A tool called sslstrip demonstrated exactly that in 2009. Our universe’s answer, for many years, was to train users to look for the padlock.

Recent findings suggest that the parallel universe would end up in much the same place. The padlock would survive as the sign that security was correctly established, and users would be trained to look for it just as ours were. (Our universe has since turned the padlock inside out. Chrome retired it in 2023, but plain HTTP pages have carried a big “Not Secure” warning since 2018. These days the sign that a connection is secure is that the warning isn’t there.).

Sources indicate that sooner or later, something like HSTS would be introduced, a header the server sends to say “from now on, never talk to me without encryption”. In our universe, HSTS arrived in 2012. In the parallel universe, with no s in the URL to fall back on, I suspect it would have been needed much sooner.

Here’s a twist. The parallel universe might end up inventing https:// anyway, but with a different meaning. It wouldn’t mean “use a different protocol on a different port”. It would mean “do HTTP on port 80 as normal, but this time, stop if security can’t be negotiated”. A link author could once again promise that a page must be encrypted, and the bank’s 404 becomes an error page instead of a shrug.

According to recent reports, our universe has even written the mirror image of this down. RFC 8164 (2017) describes “opportunistic security” for plain http:// URLs, where a browser can quietly use TLS if the server offers it, while https:// keeps its meaning of “secure or nothing”. Both universes end up with https:// making the same promise. They just got there from opposite ends.

There’s an old argument that the parallel universe would replay, from the other side.

According to recent reports, before Let’s Encrypt arrived in 2015 and made certificates free, a few people ran their servers with self-signed certificates, vouched for by nobody but themselves. Browsers greeted those servers with major scary here-be-dragons warnings. The people running them hated this, and they had a point: a website with no security at all got no warning at all. The browser was treating “encrypted, but I can’t tell who by” as worse than “not encrypted”.

In a recent development, in the parallel universe, the same struggle would happen in a different way. Connect to a site for the first time, with no https:// in the link and no HSTS history, and the opportunistic security kicks in. If the certificate checks out, you get the padlock. If it doesn’t, there’s no padlock, but there’s no need for a warning either. An unknown certificate is much the same as no security at all, and the browser treats it that way.

In a recent development, going to the effort of TLS without verifying the certificate sounds a bit pointless, but it isn’t entirely. It won’t stop an attacker who can sit in the middle and hand you a certificate of their own. It does stop anyone who can only listen, which is the cheaper and far more common kind of snooping. The IETF came round to this view in 2014, declaring that pervasive monitoring is an attack (RFC 7258) and describing opportunistic encryption as “some protection most of the time” (RFC 7435).

And if you know the magic spell to get into the experts-only configuration, you’ve got the basis for SSH-style security. Tell your browser to remember that certificate, and complain loudly if it ever changes. The first connection is a leap of faith, and every connection after that is checked against it. Our universe’s browsers half-did this already: Firefox had a “Permanently store this exception” checkbox, buried behind enough scary warnings that only the determined ever found it.

Is that a good thing? Depends how you feel about SSH.

Recent findings suggest that here’s the funny thing. Our universe keeps quietly doing it the HTTP way anyway.

Industry observers note that not every lesson points my way, though. Email went the parallel-universe route with STARTTLS, upgrading a plain connection on the normal port. In 2018, RFC 8314 recommended that email clients use a dedicated port with TLS from the very first byte instead, because of the stripping problem.

So was Netscape lazy, or right?

It has been revealed that I think the honest answer is “right for the wrong reasons”, and the parallel universe indicates which part was right. The thing that protects you from an attacker quietly downgrading your connection isn’t the separate port. It’s the s in the URL: a promise, made in advance, that this connection must be secure. Netscape almost certainly didn’t choose a new scheme for that reason. A new scheme and a new port were simply the easiest way to bolt encryption onto software that already existed. But the scheme is the part that earned its keep.

The port, I’m less sure about. I can’t help noticing how much of the past thirty years of TLS work has been spent rebuilding, inside a black box, things HTTP already had. I’d have liked to visit the universe where the s in https:// means “this must be secure” and everything else is just HTTP.

…we’ve tightened Activity Zone boundary precision on our newest wired cameras to significantly reduce false alerts from passing cars, animals, and motion just outside your zone borders. Compatible brands will include IKEA, Eve, and Aqara.

Recent findings suggest that starting in December, Nest thermostat owners in the U.S. and Canada can check the app to see estimated cumulative savings. And they can also balance hot and cold spots with compatible third-party room sensors with their 4th-gen Nest Learning Thermostat.

Dynamic Farsight already lets you see the time, temperature, weather, and air quality from across the room, and starting this December, we’re rolling out newly introduced Dynamic Farsight faces with designs that match your aesthetics. Keep an eye out for seasonal animations on the Temperature face, or switch to our new Lunar face to track the phases of the moon right on your wall.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A near-record share of young adults won’t be traveling home to visit family for the holidays—they’re already living there. One in three U.S. adults between age 18 and 34 live with their parents, according to a upcoming report from Realtor.com. That’s 25.2 million or 33% of young adults living at home in 2025, only a sliver less than the 33.6% during the pandemic-era peak in 2020. Living at home is one way that Americans who can’t afford to buy or rent on their own wrestle with the high cost of housing and other expenses. While the cost of housing is a nationwide problem, the share of adults living with their parents offers an interesting glimpse into regional affordability patterns around the country. “The pattern of young adults at home has spread beyond the most expensive markets, with the share rising most in parts of the South and West, including some that have traditionally supported an earlier launch,” Realtor.com’s chief economist, Danielle Hale, wrote in the report. “As young people adapt to high housing costs, they are delaying homeownership and the wealth creation that comes with it.” Two stories with the same ending Predictably, at least one of the country’s priciest cities is among those with the largest share of adults living with their parents—but the full story is more complicated. New York leads the list, with 41.3% of adults between the ages of 18 and 24 staying in the nest. In Philadelphia, Miami, Baltimore, and Houston, more than 38% of adults in that age range lived with their parents. Across Los Angeles, Atlanta, and Chicago, the share of adults living at home was over 35%. Houston, Atlanta, and Baltimore aren’t known for their high cost of living, unlike costly urban hubs like New York and Los Angeles, but home prices have soared in recent years in those markets. That rapid change to local affordability is freezing many young adults out of a housing market they might have been able to afford during a previous era. The share of adults living at home has grown the quickest in Las Vegas, San Francisco, and San Jose, but those metros tell different stories. In San Francisco and San Jose, two expensive cities close to the AI boom, housing prices have always been high, even as they grow higher still. In Las Vegas, once known as a relatively affordable market in the West, home prices have skyrocketed by more than 60% since 2019. “Las Vegas and the Bay Area show two different paths to the same challenge,” wrote Hannah Jones, senior economist at Realtor.com. “In Las Vegas, the sharp rise in home prices has made it harder for young adults to buy. In San Francisco and San Jose, already-high housing costs and limited inventory leave many young adults facing steep barriers to living on their own.” Living at home on the rise Regionally, the Northeast still dominates with 36.9% of young adults living at home in 2025, though that number is trending down. The West is next with a 32.4% “co-residence” rate, followed by 32.3% in the South and 31.7% in the Midwest. That share is rising everywhere except the Northeast, demonstrating that the housing affordability crisis may look distinct in different corners of the country, but it’s something that a surprising share of Americans everywhere are struggling with. “For young adults who hope to live independently or buy a home, elevated costs and limited entry-level supply can delay household formation and, for would-be buyers, the opportunity to build home equity,” Jones noted. “Until affordability improves and entry-level supply expands, the report finds that pent-up demand is likely to continue accumulating.”.

🇵🇭 FilBench - Can LLMs Understand and Generate Filipino?

📅 12 Aug 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (878 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that as large language models (LLMs) become increasingly integrated into our lives, it becomes crucial to assess whether they reflect the nuances and capabilities of specific language communities.
  • That’s why we developed FilBench: a comprehensive evaluation suite to assess the capabilities of LLMs for Tagalog, Filipino (the standardized form of Tagalog), and Cebuano, on fluency, linguistic and translation abilities, as well as specific cultural knowledge.
  • We used it to evaluate 20+ state-of-the-art LLMs on FilBench, providing a comprehensive assessment of their performance in Philippine languages:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that as large language models (LLMs) become increasingly integrated into our lives, it becomes crucial to assess whether they reflect the nuances and capabilities of specific language communities. For example, Filipinos are among the most active ChatGPT users globally, ranking fourth in ChatGPT traffic (behind the United States, India, and Brazil [1] [2]), but despite this strong usage, we lack a clear understanding of how LLMs perform for their languages, such as Tagalog and Cebuano. Most of the existing evidence is anecdotal, such as screenshots of ChatGPT responding in Filipino as proof that it is fluent. What we need instead is a systematic evaluation of LLM capabilities in Philippine languages.

That’s why we developed FilBench: a comprehensive evaluation suite to assess the capabilities of LLMs for Tagalog, Filipino (the standardized form of Tagalog), and Cebuano, on fluency, linguistic and translation abilities, as well as specific cultural knowledge.

We used it to evaluate 20+ state-of-the-art LLMs on FilBench, providing a comprehensive assessment of their performance in Philippine languages:.

The FilBench evaluation suite contains four major categories–Cultural Knowledge, Classical NLP, Reading Comprehension, and Generation–divided into 12 tasks. For example, the Classical NLP category includes tasks such as sentiment analysis, whereas Generation tasks include different aspects of translation. In order to ensure that these categories reflect the priorities and trends in NLP research and usage, we curate them based on a historical survey of NLP research on Philippine languages from 2006 to early 2024. (Most of these categories exclusively contain non-translated content to ensure faithfulness to the natural use of Philippine languages.).

Industry observers note that each of these categories provides an aggregated metric. To create a single representative score, we compute the weighted average based on the number of examples in each category, which we call the FilBench Score.

To simplify usage and set up, we built FilBench on top of Lighteval, an all-in-one framework for LLM evaluation. For language-specific evaluation, we first defined translation pairs from English to Tagalog (or Cebuano) for common terms used in evaluation such as "yes" (oo), "no" (hindi), and "true" (totoo) among others. Then, we used the provided templates to implement custom tasks for the capabilities we care about.

FilBench is now available as a set of community tasks in the official Lighteval repository!

By evaluating several LLMs on FilBench, we uncovered several insights into how they perform in Filipino.

It has been revealed that in the past few years, we have seen an increase in region-specific LLMs that target Southeast Asian languages (SEA-specific), such as SEA-LION and SeaLLM. These are open-weight LLMs that you can freely download from HuggingFace. We find that SEA-specific LLMs are often the most parameter-efficient for our languages, achieving the highest FilBench scores compared to other models of their size. However, the best SEA-specific model is still outperformed by closed-source LLMs like GPT-4o.

Building region-specific LLMs still makes sense, as we observe performance gains of 2-3% when continuously fine-tuning a base LLM with SEA-specific instruction-tuning data. This suggests that efforts to curate Filipino/SEA-specific training data for fine-tuning remain relevant, as they can lead to better performance on FilBench.

We also observe that across the four categories on FilBench, most models struggle with Generation capabilities. Upon inspecting failure modes in Generation, we find that these include cases where the model fails to follow translation instructions, generates overly verbose texts, or hallucinates another language instead of Tagalog or Cebuano.

The Philippines tends to have limited internet infrastructure and lower average incomes [3], necessitating accessible LLMs that are cost- and compute-efficient. Through FilBench, we were able to identify LLMs that are on the Pareto frontier of efficiency.

In a recent development, in general, we find that open-weight LLMs, i.e., models that you can freely download from HuggingFace, are way cheaper than commercial models without sacrificing their performance. If you want an alternative to GPT-4o for your Filipino language tasks, then try Llama 4 Maverick!

We also make this information available in the HuggingFace space of the FilBench leaderboard.

According to recent reports, we hope that FilBench provides deeper insights into LLM capabilities for Philippine languages and serves as a catalyst for advancing Filipino NLP research and development. The FilBench evaluation suite is built on top of Hugging Face's lighteval, allowing LLM developers to easily evaluate their models on our benchmark. For more information, please visit the links below:.

The authors would like to thank Cohere Labs for providing credits through the Cohere Research Grant to run the Aya model series, and Together AI for additional computational credits for running several open models. We also acknowledge the Hugging Face team, particularly the OpenEvals team (Clémentine Fourrier and Nathan Habib) and Daniel van Strien, for their support in publishing this blog post.

If you are evaluating on FilBench, please cite our work:.

Industry News: Lenovo Pro 9n review: 18-core RTX Spark in a fancy chassis

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Lenovo Pro 9n is an elegant consumer workstation with a vivid OLED screen and lots of ports, but it's expensive, and RTX Spark still needs to differentiate itself with Windows features to justify that price.
  • Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you.
  • Recent findings suggest that A lot of noise was made about the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra, but there's a handful of other premium machines running Nvidia's latest RTX Spark chips.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Lenovo Pro 9n is an elegant consumer workstation with a vivid OLED screen and lots of ports, but it's expensive, and RTX Spark still needs to differentiate itself with Windows features to justify that price.

Lighter than Surface Laptop Ultra.

ExpensiveBattery life could be better.

Included stylus doesn't work on the touchscreen.

Windows doesn't take advantage of RTX Spark.

Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Recent findings suggest that A lot of noise was made about the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra, but there's a handful of other premium machines running Nvidia's latest RTX Spark chips. Lenovo's Pro 9n follows Microsoft's lead, making a fancy laptop with its own touches, like an OLED panel and a stylus that works on the touchpad.

This is also our first time looking at the 18-core version of the RTX Spark, which has fewer CUDA cores than the last one we tested, so we'll see just what kind of changes in performance you get if you don't opt for a higher-end configuration.

It has been revealed that the Lenovo Pro 9n is clearly a tool. It's a dark gray box with a Lenovo logo and a slight extrusion to fit Lenovo's signature anti-notch for the camera. The lid is flat, with a rounded keyboard deck, like many of Lenovo's premium Yoga laptops. It's a playful look that's less noticeable when the system is matte black rather than colorful.

The keyboard deck, including a massive touchpad, is logo-free other than an Nvidia RTX Spark sticker, which keeps all of your attention on the backlit keyboard and 15.3-inch OLED screen.

Sources indicate that there are plenty of ports, and I appreciate that both sides of the laptop have both USB Type-C and Type-A. The left side also has HDMI and a 3.5 mm headphone jack, while the right side includes an SD card slot and an e-shutter for the webcam.

At 13.66 x 9.53 x 0.66 inches, this isn't a small system, but it's still one you can reasonably fit in your backpack. It's wider and deeper than the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra (12.95 x 9.40 x 0.75 inches) but it's also thinner. Apple's newly introduced 16-inch MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR is a tad sleeker at 0.63 inches thick.

Recent findings suggest that the Pro 9n measured in at 3.64 pounds pounds, less than 4.41-pound Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra. The 16-inch MacBook Pro is a bit heavier than the Pro 9n at 4.1 pounds.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

5,120 CUDA cores, Blackwell-based.

15.3-inch, 2560 x 1600, OLED, touch, 165 Hz.

MediaTek Wi-Fi 7 MT7925, Bluetooth 5.4.

HDMI 2.1, 2s USB Type-A (10Gbps), 2x USB4 Type-C (40 Gbps), 3.5 mm headphone jack, SD card reader (UHS-II).

13.66 x 9.53 x 0.66 inches / 347 mm x 242 mm x 16.7 mm.

In a recent development, the Lenovo Pro 9n features the lesser variant of the RTX Spark N1X, and this is our first look at a system with that config. This version has an 18-core CPU, down from the 20-core version we saw with the Surface Laptop Ultra. It also has 32GB of RAM and 1TB of storage.

Sources indicate that on Geekbench 6, the Pro 9n came in slightly behind the Surface Laptop in both single-core and multi-core performance (given how heavy the Surface Laptop is, some of this could come down to cooling). The MacBook Pro with M5 Max won out, while the Asus ZenBook A16 with Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme beat both RTX Sparks.

According to recent reports, the Pro 9n copied 25GB of files at a rate of 1,205.37 MBps. That's not terrible, but in the ultra-premium price band, you can get faster speeds. Every other laptop beat the Pro 9n here.

According to recent reports, on Handbrake, the Pro 9n transcoded a 4K video to 1080p in 2 minutes and 1 second, or 7 seconds behind the Surface Pro with the 20-core CPU. The Pro 9n beat the Snapdragon-powered Zenbook here.

We use Cinebench 2026 to stress test laptops, running a multi-core benchmark ten times in a row. The Pro 9n stayed largely consistent — in fact, it even got better later on, as the cooling kicked into high gear. The system started with a score of 6,219.85, and topped out on run 6 at 6,417.45. Most of the runs were in the high 6,300s. The RTX Spark's Cortex-A725 cores ran at an average of 2.81 GHz, while the Cortex-X925 cores averaged 3.57 GHz.

It's worth noting that HWinfo, which we used for monitoring, was missing a single A725 core. This also happened on the Surface Laptop Ultra, though now we can tell which cores are which.

Industry observers note that the Lenovo Pro 9n we reviewed came with the entry-level version of Nvidia's RTX Spark, which has an 18-core CPU and 5,120 CUDA cores. It can be upgraded to a 20-core / 6,144 CUDA core chip in some configurations, which is the same chip we saw in the Surface Laptop Ultra.

In a recent development, to test the difference in AI performance, we ran AgentPerf-Local using Qwen 3.8-27B-UD_IQ3_XXS in order to fit in the limited available GPU memory (both are 32GB systems, with the Surface allowing 24GB of allocated graphics memory and the Pro 9n accepting just 16GB). The benchmark simulates running conversations by playing back conversations, with a majority of the work involving processing prompts rather than generating tokens.

The difference between the two RTX Spark systems wasn't particularly significant here. The Surface Laptop Ultra completed the benchmark in 1,148.3 seconds, while the Pro 9n took 1,196.6 seconds. That's a 4.12% difference in favor of the higher-end Spark.

According to recent reports, beyond the difference in CPU cores, the version of RTX Spark in the Pro 9n we tested has 5,120 CUDA cores, down from 6,144 in the more powerful version in the Surface Laptop Ultra. (The beefier chip is also available in other configurations of the Pro 9n).

On 3DMark Steel Nomad, the Pro 9n earned a score of 2,796, falling behind the Laptop Ultra (4,355) and the MacBook Pro (3,865). It's still a more powerful system than the Zenbook with Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme (1,262).

Recent findings suggest that in gaming, the RTX Spark isn't really meant for much above 1080p (perhaps 1440p, depending on the game). So in the case of our benchmarks, the difference in CUDA cores didn't have a stark difference, with nearly identical scores on Shadow of the Tomb Raider and Cyberpunk 2077. Far Cry 6, which is more CPU-focused, ran better on the 20-core RTX Spark.

It has been revealed that when I played 007: First Light, with the game at 1920 x 1200 and settings on medium, and DLSS set to ultra performance, the game ran just over 30 frames per second. With DLSS on "dynamic," the game ran smoother, between 40 and 72 frames per second as Bond moved through a swanky hotel, though there was some jankiness to it. The game also took a long time to load, possibly due to Windows' Prism emulation.

Industry observers note that the 15.3-inch OLED touchscreen on the Pro 9n is quite nice. The 165 Hz panel is vivid and bright enough for most uses.

The trailer for Artificial demonstrated off the colors and blacks, as the trailer descends from lush greens outside of Sam Altman's home to a dark tunnel, until he arrives in a bunker with blue lights that all but jumped off the screen.

Lenovo's OLED panel was the most vivid of our test group on our colorimeter, covering 198% of the sRGB color space by volume, significantly higher than the rest of the field, though it often appeared oversaturated. In fact, it arrivees out of the box on its default wallpaper with severe pops of green and white. The MacBook Pro's PROLED XDR display has lower numbers on the colorimeter, but looks far more natural than what Lenovo is offering here.

At 440.6 nits of brightness, the Pro 9n's display is good, but the MacBook Pro has it beat at 529.5 nits, while the Surface Laptop Pro reached an astounding 944 nits in our testing.

It has been revealed that lenovo's keyboard feels great. There's 1.5 mm of key travel, and you can feel it. It's deep, but punchy. The keycaps can be a bit slippery, though I typed at 106 words per minute on the monkeytype typing test, albeit with 2% less accuracy than usual.

The haptic touchpad is huge, smooth, and responsive. Oddly enough, despite being haptic, there is a noticeable depression when you click down, especially at the bottom edge. It's an odd feeling when you notice it, especially when you can still configure how hard you have to press in Windows to register a click.

Lenovo includes a stylus in the box for use with the touch screen, which is good for signing documents. The pen, however, does not work on the touchscreen, which is an odd choice. The Yoga Pen Gen 2 (typically sold for $63 with a case that isn't included here) can attach magnetically to the Pro 9n's lid and charges over USB Type-C, so you can use the same charger as the laptop. It supports up to 8,192 points of pressure sensitivity with AES3.0, or up to 4,096 points on other protocols.

According to recent reports, lenovo's combination of two tweeters and two woofers does a decent job. They get nice and loud, easily filling a mid-sized office room with Justice's "Flower In A Hurricane.".

The song's guitars and synths sounded excellent, as did SZA and Kevin Parker's voices. The drum beat was a bit low, but going into the Dolby Settings app, switching to the "Warm" music setting with boosted lows helped there.

There are 9 screws holding the bottom of the Lenovo Pro 9n on. The four closest to the hinge are longer than the remaining five, so be sure to keep them organized. You'll need a pry tool to remove the latches and release the base.

Inside, there's not a ton to repair or replace down the line for the average person. The 92.5 WHr battery is held in place with a few screws. You can also easily access the included M.2 2242 SSD, and there's a second bay for another drive of the same length. I would always prefer a more standard 2280 drive, but if this is what lets Lenovo fit two drives on the board (or at least give you the option to add a second drive), I'll take it.

The Wi-Fi card is soldered to the board and partially obscured by the heatsink's thick heat pipes.

The Pro 9n ran for 10 hours and 30 minutes on average on our battery test, which browses the web, streams video from a server, and runs OpenGL tests with the screen set to 150 nits of brightness.

That's not too far off from other high-end Windows on Arm laptops, beating the Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme-based Zenbook A16 by 4 minutes, and it was 13 minutes behind the Surface Laptop Ultra with a more powerful version of N1X.

The MacBook Pro smoked them all though, running for 15 hours and 57 minutes on our test.

During our Cinebench stress test, we took skin temperature measurements to get an idea of how hot the Pro 9n gets during use.

The center of the keyboard measured 98.5 degrees Fahrenheit, while the touchpad was 10 degrees cooler. The hottest point on the bottom of the laptop reached 101.5 F.

HWinfo hasn't been updated to be clear on which sensors are measuring what internally. We could make educated guesses, but we'll have more specifics when the software is updated.

Sources indicate that the 9.2-megapixel webcam on the Pro 9n should be more than enough for video calling in 4K, assuming your software supports it. While making calls, I found that the camera captured fine details, like graying hairs on the side of my temples (it's been a long month).

The colors were a bit cool, however. I could do with more vibrancy and warmth to make it more realistic.

In a recent development, there’s just too much pre-loaded software on the Pro 9n. The most important app is Vantage, a catch-all app with your serial number, user guides, warranty status, a number of device settings, and access to support services. But it also houses a ton of ads.

In a recent development, the organization also has direct links in the Start menu and taskbar to the Lenovo subscription portal to buy software. An additional user guide is also in the start menu. There's also Smart Connect, to pair and transfer files between your laptop, tablet, and phone, along with a dashboard to view them all. The company also has its stylus settings app and a link in the Start Menu to its Artificial Intelligence policy, which looks more like an internal document than something meant for consumers.

Lenovo also includes some bloatware, like trials of McAfee antivirus and a promotional trial of Dropbox.

Like other RTX Spark systems, the Pro 9n is running Windows on Arm. It's better than it's ever been, but there are still times when it feels laggy. More games and apps than before are compatible, but it's still not perfect.

Lenovo sells the Pro 9n with a 1-year warranty, which can be extended with additional coverage for more money.

We tested the Lenovo Pro 9n in a $3,249.99 configuration with an 18-core RTX Spark CPU and integrated GPU using 5,120 CUDA cores, 32GB of RAM, a 1TB PCIe Gen 4 SSD, and Windows 11 Pro.

The cheapest version, at $2,999.99, uses the same processor and RAM as our review unit, comes with Windows 11 Home, and has 512GB of RAM.

Industry observers note that bumping up to the higher-end 20-core, 6,144 CUDA-core GPU costs an extra $450 but also gets you 64GB of RAM and 1TB of storage as a base. Moving to 128GB of RAM is $1,400, while moving to a 2TB PCIe Gen 5 SSD is another $450.

The Lenovo Pro 9n is a minimalist, RTX Spark-based laptop with strong port selection and a lovely OLED screen. The keyboard has deep travel, and I don't mind a design that simply gets out of the way of your work.

It has been revealed that still, it's expensive, even with the base version of RTX Spark. Battery life is just past 10 hours, which I would like to see improve across the RTX Spark platform, and there aren't any AI features in Windows that make this chip special for anyone who isn't running local models.

It has been revealed that if you are married to getting an RTX Spark machine, the Lenovo Pro 9n beats the Surface Laptop Ultra in three areas: It's lighter, has an OLED screen, and extra SSD slots (even if it is M.2 2242) for an upgrade down the line. Still, the Surface is a nicer, more premium design and has the fun, magnetic Surface Connect port.

Those who aren't running local models should probably be looking for a cheaper laptop. Those prioritizing battery life should consider a Mac. And those who like Windows on Arm can still consider Snapdragon X2, as Nvidia's entrance into this choppy sea should lift all ships.

TextQuests: How Good are LLMs at Text-Based Video Games?

📅 12 Aug 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (940 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has enabled remarkable progress on established academic and industrial benchmarks.
  • Sources indicate that two core avenues exist to evaluate autonomous agents: either use real-world environments and a limited set of specific skills, such as tool use or coding capabilities, or use simulated open-world environments.
  • Recent findings suggest that textQuests is a benchmark built upon 25 classic Infocom interactive fiction games.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The rapid advancement of Large Language Models (LLMs) has enabled remarkable progress on established academic and industrial benchmarks. Knowledge benchmarks, such as MMLU and GPQA, are now largely saturated, and frontier models are making significant progress on expert evaluations like HLE. However, this success in static, knowledge-based tasks does not always translate to effectiveness in dynamic, interactive settings, the kind of environment in which we would want effective assistants and AI agents to perform well. Developing robust methodologies for evaluating LLMs as autonomous agents in complex, exploratory environments remains a significant challenge.

Sources indicate that two core avenues exist to evaluate autonomous agents: either use real-world environments and a limited set of specific skills, such as tool use or coding capabilities, or use simulated open-world environments. The latter better captures an agent's ability to operate autonomously in exploratory environments that demand sustained, self-directed reasoning over a long and growing context, while being easy to evaluate. While this direction is still developing, it has seen growing interest through benchmarks such as Balrog, ARC-AGI, and demonstrations of models like Claude and Gemini playing Pokémon. Building on this emerging vein of work, we introduce TextQuests.

Recent findings suggest that textQuests is a benchmark built upon 25 classic Infocom interactive fiction games. These once-popular text-based video games, which can take human players over 30 hours and require hundreds of precise actions to solve, provide a compelling testbed for the challenges of agentic reasoning. They demand that an agent demonstrate:.

Long-Context Reasoning: Agents must devise and execute multi-step intends by reasoning over a long and continuously growing history of actions and observations, relying solely on their intrinsic capabilities without the aid of external tools.

Learning through Exploration: The games require agents to learn from experience, interrogating their own failures and making incremental improvements through trial-and-error as they explore the unknown world.

Success in these games requires an agent to build understanding over a long gameplay session. This allows for a more direct and accurate assessment of the LLM itself as the reasoning backbone of an AI agent system.

Recent findings suggest that for each model, we conduct two distinct evaluation runs: one with access to the game's official hints (With Clues) and one without (No Clues). Each run is executed for a maximum of 500 steps and stops early if the agent successfully completes the game. To handle the growing context, the full game history is maintained without truncation throughout the run. This long-context evaluation is computationally feasible due to the prompt caching inherent in modern LLM inference frameworks. We employ two main evaluation metrics:.

In a recent development, game Progress. The Game Progress metric is calculated based on a series of labeled checkpoints representing necessary objectives on the path to finishing a game.

According to recent reports, harm. To assess the ethical behavior of the agents, we measure Harm by tracking specific in-game actions that are considered harmful to some degree. This score is then averaged across all games to evaluate an agent's overall tendency to perform such actions.

According to recent reports, long-context Reasoning. During evaluation, the context window can exceed 100K tokens, requiring LLMs to consistently perform precise reasoning and planning over a vast history of observations and clues to effectively progress. As the context length grows, we observe that current models often hallucinate about prior interactions, such as believing they have already picked up an item when they have not or getting stuck navigating in a loop. Furthermore, similar to observations in Gemini 2.5 Plays Pokémon, LLM agents show an increased tendency to repeat actions from their history rather than synthesizing novel prepares as the context lengthens. These long-context failures are particularly stark in tasks requiring spatial reasoning. For instance, in Wishbringer, most LLMs struggled to navigate back down a cliff after climbing it. The solution simply required reversing the sequence of directions used to ascend—information available in the context history—indicating a fundamental difficulty in building and utilizing a mental map. Similarly, all frontier LLMs struggle in navigating the infamous Maze in Zork I.

Dynamic Thinking. An agent's overall effectiveness is defined by both its task success and its operational efficiency. For LLM agents, efficiency is closely tied to the number of output or reasoning tokens it generates, which directly impacts inference cost and latency. Models that utilize more test-time compute generally achieve higher performance. However, this trend starts to diminish after a certain budget. This consideration is key as many exploratory steps in TextQuests (for example, navigation steps) are intermediate and can be successfully executed without a large reasoning depth.

According to recent reports, in closing, TextQuests is an evaluation of how well models can consistently progress through a series of classic interactive fiction games that were once popular among human players. We hope that open-sourcing TextQuests helps researchers better understand and assess the current capabilities of LLM agents in challenging exploratory environments. Open-source model builders are welcome to submit to TextQuests Leaderboard by sending us an email at agibenchmark@safe.ai.

You can also plug them into MUDs (the few that still exist at least!) check out this script I put together last year that hooks up LLMs to telnet: https://github.com/CharlesCNorton/Language-Model-Tools/tree/main/AutoMUD.

Elementor made your site easy to build. It may also be making it slow. Here's how to move a site onto the Block Editor without breaking URLs, losing content or dropping out of Google.

According to recent reports, page builders solved a real problem. Before the Block Editor matured, they were the easiest way to give clients drag-and-drop layouts. Many of those sites are still running today, and a lot of them are slow on phones.

The data backs that up. According to the HTTP Archive Core Web Vitals Technology Report for June 2026, 36.8% of Elementor sites pass Core Web Vitals on mobile. Sites built with the Block Editor pass 53.0% of the time. That's correlation, not proof, since hosting and setup matter too. But in my experience, it matches what happens when you remove the builder from a slow site.

Industry observers note that my reason for migrating sites off Elementor is simple: **page builders make websites heavy. **Having stated that, Elementor has improved a lot. Its performance settings, Flexbox Containers, and asset-loading options cut much of the bloat, and a carefully tuned Elementor site can pass Core Web Vitals. But tuning only goes so far. You’re still shipping the builder’s framework, wrapper markup and scripts, and every plugin or Elementor revision is a chance for the speed to slip again.

For small business sites that don’t need drag-and-drop editing, rebuilding the same design on the WordPress Block Editor (Gutenberg) removes that weight at the source, without changing what the client sees.

This guide follows the order I use. It assumes you're comfortable with WordPress admin, WP-CLI and a staging site. If you need to set those up first, SitePoint's guide to the ultimate WordPress development environment covers the tooling.

Not every Elementor site needs to move. Migration makes sense when:.

Industry observers note that it's harder to justify when the site leans on Elementor Pro features you'd need to replace, such as complex popups, dynamic loops or WooCommerce templates. Those can all be rebuilt, but the job gets bigger fast.

It has been revealed that you can't prove a migration worked without "before" numbers. Capture these on the live site first.

Crawl the site with a tool such as Screaming Frog, and export every indexable URL with its title, meta description, H1 and canonical tag. You can also pull published pages and posts with WP-CLI:.

Run Google PageSpeed Insights, which uses Lighthouse for its lab scores, on the homepage and two or three key templates. Save the mobile lab scores and, if the site has enough traffic, the field data from real users.

Sources indicate that export the last three months of pages and queries from Google Search Console. That's what you'll compare against after launch.

Elementor stores each page's layout as JSON in the elementordata post meta field, and marks builder pages with elementoredit_mode. This command lists every page that uses the builder:.

Then list everything else Elementor controls, which is easy to miss:.

Sources indicate that on the small business sites I've migrated, the inventory usually turns up more than the owner expects. The pages are the easy part. The surprises are saved templates nobody remembers creating, a popup still running on every page, add-on widgets from plugins that were installed once and forgotten, and contact forms that live inside Elementor Pro rather than a form plugin. Finding those before the rebuild saves a broken launch.

According to recent reports, work on a staging copy. Install a block theme, such as Twenty Twenty-Five or a lightweight starter theme, and move the Elementor global styles into theme.json. That way colors, fonts and spacing are defined once, instead of in every widget.

Copy the hex values and font names from Elementor's Site Settings so the newly introduced site matches the old one. Rebuild the header and footer as template parts in the Site Editor. If you'd rather write a theme yourself, SitePoint's series on building a WordPress theme from scratch covers the basics.

Most Elementor sites repeat the same few sections: a hero, a services grid, testimonials and a call to action. Build each one once as a block pattern, then reuse it on every page. Patterns are plain block markup, so you don't need React to write them, whatever you may have heard about React and WordPress development.

In a block theme, any PHP file in the /patterns folder with a header comment is registered automatically:.

Sources indicate that for page content, there's a useful shortcut. Elementor saves a plain HTML copy of each page into post_content. Open a page in the Block Editor, and the old content usually appears in a Classic block. Choose Convert to blocks, then delete the leftovers and rebuild the layout with your patterns. It keeps the copy and images, so you only redo the design.

It has been revealed that the difference highlights up in the page source. Here's typical front-end markup for a single heading on an Elementor page, using the older section and column layout:.

And the same heading as a block:.

Recent findings suggest that newer Elementor versions with Flexbox containers and the optimized markup settings trim some of those wrappers, but most older sites still carry all of them. Multiply that by every element on every page, and the weight adds up.

To speed up this step, I built a free Elementor to Gutenberg converter. Paste in a page's elementordata JSON from Step 2, and it returns block markup you can paste into the Block Editor's code editor. It handles headings, text, images, buttons, spacers, dividers and column layouts, and lists anything it can't convert, such as forms and popups, for you to rebuild by hand. It runs entirely in your browser, so the page data never leaves your computer.

Sources indicate that the code is rarely what holds a migration up. Content is. Once clients see their site being rebuilt, many decide it's time to rewrite their pages too, and the project ends up waiting on copywriters and approvals. My fix is to separate the two: migrate the existing content as it is, launch, then update the copy afterwards. That keeps the speed and SEO gains on schedule, and it means any ranking change can be traced to either the migration or the new copy, not both at once.

This is the step that decides whether rankings hold.

To spot-check a redirect or a status code from the command line:.

When staging matches the live site, deploy it. Then:.

Leave the old elementordata meta in place for a few weeks, in case you need to roll back. Once you're confident, take a backup and remove it to shrink the database.

Run PageSpeed Insights again straight away for lab scores. Field data takes longer: the Chrome UX Report uses a rolling 28-day window, so give it a month before judging real-user results. Compare Search Console clicks for the same period before and after launch.

Industry observers note that in my migrations, the biggest change is usually page weight and loading time, because the builder's CSS, JavaScript and wrapper markup are gone. What doesn't always improve is server response time. If the site is on slow shared hosting, the first byte still arrives late, and that needs a hosting fix, not a rebuild. Search traffic should hold steady if the URLs and metadata were protected. If it drops, the Step 5 crawl comparison is the first place to look.

Moving off Elementor isn't a one-click job, but it isn't a full redesign either. Record a baseline, inventory what the builder controls, rebuild with patterns, and protect every URL. Most of the speed gain comes from removing code the site never needed. For what to tackle after that, see these practical web performance techniques. Most of the risk comes from rushing the SEO checks. Done carefully, the client gets the same site, a faster one, and an editor that comes with WordPress itself.

Viture’s smart display glasses offer official Switch 2 compatibility with the Mobile Dock Mini, and these Black Friday deals even come with free bonus controllers and other accessories.

One of the most annoying things about playing Ocarina of Time right now is that everyone in my home is at a different point in their save file. This makes it tough to be in the same room with others and not spoil something for them, but plugging in a pair of Viture glasses makes this much easier since no one else can see the screen inside the glasses I’m wearing.

You can get your own pair of Viture glasses with the Switch 2 Mobile Dock Mini for as low as $375. This pack comes with Viture Pro 2 glasses, which sport a pair of 120Hz micro-OLED displays with 1,600-nit peak brightness and built-in myopia adjustment diopters. They also weigh just 63g, making them comfortable for long gaming sessions.

The Mobile Dock Mini (on sale for $99 on its own) in the pack comes with a magnetic mount that attaches to the back of the Switch 2. This Dock lets you plug your Viture glasses in and also charges the Switch 2, thanks to the built-in 10,000mAh battery. That delivers more than double the Switch 2’s battery life, so you can clear several temples in Ocarina before even thinking of stopping to charge.

Most of Viture’s glasses are on sale and have extra free gifts, which you can see in the image above. This includes the company’s high-end Viture Beast model, which is on sale for $489 ($60 off). That’s the lowest price ever for the glasses.

Viture Beast upgrades the experience with a wider field of view (58 degrees), native 3DoF spatial tracking, and 9-level electrochromic lens dimming. Native spatial tracking means that you can pin the virtual monitor in space and move around as if it were a TV mounted on a wall. Beast doesn’t have diopters, so you’ll need to order prescription lenses if you need myopia adjustment.

The biggest discount of all is on Viture Luma Pro, which is down to $339 ($160 off). Luma Pro is Viture’s “Goldilocks” pair with excellent image quality and RGB lighting along the frames for some extra style, and even includes myopia adjustment diopters. Pair any of these Viture glasses with the Mobile Dock Mini for Switch 2 compatibility, making them the only pair of smart glasses with official Switch 2 support.

Sources indicate that lastly is Viture Luma Ultra, down to $449 ($150 off). Luma Ultra sports the best image quality of all Viture glasses and includes myopia-adjusting diopters. These are the only pair that support 6DoF tracking when using the Viture Spacewalker app thanks to the cameras on the front, but there’s no native 3DoF support like Beast has, so this functionality is limited to content you view through the app.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A wall of 100 Noctua PC fans was built by maker Sasa Karanovic because "why not." There's a little more to it, though, as the Toronto-based electronics and 3D printing expert wanted to test the capabilities of his upcoming open-source open-hardware OpenFAN XL fan controller. A video shows the setup and control of a 10x10 Noctua fan grid controlled via the 10 headers on the controller. A 50x2 setup was also shown working off the controller. Karanovic indicates that 100 fans was "no sweat" for the new controller, but it would max out at around 200 spinners in its current iteration.

In a recent development, the maker explains in the video that they had this demo idea a while back but recently acquired 100 fans through a combination of "a ton of luck and a good friend." As the new OpenFAN XL controller has 10 headers, the natural first step in controlling them all was to make a grid of 10 x 10 units. That's a lot of fans, but there's also 200 fan grills, 800 screws, and oodles of wiring, including tens of fan splitters.

In a recent development, so, the 100 fans aren't individually controllable, they are controlled in banks of 10 due to the 10 header channels. Thus, the granularity of control on offer here can only apply to 10 fans at the fewest in an array of 100 fans. The maker insisted that with 100 fans "our fan controller is not even breaking a sweat." Incidentally, the controller supports up to four integrated temperature probes to check if it is, actually, sweating.

It has been revealed that karanovic also sought to show the flexibility of his system by using wiring/splitters so that the first two headers controlled 50 fans each. If he'd had enough fans he could have theoretically expanded the cooling wall to 500 fans controlled by his OpenFan software in this way. But there are some other limits to the controller which means it tops out at around 200 fans.

According to recent reports, in summary, this beastly cooling "contraption probably makes no sense," admitted the OpenFAN XL controller designer. However, he could have demonstrated it with some TrashBench-style shenanigans (or in an actual collab) by funneling a 100 fan-powered gust of air at a GPU, PC, laptop or so on.

Sources indicate that if you can think of a use for the OpenFan XL, you can make one yourself or grab one from Karanovic Research for $2,355, presently discounted from $2,926 on pre-order, by following the link in the intro. The product retail page more seriously pitches the controller as a useful product for server or other high-power device builders.

Neural Super Sampling (NSS), a next-generation AI-powered upscaling solution from Arm is released for graphics and gaming developers to start experimenting today!

Sources indicate that NSS is designed for real-time performance on future mobile devices with Arm Neural Technology. However, latency depends on implementation factors such as GPU configuration, resolution, and use case. In our Enchanted Castle demo video below, NSS reduced GPU workload by 50 percent. The model rendered at 540p and upscaled to 1080p in just 4ms in sustained performance setup.

It has been revealed that neural Super Sampling (NSS) is a parameter prediction model for real-time temporal super sampling developed by Arm, optimized for execution on Neural Accelerators (NX) in mobile GPUs. It enables high-resolution rendering at a lower compute cost by reconstructing high-quality output frames from low-resolution temporal inputs. NSS is particularly suited for mobile gaming, XR, and other power-constrained graphics use cases.

Get started with our NSS model today.

If you want to go deeper check out the following resources:.

Check out the Neural Graphics Dataset: A collection of reference images and image sequences along with the corresponding motion, depth and other data required to train, validate and test neural super sampling algorithms.

According to recent reports, the current version of the dataset includes a limited set of data for Neural Super Sampling to demonstrate how the NSS model development flow works. While this flow does not yet provide a comprehensive dataset for complete model (re)training, stay tuned for future releases of the Neural Graphics Model Gym where Arm will provide tools to capture and convert content for use in model training and retraining.

NSS has been integrated into Unreal Engine via two plugins, the NSS Plugin for Unreal® Engine and Unreal® NNE Plugin for ML extensions for Vulkan.

#149399. Arm & ExecuTorch 0.7: Bringing Generative AI to the masses

📅 13 Aug 2025 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (895 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Arm & ExecuTorch 0.7: Bringing Generative AI to the masses

📅 13 Aug 2025 | ⏱️ 4 min read (895 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With Arm’s recent SME2 announcement, the role of Arm KleidiAI is increasingly clear as Arm’s AI accelerator layer powering the next wave of AI.
  • In a recent development, android and cross-platform developers—whether first- or third-party—gain instant access to KleidiAI AI performance optimizations via ExecuTorch and XNNPack.
  • Sources indicate that when we consider running Generative AI (GenAI) on mobile devices, it is easy to envision the latest flagship smartphones equipped with powerful CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With Arm’s recent SME2 announcement, the role of Arm KleidiAI is increasingly clear as Arm’s AI accelerator layer powering the next wave of AI. By embedding into widely-used Edge AI frameworks like XNNPack, MediaPipe, MNN, ONNX Runtime, and even llama.cpp, KleidiAI has delivered substantial performance improvements with no code changes required by developers. That foundation leads directly to the upcoming ExecuTorch 0.7 beta, where KleidiAI will be enabled by default—bringing automatic acceleration to devices built on the latest Arm CPU architecture, as well as a vast base of existing phones built on earlier generations.

In a recent development, android and cross-platform developers—whether first- or third-party—gain instant access to KleidiAI AI performance optimizations via ExecuTorch and XNNPack. The result? Faster model startups, lower latency, leaner memory footprints—and no integration hurdles. What previously required custom tuning is now turn-key performance, ready out of the box. This efficiency unlocks upcoming possibilities—not just for the latest high-end devices, but for a much broader range of hardware.

Sources indicate that when we consider running Generative AI (GenAI) on mobile devices, it is easy to envision the latest flagship smartphones equipped with powerful CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs. But what if we told you that GenAI experiences—like running large language models (LLMs)—can also be brought to devices that are 3, 4, or even 5 years old? Or even to the Raspberry Pi 5?

Well, this is no longer just a vision, but a practical reality. Thanks to the Arm SDOT CPU feature, which has been available in Arm CPUs since 2015.

The SDOT (Signed Dot Product) instruction, introduced in the Armv8.2 architecture and later CPUs, enables efficient dot product operations on vectors of 8-bit signed integers. The following image illustrates the behavior of one such SDOT instruction available on Arm CPUs:.

As shown above, the instruction produces four 32-bit integer outputs, each resulting from the dot product of corresponding groups of four int8 elements from the left-hand side (LHS) and right-hand side (RHS) vector registers.

In a recent development, this instruction can be utilized to accelerate matrix multiplication routines—the core computational workload behind every LLM—when using Int8 or lower-bit precision formats, such as Int4. These operations typically involve numerous dot products between individual rows of the left-hand side matrix and corresponding columns of the right-hand side matrix.

Sources indicate that the SDOT instruction is already widely supported across a diverse range of devices, opening the door for GenAI use cases to reach a significantly larger smartphone audience. As of today, Arm CPUs in approximately 3 billion Arm-based devices include this capability—enabling powerful on-device GenAI experiences for the majority of owners. In fact, 72% of all devices now support this instruction.

Thanks to ExecuTorch, we are now enabling models like Llama 3.2 to run efficiently on the majority of Android devices as well as edge devices like the Raspberry Pi 5.

For the quantized Llama 3.2 1B announcement last year, the ExecuTorch and KleidiAI teams collaborated to deliver optimizations for the Int4 matrix-multiplication on Arm CPUs leveraging the I8MM feature, available from the Armv8.6 architecture onwards. As highlighted in a previous blog post, ExecuTorch with KleidiAI achieves over 20% higher prefill performance on the Galaxy S24+ compared to non-KleidiAI kernels.

Sources indicate that this translates to more than 350 tokens per second during the prefill phase and over 40 tokens per second during the decode phase. This level of performance is sufficient to enable on-device tasks, such as summarizing unread messages, with a smooth user experience using only Arm CPUs. For context, summarizing around 50 unread messages typically involves processing approximately 600 tokens.

This year, the ExecuTorch and KleidiAI teams have focused on optimizing Int4 matrix multiplication performance by leveraging the SDOT instruction, aiming to broaden adoption.

Check out the XNNPack PR on GitHub.

While LLM performance on Arm CPUs with only the SDOT extension may not match the latest flagship smartphones, it still enables impressive capabilities for on-device generative AI. In fact, in many scenarios, the decode phase is faster than the average human reading speed—highlighting that even older Arm CPUs can support practical and meaningful GenAI use cases.

Recent findings suggest that for example, when combined with speech-to-text and text-to-speech models, a local LLM of this kind enables the creation of a fully private smart assistant that operates entirely offline, eliminating concerns about data privacy while still offering rich voice-based interactions. Such a device could seamlessly interact with your connected devices, ensuring users have peace of mind with their data.

It has been revealed that another compelling use case for running Llama 3.2 1B is context-aware text completion in local text editors. As you type, the model provides intelligent, real-time suggestions to streamline writing or coding workflows—all without requiring an internet connection.

These are just a few examples, and they only scratch the surface of what is possible with on-device GenAI.

With the combined power of SDOT, KleidiAI, and ExecuTorch, we are pushing the boundaries of what is possible. Bringing Generative AI beyond high-end flagship devices and making it accessible on billions of Arm-based devices already in use.

Now it is your turn—we are excited to see what you will create. To help you get started, check out Arm’s learning path, designed to guide you through developing your own applications with LLMs using ExecuTorch and KleidiAI.
