Sending a document for signature is the easy part of an e-signature integration. One POST request and the signer gets an email. The work that actually breaks in production happens afterwards: knowing when the document was signed, trusting the notification that told you so, handling the same notification twice, and getting the final PDF into storage before the download link expires.

In a recent development, this tutorial builds that whole loop in Node.js with Express. An event in your app (a deal is approved, a client is onboarded, a task moves to "ready to sign") sends a contract from a template. When the signer finishes, a webhook arrives, your server verifies it, and the signed PDF plus its audit trail get saved without anyone touching them.

The code uses Firma.dev, the e-signature API I work on, because I needed a real API to make the examples runnable. The patterns are not specific to it, though. Signature verification, idempotent handlers, short-lived download URLs, and reconciliation jobs show up in almost every webhook-driven integration, and the same structure applies whether you're receiving events from a payment processor, a CI system, or another signing provider.

There's a fifth part that tutorials usually skip: a reconciliation job that catches anything the webhooks missed. We'll build that too, because webhooks are a notification mechanism, not a delivery guarantee.

Set three environment variables:.

Industry observers note that before sending anything, wrap the HTTP calls in one place. This is where authentication lives, and it's also where you handle 429 Too Many Requests once instead of in every caller. Most APIs, this one included, return a Retry-After header on a 429, so the client should honour it rather than guessing a backoff.

The 503 branch matters later. When a document has just been completed, the final PDF and its completion certificate take a moment to generate, and the download endpoint says so with a 503 and a Retry-After instead of handing you a half-built file.

Sources indicate that the trigger depends on your product. It might be a route handler, a queue consumer, or a CRM automation calling into your service. What matters is that the function doing the sending is small and takes plain data:.

Two design choices are worth calling out.

Use a single create-and-send call when you can. Many signing APIs split this into "create a draft" and "send the draft." That's useful when a human needs to review the document first, but for automation it creates a window where your process can crash between the two calls and leave an orphaned draft. A combined endpoint makes the operation atomic from your side.

Store the provider's ID on your own record immediately. Webhook payloads reference the signing request, not your deal or customer. Without that mapping you'll end up searching by email address, which falls apart as soon as one client signs two documents.

Sources indicate that here's the first place integrations quietly go wrong. Webhook signatures are computed over the exact bytes the sender transmitted. If Express parses the body as JSON first, you lose those bytes, and re-serialising the object won't reproduce them (key order, whitespace, and number formatting can all change). Signature checks then fail intermittently, which is the worst kind of failure.

The fix is to use express.raw() on the webhook route only, so the handler receives a Buffer:.

In a recent development, most webhook providers sign payloads with HMAC-SHA256 using a shared secret. The details vary, so read your provider's docs for the exact header format, but the scheme here is common: the header looks like t=1731456000,v1=5f2b..., and the signed string is the timestamp, a dot, and the raw body. Stripe uses a very similar format, and the Standard Webhooks spec describes the same idea as a vendor-neutral convention.

Each line here defends against something specific.

The OWASP guidance on cryptographic storage covers the other half of this: the secret belongs in an environment variable or secrets manager, never in the repository.

Sources indicate that every serious webhook system delivers at least once, not exactly once. If your endpoint is slow, returns a 5xx, or the network drops the response, the sender retries. Firma.dev, for example, makes up to three attempts per event (immediately, then after at least five minutes, then after at least an hour) and treats anything other than a 2xx as a failure, including redirects. Other providers retry more aggressively. Either way, your handler will eventually see the same event twice.

Industry observers note that the defence is to record each event's unique ID and skip ones you've seen. In the server above that's alreadyProcessed and markProcessed. For a demo, a Set works:.

In production, use your database and let a unique constraint do the work, so two concurrent deliveries can't both pass the check:.

Also notice the order in the route: respond with 200, then do the work. Many providers time out deliveries after a few seconds (five, in this case). Downloading a PDF and uploading it to object storage can easily take longer than that, and a timeout counts as a failure, which triggers a retry, which triggers duplicate work. Acknowledging fast and processing asynchronously avoids that loop.

According to recent reports, setImmediate is fine for a tutorial, but it has a real weakness: if the process dies after sending the 200 and before finishing the work, the event is acknowledged and lost. In production, push the event onto a durable queue (BullMQ, SQS, a jobs table) before responding. Step 7 covers the safety net for whatever still slips through.

Now the actual business logic. You'll usually see several event types (sent, viewed, a signer signed, declined, expired, completed). Only one of them means "the document is final":.

Three things in here are easy to get wrong.

Don't treat "a signer signed" as "the document is done." With multiple signers, each one triggers its own event, and a per-signer "all complete" flag can be true on more than one of them. Key your storage logic off the single completion event.

Don't persist the download URL. Pre-signed URLs expire (this one carries an expires_at). Saving the link to your database and serving it to owners later produces broken links a few minutes or hours later. Download the bytes and store them in storage you control. Swapping the fs.writeFile calls for an S3 PutObject or a Google Drive upload is a drop-in change.

Store the audit trail, not just the PDF. If a signature is ever disputed, the PDF reveals what was signed, and the audit trail shows who signed it, when, and from where (timestamps, IP addresses, the sequence of views and signatures). That evidence is what makes an electronic signature defensible, which brings us to the legal side.

Retries are finite. Endpoints go down during deploys. Some providers auto-disable a webhook after enough consecutive failures, and events aren't guaranteed to arrive in order. Any one of these can leave a completed document sitting unsaved.

A small scheduled job closes that gap. Keep a list of signing requests your app considers "pending," and periodically ask the API for their real status:.

Since storeSignedDocument overwrites by ID, running it twice for the same document is harmless. That's the property you want from every step in a webhook pipeline: doing it again shouldn't change the result.

None of this is legal advice, but a few facts shape how you build.

In a recent development, in the US, the ESIGN Act and the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (adopted by 49 states) give electronic signatures the same legal standing as handwritten ones for most commercial documents. ESIGN also has requirements around consumer consent and record retention, which is part of why you store the final PDF yourself rather than relying on a third-party link.

In the EU, eIDAS defines three levels: simple (SES), advanced (AdES), and qualified (QES). SES and AdES cover most business contracts. QES requires a qualified trust service provider and certificate-based identity, and some documents (certain property transfers and court filings, depending on the country) require it or exclude e-signatures entirely. Check which level your document types need before you pick a provider, since not every API offers every level.

Industry observers note that across jurisdictions, the evidence that holds up is the same: who signed, how they were identified, when it happened, and proof the document hasn't changed since. That's the audit trail and the completion certificate, which is why Step 6 stores both.

If you're evaluating providers for a workflow like this, the questions that matter at the integration level are mostly not on the pricing page:.

In a recent development, the send call is one line. The reliability comes from everything around it: keeping the raw body for verification, checking timestamps and comparing in constant time, acknowledging fast and deduplicating by event ID, downloading files before their links expire, and running a reconciliation job for the events that never arrive. Get those right and contract signing becomes something your app does in the background, with no one chasing signatures or copying PDFs between folders.

For the Firma.dev-specific details used here (event names, header format, rate limits), see the webhooks guide.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Nest app is officially dead, but it’s worth taking a step back and remembering that, while there are some rough edges, the Google Home app is a better smart home experience than Nest alone ever could have been.

The Nest app has been on life support for years now. Google has been migrating legacy products into the Home app for a while and the last few puzzle pieces came in Nest Protect support, the death of the earliest Nest Thermostats, and other assorted adjustments.

Realistically, even long-time Nest consumers have had no reason to continue using the app over Google Home.

According to recent reports, having been personally, deeply invested in Google’s vision for the smart home over the past decade, I’ll say that the Google Home app we have today is better than the Nest app ever was or ever could be. A huge part of that comes from Google Home’s ability to pull together devices from third-party ecosystems. Being able to control your entire smart home from a single app is how the smart home always should have been, and between Google’s work and the Matter standard, we’re finally able to enjoy that pretty seamlessly for the most part. Automations, Google’s actually-useful AI features, and more only sweeten the deal. I’m also a big fan of what the Home app has become from a UX perspective. While there are always rough edges and bugs to clean up, the customizable homepage and well-organized sections make for a good – not perfect, but good – experience for the end user.

That mentioned, there is one thing that the Nest app’s limited scope benefitted from, and that’s a focus on making your own product great.

Sources indicate that google’s move to the Home app for Nest devices has been a 5-year run of trying to clean things up, improve on the app, and basically bring back the way things were in the Nest app as far as the first-party cameras and thermostats are concerned. It’s taken ages, but we’re finally up to speed, mostly. I still hate that you have to reset Nest Cams to change Wi-Fi when the Nest app just let you change it, and the Nest app’s settings were much less overwhelming, but I’d say the pros far outweigh the cons at this point.

The Nest app was good at its job, but the Google Home app is a worthy successor, finally, and now the Nest app can finally rest. I mostly think the same applies to Gemini vs Google Assistant, with the newer assistant a better overall experience, but it’s easier to poke holes in that argument.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that nintendo raised the price of the Switch 2 earlier this year in response to rising NAND and DRAM prices, but on Black Friday, you can wipe out that hike with a variety of bundles available on Amazon. The core deal is the Mario Kart World Switch 2 bundle, which includes the game, the console, and three months of Nintendo Switch Online. It normally sells for $550, but Amazon has it marked down by $50, bringing the bundle down to its original price of $499.

Amazon is extending that sale to a variety of bundles it has available. You can pick up the kit alongside a Switch 2 Pro Controller, the fresh Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake, or a microSD Express card with the same discount. Note that with the base Mario Kart World bundle, the game is included as a redeemable code, not a physical cartridge.

This bundle includes the Nintendo Switch 2 console, a code for Mario Kart World, and three months of a Nintendo Switch Online Individual membership.

As you can read about in our Nintendo Switch 2 review published last year, the console is a major upgrade over the original version. The heart of the handheld is a custom Nvidia SoC that includes eight Arm Cortex-A78C CPU cores alongside an Nvidia GPU with 1,536 CUDA cores, hailing from the firm's Ampere generation. Alongside the SoC, the handheld sports 12GB of LPDDR5X memory along with 256GB of storage.

According to recent reports, showing off the capabilities of these upgraded internals is a larger 7.9-inch, 1080p LCD display. It's larger and brighter than the original Switch display, but it also comes with far greater capabilities, including variable refresh rate, HDR10 support, and a 120 Hz panel.

Sources indicate that the handheld is much larger overall, and it sports a redesigned Joy-Con mechanism that's far more resilient than the original Switch design. The kickstand more closely aligns with the Switch OLED, running along most of the edge of the display; the original Switch props up the console on one side, where it can easily fall over.

Overall, the performance jump is what stands out most. Nintendo has released several Switch 2 updates for flagship titles like Metroid Prime 4 and The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom with support for higher resolutions and frame rates. Titles like the recent Ocarina of Time Remake and Donkey Kong Bananza target 60 FPS, though occasionally fall short of that mark.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • We are happy to introduce kimina-prover-rl, an open-source training pipeline for formal theorem proving in Lean 4, based on a structured reasoning-then-generation paradigm inspired by DeepSeek-R1.
  • This training pipelinee is a simplified version of the system we used to train Kimina Prover, preserving the key components of the system and offering full compatibility with the open-source Verl framework.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A slimmed-down training pipeline from Kimina Prover, with core features and full compatibility with verl.

We are happy to introduce kimina-prover-rl, an open-source training pipeline for formal theorem proving in Lean 4, based on a structured reasoning-then-generation paradigm inspired by DeepSeek-R1.

This training pipelinee is a simplified version of the system we used to train Kimina Prover, preserving the key components of the system and offering full compatibility with the open-source Verl framework.

It is released as part of a fork of Verl containing the complete training recipe in recipe/kimina-prover-rl, allowing anyone to reproduce our experiments or adapt the setup to their own models and datasets. All information to setup and launch the pipeline can be found in the README of the recipe.

As a result of this training pipeline, we are releasing two models:.

kimina-prover-rl is a training pipeline designed to teach large language models to solve formal proof goals in Lean 4, using a two-stage output structure: a natural language reasoning trace followed by corresponding Lean code.

This paradigm, inspired by DeepSeek-R1, enables the model to separate planning from execution, promoting explainability, error recovery, and stronger generalization.

To train models under this reasoning framework, we apply GRPO — a reinforcement learning approach tailored for LLMs. This open-source version of the training pipeline of Kimina-prover is implemented using the RL library Verl.

According to recent reports, during the rollout phase of GRPO, the model generates N outputs for each prompt. A reward of 1 is assigned to any output whose Lean code is successfully verified by Lean using our kimina-lean-server.

Two main features are added to this framework:.

During training, a large number of Lean 4 proof candidates must be verified simultaneously. To handle this efficiently, we require a high-throughput verification system.

To meet this need, Numina and Kimi have developed an open-source server called kimina-lean-server, which supports parallel proof checking at scale using Lean 4.

To simplify integration, we also provide kimina-client, a lightweight Python package (available on PyPI) that offers a clean interface for interacting with the server’s API.

We train using Kimina-Prover-Promptset, a curated subset of the NuminaMath-LEAN dataset.

For this training setup, we filter and preprocess the dataset as follows:.

The resulting dataset contains challenging, high-value problems for improving Lean 4 theorem proving models.

NuminaMath-LEAN-RL is also the dataset used to train AI-MO/Kimina-Prover-RL-1.7B and AI-MO/Kimina-Prover-RL-0.6B.

The core idea of our reasoning training pipeline is to structure the LLM output into two stages. One thinking block followed by one lean4 block:.

Each rollout is verified to ensure that this format is respected. If the output is malformed — e.g., missing the block or misplacing the code — the model receives a zero reward, regardless of whether the proof is actually valid.

This enforces consistency and teaches the model to structure its outputs reliably.

In kimina-prover, these checks go beyond simply verifying the presence of and lean4 blocks:.

Only generations that pass all these checks are considered well-formatted and can receive a reward. This structured filtering improves training stability and encourages clean reasoning.

To make training more informative, we have added an error correction mechanism that gives the model a chance to fix its own failed proofs.

When a rollout fails (e.g., due to a Lean error or incorrect proof), we:.

This encourages the model to learn from failure signals as lean feedback is provided during the training.

It also enables multi-turn interaction chains, where feedback from Lean is injected as part of the prompt, and the model is rewarded for successfully debugging its own output.

Because multi-turn responses can get long, we allow only one error-fix turn and cap the error message at a set number of tokens.

The work Understanding R1-Zero-Like Training: A Critical Perspective claims there's optimization bias in GRPO, that leads to artificially longer responses, especially for incorrect outputs.

Recent findings suggest that we also noticed this behaviour during our experimentations and we used DrGPO for our optimization. DrGRPO aggregates token-level losses by normalizing with a global constant to eliminate length bias.

The configuration file provided in the repository is for a 8 GPUs setup.

In a recent development, the model that we are finetunning is the AI-MO/Kimina-Prover-Distill-1.7B. This model is a finetuned version of Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B with cold start data generated from our AI-MO/Kimina-Prover-72B model.

It has been revealed that at every step, 256 samples are fetched in the training dataset. One out of two is an error correction sample. We generate 8 rollout per samples so 2048 generations. You can increase to 16 or 32 rollouts if you are using more than one node.

According to recent reports, we evaluate the model every 5 training steps, using the best@8 metric from verl to have fast validation steps. You can increase to best@16 or 32 if you are using more than one node. We are evaluating the performance before and the after the error correction turn. For each failed reponse we allow the model to do one more tentative to fix its proof.

After a few training steps, we observe a consistent improvement in performance. In this section we will discuss the training metrics after 48 hours of training on 8 H100 GPUs.

By step 85, the pipeline improves the model's accuracy by 4 points, reaching 70% for the best@8 metric and 74% after the error correction turn:.

In parallel, we observe that the number of format errors steadily decreases over the course of training, indicating that the model is learning to produce structurally valid outputs.

Finally, and as expected under the DeepSeek-R1-style training setup, the average token length of the model’s outputs increases with training — a signal that the model is learning to reason in longer, more structured traces.

According to recent reports, after the training, we evaluated the model using pass@32 with and without error fixing. We were able to improve the performances of our 1.7B model by more than 3% at pass@32 on MiniF2F:.

Using this training pipeline we also finetuned a 0.6B model, improving its performances by more than 2%.

With Kimina-Prover-RL, we provide a lightweight yet powerful reinforcement learning pipeline for training Lean 4 theorem provers.

By combining structured reasoning, format rewards, and error correction, we achieve state-of-the-art results for open-source models in the 0.6B–1.7B parameter range.

Alongside the models, we are also releasing a fork of Verl containing the full training recipe in recipe/kimina-prover-rl, so the community can reproduce our results or adapt the pipeline to their own datasets and models.

We hope this release will serve as a solid foundation for the community to experiment with RL training in formal reasoning, and to push the limits of open-source automated theorem proving in Lean 4.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Steadfast is a new Ruby project that aims to provide a new way to dynamically generate Ruby code at runtime by synthesizing and manipulating ASTs, as an alternative to the common technique of calling eval with a dynamically generated string containing Ruby source code.

In the last Steadfast update I discussed the foundations of the project, its general API design, and my work on implementing the basic capacity of turning ASTs back to source code (using Steadfast.to_source), as well as providing some facilities for translating backtrace locations for code derived from AST that were composed of pieces of code from different locations.

Over the last few days, I’ve concentrated on implementing the ability to transform an existing AST by replacing specific nodes therein. Previously, I called this “mutating” an AST, but actually I realized this term might be confusing, since Prism ASTs are inherently immutable, that is, they cannot be modified. Instead, you need to create a copy of an AST node with the requisite changes, so using the verb “mutate” is in fact incorrect. So henceforth I’ll use the term “rewrite” instead, which seems more fitting, since we’re basically taking existing code and rewriting it.

Industry observers note that so, if Prism nodes are immutable, how can we rewrite them? Basically, Prism lets us create a copy of a given node, with specific attributes assigned newly introduced values:.

Now, there are some interesting nuances to this, because Prism nodes basically have three different kinds of attributes:.

In a recent development, that last group of node attributes, locations, is actually what Steadfast uses in order to convert a given AST back to a string containing Ruby code. So, if we want to rewrite a given node, we can’t just create a copy of it with its plain value attributes changed. For example, if we have a method call foo, which we want to change to bar, we can’t just rewrite the corresponding CallNode with a modified name attribute, because the location attribute for this (called message_loc) will still point to the original source code containing the string foo. We actually need to replace the CallNode with a another CallNode that actually represents a call to bar.

In the above example, we acquire the lambda AST, then we get its body, create a copy of it containing the synthesized call to bar, and create a copy of the original AST, with the rewritten body.

As you can see, this is not very convenient. We need to reach into the AST to extract the body of the lambda, which is a StatementsNode, and we then need to inject the replacement method call into it. Once the body is rewritten, we need to create a copy of the lambda node itself, so it will point to the new body.

In the above example, we just needed to touch the body node, which is a subnode of the lambda root node, but in other cases we might need to drill down and make changes to some subnodes that are nested a lot deeper in the AST, which means that for any node that was replaced, we also need to replace all its parent nodes.

In a recent development, so this is what I set out to solve with Steadfast.rewrite. The implementation is quite simple: for any modification (rewrite) of a subnode, we automatically create modified copies of all its parent right up to the root. That’s why Steadfast.rewrite trakes an AST as its first argument, and returns a rewritten AST as its return value.

Industry observers note that the method above extracts the AST for the given method, separates the method body into a body (containing all statements but the tail), and a tail which references the last statement. We then synthesize a loop node containing the body and the converted tail, and call Steadfast.rewrite to replace the original body with the loop. Finally, we call eval with the rewritten source code, which effectively redefines the method. Here’s how we make the loop node:.

Industry observers note that we synthesize a call to loop, and then use Steadfast.rewrite to inject the given list of statements into its body. To convert the tail call, we use a similar technique:.

We synthesize a multi-write node (representing assignment to multiple local variables) with the given variable names, and we use Steadfast.rewrite to inject the tail call arguments into the assignment as an array.

This does not really exist in Ruby, though you can use the somewhat unwieldy syntax .then { ... }. While method chaining is quite useful for many kinds of computations, sometimes you wish you had something like a pipe operator in Ruby, the idea being that at each step of the pipe, we inject the last return value as the first argument to the next method call. What if we could do something like the following:.

Interestingly, the AST representation of the code will have the call to pow at the top of the AST (that is, on the outside), with the preceding calls being expressed as the receiver of that method call, something like the following:.

We need to be able to transform this syntax into a sequence of method calls where the result of each method call is injected as an argument into the next one.

The rewrite operation we need to do is to flip the receiver and the argument for each call to >>, such that the argument becomes the method call, and the receiver is injected as an additional first argument into that method call, in order to achieve the following:.

Here again, we can use Steadfast.rewrite to do just that:.

Sources indicate that in this example, instead of providing Steadfast.rewrite with a list of specific node replacements, we give it a block that is invoked for each node in the AST. The block should return either a replacement node, or the original node, in which case no replacement is made.

It has been revealed that in the rewriter block, we filter out anything that is not a call to >> (since in Ruby, binary operators are actually method calls). Notice how we use next n to tell Steadfast.rewrite that no replacement is made and that we want to continue visiting other nodes. We then extract the call_node to the right of the >> operator (its argument), and replace the operator call with this call node, with its arguments rewritten so as to inject the value to the left of the operator into the call.

In a recent development, notice how we recursively call Steadfast.rewrite(n.receiver, &r). In order to make it possible for us to recurse inside the block, Steadfast.rewrite yields, along with the node, a reference to the block itself, which lets us call Steadfast.rewrite recursively with the same block. This technique is interesting in and of itself, and is quite useful as you can see, since working with ASTs is inherently recursive.

Pipe operator syntax transformation and tail call optimization are but two possible applications of AST rewriting, but Steadfast.rewrite can also be used for inlining method calls, and more generally, for such things as wrapping code in a loop, or in a begin/rescue block, unrolling loops, injecting arguments into method calls… the possibilities are endless!

In the upcoming stages of this project, I’ll use Steadfast.rewrite to implement the code quoting tool (aka quote/unquote), as well as for synthesizing different kinds of AST nodes.

In a recent development, the Steadfast.rewrite implementation is surprisigingly succint, about 35LOC. At the heart of it is the following method that visits each node in the AST:.

It has been revealed that we start the visit by invoking the rewrite block with the given node. If a replacement node was returned by the block, we return it immediately. Otherwise, we dive into the node attributes (using deconstruct_keys), and visit each subnode, or array of subnodes. If any replacements were returned for any of the attributes, we make a copy of the node with the relevant changes. Thus we ensure that any replacement to a nested node will result in its parent being replaced as well, all the way up to the root of the AST.

The Samsung Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 is worth spending more on if you want longer battery life, a brighter outdoor display, and specialized features for trail running and diving. The Galaxy Watch 9 is the better fit if you want Samsung’s latest everyday health tools in a smaller, lighter watch.

Both, however, are fantastic smartwatches with limitless potential. They share a Snapdragon Wear Elite processor and many of Samsung’s newest wellness features, so deciding between them is really about figuring out your priorities when it comes to buying a wearable this holiday season. We’re here to help you figure that out.

This post is sponsored by Samsung.

As we covered in our Galaxy Watch 9 and Watch Ultra 2 comparison, both watches move to Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Wear Elite platform. Both also ship with Wear OS 7 and One UI 8 Watch.

It has been revealed that that shared foundation includes useful health insights. Vitals brings overnight measurements together to establish your personal baseline, while Daily Cardio Load helps you understand training demands and recovery. Hearing monitoring can flag potentially unsafe noise levels, whether you’re at a concert or somewhere unexpectedly loud.

Both also get five years of Wear OS updates and security patches, making either a useful long-term partner for your Samsung device, like the Galaxy S26 Ultra or Galaxy Z Fold8.

Recent findings suggest that the clearest differences are size, battery capacity, display brightness, and outdoor capabilities. Here’s how the lineup breaks down:.

As you can tell, the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 is considerably bigger and heavier, but you get a lot more capability for that additional size.

The Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 makes its strongest case when your plans regularly take you beyond a desk, a gym, or a charger.

Samsung rates the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 for up to 60 hours with the always-on display enabled, compared with up to 30 hours for the Watch 9, and that extra headroom is appealing when your day starts with a workout and finishes well into the evening.

Then there’s the screen. In our hands-on with both watches, the Ultra 2’s brightness stood out immediately, with a higher peak that gives it an advantage when checking workout information outdoors, even in the bright sun. And its titanium frame provides added durability.

The Ultra 2 also adds Trail Run tracking for elevation and terrain impact, route guidance using compatible GPX files, and Nutrition Alert hydration guidance. These are tangible reasons to upgrade if your usual run involves trails instead of pavement.

Sources indicate that diving is another differentiator. Samsung specifies recreational diving support to depths of up to 40 meters, with automatic tracking of depth, dive time and water temperature — a remarkable feat for a piece of technology that lives on your wrist.

The best choice becomes clearer when you picture your own routine:.

Choose the Galaxy Watch 9 for everyday wellness, a lighter fit, and strong value. Choose the Galaxy Watch Ultra 2 for longer adventures, more demanding outdoor activities, and greater freedom between charges.

In a recent development, if you’re replacing an older Galaxy Watch, both offer a compelling fresh generation of health insights and long-term support. Both last a long time and look absolutely awesome with running shorts or a business suit. But the Watch Ultra 2 can take you that extra mile, literally and figuratively, and may be worth spending more on during Best Buy’s Holiday Deals event.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that academic research involves frequent research discovery: finding papers, code, related models and datasets. This typically means switching between platforms like arXiv, GitHub, and Hugging Face, manually piecing together connections.

In a recent development, the Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a standard that allows agentic models to communicate with external tools and data sources. For research discovery, this means AI can use research tools through natural language requests, automating platform switching and cross-referencing.

Much like software development, research discovery can be framed in terms of layers of abstraction.

At the lowest level of abstraction, researchers search manually and cross-reference by hand.

According to recent reports, this manual approach becomes inefficient when tracking multiple research threads or conducting systematic literature reviews. The repetitive nature of searching across platforms, extracting metadata, and cross-referencing information naturally leads to automation through scripting.

Python scripts automate research discovery by handling web requests, parsing responses, and organizing results.

The research tracker demonstrates systematic research discovery built from these types of scripts.

While scripts are faster than manual research, they often fail to automatically collect data due to changing APIs, rate limits, or parsing errors. Without human oversight, scripts may miss relevant results or return incomplete information.

MCP makes these same Python tools accessible to AI systems through natural language.

The AI orchestrates multiple tools, fills information gaps, and reasons about results:.

This can be viewed as an additional layer of abstraction above scripting, where the "programming language" is natural language. This follows the Software 3.0 Analogy, where the natural language research direction is the software implementation.

This comes with the same caveats as scripting:.

The easiest way to add the Research Tracker MCP is through Hugging Face MCP Settings:.

Recent findings suggest that this workflow leverages the Hugging Face MCP server, which is the standard way to use Hugging Face Spaces as MCP tools. The settings page provides client-specific configuration that's automatically generated and always up-to-date.

According to recent reports, ready to automate your research discovery? Try the Research Tracker MCP or build your own research tools with the resources above.

I might be biased:https://github.com/mixelpixx/Google-Search-MCP-Server.

This is a really interesting explanation of how MCP can simplify research discovery. I particularly liked the progression from manual research to scripted tools and finally MCP integration, because it clearly demonstrates how AI agents can coordinate multiple tools instead of relying on separate manual searches. The ability to discover papers, locate related code, and cross-reference models and datasets through natural language is especially useful. I think this approach has great potential beyond research as well, particularly for businesses looking to connect their internal applications and external services with AI agents. A well-designed custom MCP server architecture and reliable MCP server integration can make these workflows more scalable and secure. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Windows 7 may have been retired years ago, but that hasn’t stopped enthusiasts from finding ways to bring modern hardware and features to Microsoft’s beloved operating system.
  • Developed by enthusiasts EAZY BLACK, kryptik, and VisualEhrmanntraut, the project backports WDDM 2.2 from Windows 10.
  • It has been revealed that according to a post by @TheBobPony on X, Nvidia's RTX 40 and RTX 50 series, AMD's Radeon RX 7000 and RX 9000 series, and select Intel Arc graphics cards are supported.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Windows 7 may have been retired years ago, but that hasn’t stopped enthusiasts from finding ways to bring modern hardware and features to Microsoft’s beloved operating system. A new community project is now giving Windows 7 the ability to support modern Nvidia, AMD, and Intel graphics cards, along with DirectX 12 and Vulkan 1.4 capabilities.

Developed by enthusiasts EAZY BLACK, kryptik, and VisualEhrmanntraut, the project backports WDDM 2.2 from Windows 10. Interestingly, Windows 7 originally launched with WDDM 1.1, while Microsoft introduced WDDM 2.0 with Windows 10 in 2015 and WDDM 2.2 with the Creators Enhancement in 2017. Microsoft also introduced a limited version of DirectX 12 for Windows 7 in 2019; however, that implementation was only meant for developers to port select games to the older operating system.

It has been revealed that according to a post by @TheBobPony on X, Nvidia's RTX 40 and RTX 50 series, AMD's Radeon RX 7000 and RX 9000 series, and select Intel Arc graphics cards are supported. Screenshots confirm that the backport enables GPUs to be recognized by Windows 7 as well as third-party apps like GPU-Z. It is also claimed that features such as ray tracing and DLSS also work on compatible hardware. Older GPUs, including Nvidia's RTX 30 series and AMD's Radeon RX 6000 series, may also benefit from the project. That said, actual feature support depends on the graphics card, driver implementation, and application.

According to recent reports, for anyone who still prefers Windows 7 or relies on older software and hardware, this project is worth exploring, especially if you intend to extend the usefulness of the operating system. Customers can also combine it with the VxKex compatibility layer, allowing newer Windows apps to run on older operating systems. You can grab the project files and modified drivers by heading to the W7Revived website.

There’s a reason why enthusiasts continue to keep Windows 7 alive. Released in 2009 as a successor to Windows Vista, it offered a familiar interface, solid performance, and a straightforward desktop experience. It became one of Microsoft’s most popular operating systems and remained a favorite among PC enthusiasts and everyday people long after the arrival of Windows 10.

In fact, Windows 7 still has some life left in it. We recently tested the aging operating system against Windows 11 on a modern PC running on an AMD Ryzen 7 9800X3D, Radeon RX 6950 XT, and 64GB of DDR5 memory. The tests included eight DirectX 11 and two DirectX 9 titles, with Windows 7 delivering better performance in certain scenarios, particularly CPU-bound games, along with stronger 1% lows in some titles.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google this weekend rolled out the latest patch to Pixel Weather with a new reporting feature and small interface tweaks.

On the homepage, cities that have active weather warnings no longer have bright red card backgrounds. The pill-shaped container retains its Dynamic Color theming with just the text of the warning in red. This change also extends to the card on the city page. Finally, the source, like “Google Weather,” at the very bottom is now themed.

The main change today is a “Report current weather” feature to “Share the current weather condition to improve local forecasts.” The card appears at the very bottom of your current location and can be moved up the feed.

Google states to “Submit a report if the weather conditions don’t look right.” Tapping “Submit a report” brings up a “Report weather in [city]” sheet. You can submit two pieces of information:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We have revamped the Kernels project since the publication of this post. Check out the updates here.

Recent findings suggest that custom CUDA kernels give your models a serious performance edge, but building them for the real world can feel daunting. How do you move beyond a simple GPU function to create a robust, scalable system without getting bogged down by endless build times and dependency nightmares?

It has been revealed that we created the kernel-builder library for this purpose. You can develop a custom kernel locally, and then build it for multiple architectures and make it available for the world to use.

In this guide we'll show you how to build a complete, modern CUDA kernel from the ground up. Then, we’ll tackle the tough production and deployment challenges, drawing on real-world engineering strategies to show you how to build systems that are not just fast, but also efficient and maintainable.

When you're done, other developers will be able to use your kernels directly from the hub like this:.

Rather watch a video? Check out the YouTube video that accompanies this guide.

Let's build a practical kernel that converts an image from RGB to grayscale. This example uses PyTorch's modern C++ API to register our function as a first-class, native operator.

It has been revealed that A clean, predictable structure is the foundation of a good project. The Hugging Face Kernel Builder expects your files to be organized like this:.

Industry observers note that this file orchestrates the entire build. It tells the kernel-builder what to compile and how everything connects.

To ensure anyone can build your kernel on any machine, we use a flake.nix file. It locks the exact version of the kernel-builder and its dependencies, eliminating "it works on my machine" challenges.

In a recent development, now for the GPU code. Inside csrc/img2gray.cu, we'll define a kernel that uses a 2D grid of threads—a natural and efficient fit for processing images.

In a recent development, this is the most notable step. We're not just binding to Python; we're registering our function as a native PyTorch operator. This makes it a first-class citizen in the PyTorch ecosystem, visible under the torch.ops namespace.

The file torch-ext/torch_binding.cpp handles this registration.

In simple terms, TORCH_LIBRARY_EXPAND allows us to define our operator in a way that can be easily extended or modified in the future.

This approach is crucial for two main reasons:.

It has been revealed that compatibility with torch.compile: By registering our kernel this way, torch.compile can "see" it. This allows PyTorch to fuse your custom operator into larger computation graphs, minimizing overhead and maximizing performance. It's the key to making your custom code work seamlessly with PyTorch's broader performance ecosystem.

Hardware-Specific Implementations: This system allows you to provide different backends for the same operator. You could add another TORCH_LIBRARY_IMPL(img2gray, CPU, ...) block pointing to a C++ CPU function. PyTorch's dispatcher would then automatically call the correct implementation (CUDA or CPU) based on the input tensor's device, making your code powerful and portable.

Setting up the __init__.py wrapper.

In torch-ext/img2gray/ we need an __init__.py file to make this directory a Python package and to expose our custom operator in a user-friendly way.

The _ops module is auto-generated by kernel-builder from a template to provide a standard namespace for your registered C++ functions.

Now that our kernel and its bindings are ready, it's time to build them. The kernel-builder tool simplifies this process.

You can build your kernel with a single command, nix build . -L; however, as developers, we'll want a faster, more iterative workflow. For that, we'll use the nix develop command to enter a development shell with all the necessary dependencies pre-installed.

It has been revealed that more specifically, we can choose the exact CUDA and PyTorch versions we want to use. For example, to build our kernel for PyTorch 2.7 with CUDA 12.6, we can use the following command:.

Note that the devShell name above can be deciphered as:.

Recent findings suggest that at this point, we'll be inside a Nix shell with all dependencies installed. We can now build the kernel for this particular architecture and test it. Later on, we'll deal with multiple architectures before distributing the final version of the kernel.

This command creates a handful of files used to build the kernel: CMakeLists.txt, pyproject.toml, setup.py, and a cmake directory. The CMakeLists.txt file is the main entry point for CMake to build the kernel.

Now you can install the kernel in editable mode.

According to recent reports, 🙌 Amazing! We now have a custom built kernel that follows best practices for PyTorch bindings, with a fully reproducible build process.

Recent findings suggest that to ensure everything is working correctly, we can run a simple test to check that the kernel is registered and it works as expected. If it doesn't, you can iterate by editing the source files and repeating the build, reusing the nix environment you created.

Now that we have a working kernel, it's time to share it with other developers and the world!

One small thing we'll want to do before we share, is clean up all of the development artifacts that were generated during the build process to avoid uploading unnecessary files.

It has been revealed that earlier, we built the kernel for a specific version of PyTorch and CUDA. However, to make it available to a wider audience, we need to build it for all supported versions. The kernel-builder tool can help us with that.

This is also where the concept of a compliant kernel comes into play. A compliant kernel is one that can be built and run for all supported versions of PyTorch and CUDA. Generally, this requires custom configuration; however, in our case, the kernel-builder tool will automate the process.

This process may take a while, as it will build the kernel for all supported versions of PyTorch and CUDA. The output will be in the result directory.

The kernel-builder team actively maintains the supported build variants, keeping them current with the latest PyTorch and CUDA releases while also supporting trailing versions for broader compatibility.

The last step is to move the results into the expected build directory (this is where the kernels library will look for them).

According to recent reports, pushing the build artifacts to the Hub will make it straightforward for other developers to use your kernel, as we saw in our previous post. We can use the kernels upload command for this:.

Make sure you are logged in to the Hugging Face Hub using huggingface-cli login.

Now, in your project directory, connect your project to the fresh repository and push your code:.

Fantastic! Your kernel is now on the Hugging Face Hub, ready for others to use and fully compliant with the kernels library. Our kernel and all of its build variants are now available at drbh/img2gray.

Sources indicate that with the kernels library, you don't "install" the kernel in the traditional sense. You load it directly from its Hub repository, which automatically registers the new operator.

According to recent reports, once you have a ready-to-use kernel, there are some things you can do to make it easier to deploy your kernel. We will discuss using versioning as a tool to make API changes without breaking downstream use of kernels. After that, we will wrap up showing how you can make Python wheels for your kernel.

In a recent development, you might decide to update your kernel after a while. Maybe you have found new ways of improving performance or perhaps you would like to extend the kernel's functionality. Some changes will require you to change the API of your kernel. For instance, a newer version might add a new mandatory argument to one of the public functions. This can be inconvenient to downstream people, because their code would break until they add this new argument.

A downstream user of a kernel can avoid such breakage by pinning the kernel that they use to a particular revision. For instance, since each Hub repository is also a Git repository, they could use a git commit shorthash to pin the kernel to a revision:.

According to recent reports, using a Git shorthash will reduce the chance of breakage; however, it is hard to interpret and does not allow graceful upgrades within a version range. We therefore recommend using the familiar semantic versioning system for Hub kernels. Adding a version to a kernel is easy: you simply add a Git tag of the form vx.y.z where x.y.z is the version. For instance, if the current version of the kernel is 1.1.2, you can tag it as v1.1.2. You can then get that version with get_kernel:.

Versioning becomes even more powerful with version bounds. In semantic versioning, the version 1.y.z, must not have backward-incompatible changes in the public API for each succeeding x and y. So, if the kernel's version was 1.1.2 at the time of writing your code, you can ask the version to be at least 1.1.2, but less than 2.0.0:.

It has been revealed that this will ensure that the code will always fetch the latest kernel from the 1.y.z series. The version bound can be a Python-style version specifier.

You can tag a version with huggingface-cli:.

Recent findings suggest that in large projects, you may want to coordinate the kernel versions globally rather than in each get_kernel call. Moreover, it is often useful to lock kernels, so that all your customers have the same kernel versions, which aids handling bug reports.

Sources indicate that the kernels library offers a nice way of managing kernels at the project-level. To do so, add the kernels package to the build-system requirements of your project, in the pyproject.toml file. After doing so, you can specify your project's kernel requirements in the tools.kernels section:.

Industry observers note that the version can be specified with the same type of version specifiers as Python dependencies. This is another place where the version tags (va.b.c) come handy -- kernels will use a repository's version tags to query what versions are available. After specifying a kernel in pyproject.toml, you can lock it to a specific version using the kernels command-line utility. This utility is part of the kernels Python package:.

Industry observers note that this generates a kernels.lock file with the latest kernel versions that are compatible with the bounds that are specified in pyproject.toml. kernels.lock should be committed to your project's Git repository, so that every user of the project will get the locked kernel versions. When newer kernels versions are released, you can run kernels lock again to upgrade the lock file.

You need one last bit to fully implement locked kernels in a project. The get_locked_kernel is the counterpart to get_kernel that uses locked kernels. So to use locked kernels, replace every occurrence of get_kernel with get_locked_kernel:.

That's it! Every call of get_locked_kernel("drbh/img2gray") in the project will now use the version specified in kernels.lock.

Sources indicate that the get_locked_kernel function will download the kernel when it is not available in the local Hub cache. This is not ideal for applications where you do not want to download binaries at runtime. For example, when you are building a Docker image for an application, you usually want the kernels to be stored in the image along with the application. This can be done in two simple steps.

First, use the load_kernel function in place of get_locked_kernel:.

Industry observers note that as the name suggests, this function will only load a kernel, it will never try to download the kernel from the Hub. load_kernel will raise an exception if the kernel is not locally available. So, how do you make the kernels locally available? The kernels utility has you covered! Running kernels download . will download the kernels that are specified in kernels.lock. So e.g. in a Docker container you could add a step:.

and the kernels will get baked into your Docker image.

Kernels use the standard Hugging Face cache, so all HF_HOME caching rules apply.

Sources indicate that we strongly recommend downloading kernels from the Hub using the kernels package. This has many benefits:.

It has been revealed that that stated, some projects may require deployment of kernels as wheels. The kernels utility provides a simple solution to this. You can convert any Hub kernel into a set of wheels with a single command:.

Each of these wheels will behave like any other Python wheel: the kernel can be imported using a simple import img2grey.

Recent findings suggest that this guide has walked you through the entire lifecycle of a production-ready CUDA kernel. You’ve seen how to build a custom kernel from the ground up, register it as a native PyTorch operator, and share it with the community on the Hugging Face Hub. We also explored best practices for versioning, dependency management, and deployment, ensuring your work is both powerful and easy to maintain.

Recent findings suggest that we believe that open and collaborative development is the key to innovation. Now that you have the tools and knowledge to build your own high-performance kernels, we're excited to see what you create! We warmly invite you to share your work, ask questions, and start discussions on the Kernel Hub or in our mono repo for kernels and kernel-builder. Whether you’re a seasoned developer or just starting out, the community is here to support you.

A frontend application can compile successfully and still fail when it communicates with the backend.

Imagine a backend developer changes an API response from:.

The backend works correctly. The frontend also builds without errors. However, a component expecting user.name now receives undefined.

This is an example of API contract drift: the frontend and backend no longer agree on the structure or behavior of an API.

According to recent reports, the problem becomes more difficult when several developers or teams work on different parts of an application. A change made by one team may affect another team's assumptions without producing an obvious error during development.

TypeScript helps catch many programming mistakes, but its types do not automatically validate data received over HTTP. A type declaration can describe what the application expects without proving that the server actually returns it.

In this tutorial, we'll look at a practical way to make API contracts more reliable.

Consider a typical frontend API function:.

At first glance, this looks reasonable.

The function promises to return a User, so TypeScript allows the application to access properties such as name and email.

According to recent reports, the return value of response.json() is not automatically checked against the User interface. The interface only provides compile-time information; it does not validate the actual JSON received from the server.

the frontend may still treat the response as a User even though the data has a different structure.

This is particularly important when working with:.

Independently deployed frontend and backend applications.

APIs maintained by different engineering teams.

The solution is to validate data at the boundary where it enters the application.

Recent findings suggest that zod is a TypeScript-first schema validation library. It allows developers to describe expected data structures and validate actual values against those definitions.

Now create a schema for the user response:.

There are two vital parts here.

First, UserSchema describes the structure that the application expects at runtime.

Second, z.infer generates the corresponding TypeScript type from the schema.

This means developers do not need to maintain a separate interface and validation definition for the same data structure.

The response is initially treated as unknown, which prevents the application from assuming that untrusted data already has the expected structure.

UserSchema.parse() validates the actual response.

If the backend returns an unexpected property type or misses a required field, Zod throws a validation error instead of allowing invalid data to move silently through the application.

You can also use safeParse() when you prefer to handle validation errors without exceptions:.

This approach is useful when API responses are external or when a frontend must provide more controlled error handling.

One common mistake is placing API validation logic directly inside React components.

Industry observers note that for a small application, this may seem convenient. As the project grows, however, it becomes difficult to reuse validation rules and identify where data transformations happen.

A better approach is to separate API schemas, service functions, and UI components.

The responsibilities are straightforward:.

schemas/user.ts defines the expected user data.

api/client.ts handles common HTTP configuration.

api/owners.ts contains user-related API requests.

hooks/useUser.ts manages data fetching for React.

components/UserProfile.tsx displays the validated data.

This structure makes it easier to change an API implementation without rewriting the UI.

It also makes testing more manageable because validation logic can be tested independently of React rendering.

For more ideas on organizing application code, see SitePoint's guide to modern JavaScript modules.

Runtime validation protects an application when data arrives. However, teams also need a shared description of what an API is supposed to accept and return.

This is where OpenAPI becomes useful.

OpenAPI provides a standard format for describing HTTP APIs, including:.

Request and response structures.

Data types and validation constraints.

For example, an endpoint can be described using an OpenAPI document:.

This document describes what the endpoint should return.

Both frontend and backend developers can refer to the same contract instead of relying on separate assumptions or outdated documentation.

Recent findings suggest that swagger Editor helps developers write and validate OpenAPI documents. It also provides a convenient way to inspect API definitions.

Swagger UI turns an OpenAPI document into interactive API documentation, allowing developers to explore endpoints and test requests.

Redoc provides another way to generate readable API documentation from an OpenAPI specification.

These tools are particularly useful when APIs are maintained by multiple developers or consumed by several applications.

Maintaining API types manually across frontend and backend repositories creates opportunities for inconsistencies.

For example, a backend developer might add a fresh optional property while the frontend continues using an older interface.

One way to reduce this duplication is to generate TypeScript definitions and API clients from an OpenAPI specification.

Orval is a useful tool for this workflow.

It can generate TypeScript clients and types from an OpenAPI document, helping frontend developers work with consistent endpoint definitions.

A simplified workflow looks like this:.

A typical configuration might look like this:.

The exact configuration depends on the Orval version and the structure of the OpenAPI document.

Once configured, the client can be regenerated when the API specification changes.

This reduces the amount of repetitive code developers need to maintain manually.

However, generated types should not be confused with runtime validation. They improve consistency during development, but an application may still need to validate responses received from external systems or services that cannot be fully trusted.

Frontend developers often need to build or test features before the corresponding backend endpoint is ready.

Waiting for a complete backend implementation can slow down development, particularly when multiple teams work independently.

Mock Service Worker (MSW) helps solve this problem by intercepting network requests and returning controlled responses.

You can define a mock handler for the user endpoint:.

The frontend can now make normal HTTP requests while MSW supplies predictable responses during development or testing.

You can also simulate an invalid response:.

This makes it possible to check whether the application's validation and error-handling logic behave as expected.

MSW is particularly valuable because it allows frontend tests to run without requiring a live backend environment.

Runtime validation and generated clients improve reliability, but they do not automatically guarantee that independently developed services remain compatible.

For systems with multiple services, contract testing can provide another layer of protection.

Pact is a contract-testing tool that allows consumers and providers to verify their expectations about API interactions.

Consider a frontend application that expects the user endpoint to return:.

The consumer defines the expected interaction.

The backend provider can then run verification against that contract to check whether its actual response satisfies the consumer's expectations.

This helps identify breaking changes before they reach production.

In a recent development, these tools solve different problems. A project does not necessarily need all of them, but larger applications can benefit from combining the approaches that match their architecture.

A contract is only useful if developers consistently check it when making changes.

A practical approach is to run validation and tests automatically whenever someone opens a pull request.

For example, a GitHub Actions workflow might look like this:.

The api:validate script should be configured to validate the project's OpenAPI document or run the relevant contract checks.

The test command should execute the application's automated tests.

For a production project, you may also want to include:.

Generated-client consistency checks.

Consumer-provider contract verification.

The objective is to detect incompatible changes before they are merged.

A failed pipeline gives developers an opportunity to investigate the change while the context is still fresh.

API contracts become harder to maintain when several teams contribute to the same system.

For example, a manufacturer might have separate teams responsible for:.

Customer-facing frontend applications.

If nobody owns an API contract, small changes can create unexpected problems for other teams.

Assigning clear ownership helps establish who reviews changes, maintains documentation, and coordinates breaking updates.

Industry observers note that this becomes particularly important when an organization expands its engineering capacity across locations or adds several specialized teams. Companies planning that kind of growth may also need to consider enterprise IT recruitment as part of their wider engineering workforce strategy.

Regardless of how a team is assembled, its development process should establish clear responsibilities for API design, versioning, testing, and release coordination.

A few practical conventions can make a significant difference:.

Assign an owner to every notable API or service.

Document breaking changes before implementation.

Require contract-related tests in pull requests.

Keep generated clients synchronized with the API specification.

Communicate deprecations before removing existing fields.

Monitor production errors after deploying API changes.

These practices help prevent a growing engineering organization from becoming a collection of disconnected services.

Sources indicate that API contract drift is not simply a TypeScript problem. It is a coordination problem that becomes visible when applications and services develop different expectations about the same data.

TypeScript provides useful compile-time checks, but it cannot guarantee that an HTTP response matches a declared interface.

A more reliable approach combines several techniques:.

Use Zod to validate incoming data.

Use OpenAPI to document API expectations.

Generate TypeScript clients with tools such as Orval.

Use MSW to test frontend behavior without a live backend.

Use Pact when consumer-provider contract verification is appropriate.

Run validation and tests automatically in CI/CD.

Recent findings suggest that you do not need to introduce every tool at once. Start by validating external API responses, document vital endpoints, and gradually automate contract checks as the application grows.

The result is a codebase where developers can make changes with greater confidence and where frontend and backend teams have a shared understanding of how their systems communicate.

Anthropic researcher tunes chess software to turn a 200 MHz Pentium Pro into a behemoth that would handily defeat Kasparov and Carlsen

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Readers with back pain probably recall the much-discussed 1996 chess challenge, wherein the world champion Gerry Kasparov faced off against IBM's Deep Blue chess-optimized computer.
  • In a recent development, to understand the task, here's a quick primer on chess scoreboards.
  • According to recent reports, at his prime, Kasparov ranked about 2800 points.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Readers with back pain probably recall the much-discussed 1996 chess challenge, wherein the world champion Gerry Kasparov faced off against IBM's Deep Blue chess-optimized computer. The nascent clanker lost the match with a 4-2 total, but still stunned the world by being the first piece of electric sand to win a single game against a grandmaster. Modern chess engines will utterly destroy any human, but Anthropic engineer Nicholas Carlini wondered if granting old hardware new bytes would give the machine a better chance. Spoiler: yes, indeed it would.

In a recent development, to understand the task, here's a quick primer on chess scoreboards. A player is rated worldwide with an Elo system (first devised for chess), wherein they lose or gain points in proportion to the difference to their opponent's rating — meaning that winning a match against Magnus Carlsen would net you a lot of points versus defeating me, who only learned about the en passant rule a handful of years ago.

According to recent reports, at his prime, Kasparov ranked about 2800 points. Given that Deep Blue eventually barely won against him in a subsequent rematch, that is a good starting point for any. Contemporary chess engines like Stockfish have an estimated Elo of about 3,300, far higher than any human — guaranteeing it'll win most matches against a human.

Nicholas Carlini got hold of a 1995-era machine, packing a Pentium Pro CPU with all of its 200 MHz of clock speed, and 64 MB of RAM. For his first experiment, he grabbed Crafty, a 1996 chess engine, and measured how well it would do. It came in at 2,000 Elo with 1 second allotted, and 2,400 @ 10s. Running that software on a Ryzen 7 resulted in a 2,600 rating — good, but not enough.

Since Crafty's source code is available, he got Claude to mod it with modern features, and eventually reached a ceiling of 3,000 Elo @ 10s per move. That's quite an impressive feat already, especially considering that the lone Pentium Pro represented but a small fraction of the hardware that Deep Blue had. An Elo delta of +200 means this iteration would defeat Kasparov three out of every four games, while a +400 delta means a victory nine out of ten times.

Carlini then pulled out the big gun: Stockfish. He had to ask Claude to modify it to use only 32-bit arithmetic instead of 64-bit, and limit its workspace to the measly 64 MB of RAM, minus whatever the system harness took. Right off the bat, the figures were revealing: 2,500 @ 1s, and 3000 @ 10s.

The engineer performed a few optimization passes, and eventually got 2,850 @ 1s; 3,100 @ 10s; and almost 3,200 @ 30s — enough to put every human in their place, especially in a grandmaster tournament setting where there's no fixed time per move. You can play the bot using the link on the respective blog post. We'd wish you the best of luck, but there's no such concept in chess.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that folding phones are entering a newly introduced chapter and, if you’re looking to try one for the first time, you might not know exactly where to start. In this guide, we’ll take a look at some of the most notable questions to answer when buying a foldable, and dissect how Samsung’s Galaxy Z Fold 8, Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, and Galaxy Z Flip 8 fit the bill to figure out which is the best for you, especially if you’re interested in one this holiday season.

This post is sponsored by Samsung.

In a recent development, samsung has three foldables in its lineup this year, two of which are pretty familiar. The Galaxy Z Flip 8 continues the lineup of clamshell-style foldables, offering a form factor similar to that of a classic flip phone. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, meanwhile, is designed to be a normal smartphone on the outside, hiding a tablet within. Finally, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 is the fresh kid on the block, offering a compact outer display that opens up to a media-friendly, wider inner panel.

Recent findings suggest that each one serves a different need, but they all share similar performance and core specs. Here’s a quick rundown of the key details on each device:.

Starting with the displays, the book-style Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Fold 8 Ultra both provide outer displays that are fully usable as standard smartphones, while the inner display is useful for multitasking, media, or just getting more space for reading a website or e-book. Samsung’s top-tier specs deliver performance for everything you’d need, with Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy powering everything from demanding games or media-editing apps to day-to-day use.

With each Samsung foldable, you’re getting a fully capable smartphone, but finding the one that’s best for you is a matter of picking your most important priorities. Cameras, battery life, content consumption, and size are some of the most important points to consider, so let’s take a look one-by-one.

When it comes to cameras, foldables have a tough time. There’s only so much physical space to fit the camera sensors and, with cameras, having more space generally results in a battery overall camera.

That said, the best camera on a Samsung foldable is undoubtedly on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra.

The Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra has a 200MP main camera that’s similar to the Galaxy S26 Ultra, while it also packs a 50MP ultrawide and something neither of the others offer, a telephoto lens. The 10MP telephoto shooter captures faraway subjects at 3x optical zoom, meaning you’re not giving up on quality when you zoom in. Two 10MP cameras can be found on the displays, with neither sacrificing quality for an under-display look.

Runner-up here is the Galaxy Z Fold 8, which offers a pair of 50MP cameras for wide and ultrawide shots. You can get 2x optical-quality zoom out of the main sensor to still get a good zoom shot, while the main camera still offers good quality and Samsung’s best camera features including 2x optical-quality zoom and the subject-tracking My FanCam.

The Galaxy Z Flip 8 may not have the best camera hardware, but what it lacks in hardware it makes up for in flexibility. This is definitely the best form factor of the bunch for using the foldable design as a tripod for capturing clips. All three devices also use their foldable nature to let you capture full-quality selfies using the rear cameras, which always have better quality than the 10MP dedicated front-facing cameras.

Here’s where specs on paper can tell a different story compared to real life.

According to recent reports, the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra may offer the biggest battery of the bunch at 5,000 mAh, but its battery life is on par with the smaller Galaxy Z Fold 8. Both foldables are designed to last you through a full day, though sticking to the outer display only on the Fold 8 Ultra may bring you slightly better battery life overall.

Industry observers note that in either case, you’re also getting 45W fast charging over USB-C, granting you speedy recharging if your device happens to get low through the course of a busy day. These are also “Qi2 Ready,” meaning you can use magnetic wireless chargers if you use a compatible magnetic case.

One of the most notable things you’ll want to ask yourself when buying a foldable phone is why you want to opt for a foldable in the first place, and each of these devices gives a different answer.

Sources indicate that the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra is a productivity powerhouse, delivering more space on its inner display for you to get work done through the web, apps, and more. You can run up to three apps at once on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra’s display, as well as floating apps, and more.

Recent findings suggest that galaxy Z Fold 8 is great for media consumption. The wider aspect ratio is perfect for watching videos, playing games, reading books, and more, all while still giving you plenty of space for productivity just like the Ultra.

Galaxy Z Flip 8, meanwhile, is all about giving you a more compact device. The outer display lets you quickly reply to messages or keep up with directions, while you can unfold it to do everything you want to on a normal phone. Close it up to more easily stow it away in your pocket or your bag.

If you are moving into a new Galaxy foldable, the good news is that you don’t have to start from scratch. Thanks to Samsung’s Smart Switch app, you can easily transfer supported content including pictures, contacts, messages, and more from an older Galaxy phone, another Android phone, or even an iPhone over to a Galaxy foldable. Apps, messages, photos, and more can all make the move wirelessly, without the need of a cable.

You can get the Galaxy Z Fold 8, Fold 8 Ultra, and Flip 8 from your favorite carriers and retailers, but Best Buy is one of the best places to score a great deal with solid trade-in values and deep discounts around Black Friday and throughout the holiday season.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The lowest rungs of hell may be reserved for politicians, yes, but scalpers have a gated community somewhere in the same area code. The latest emotion-inducing story on this topic comes from Ontario, Canada, wherein a person from Oakville had an ad listing what appear to be over forty RTX 5090s for sale, priced at 9,500 CAD (over $6,600 USD) for the cheapest, and also having the gall to demand an extra 500 CAD (about $350 USD) for one with a sealed box.

Recent findings suggest that the magnanimous magnate wanted to perform the transactions at his nearby police station, and claimed that "testing is available." Some Canadian police stations do open their lobbies for this purpose for added public safety. The scalper mentioned in his ad that he had models from most every manufacturer, including Nvidia's Founders Edition and even Dell.

Sources indicate that should the statements by commenter "goudacheeseguy" be true, the person selling the card is their business partner. The cards purportedly came from their small neocloud outfit and are being sold as they eventually got their hands on Nvidia B300, B200, and Pro 6000 servers "with the money [they] made shorting AI funnily enough." It's possible they're telling the truth, as the presence of the Dell and Nvidia FE cards, plus the fact they're apparently mostly open-box units, would fit with that story.

Recent findings suggest that nevertheless, the response from commenters was swift and harsh. Some pointed out that the photograph depicting windows of a street-level basement, coupled with the fact that Oakville isn't that huge, could have a master geo-guesser like Rainbolt pinpointed where the scalper was.

According to recent reports, in a similar vein, other people remarked on the danger of the seller being followed home for discussing a five-finger discount. His laissez-faire attitude infuriated some commenters, as he stated that "[he has] other models too probably missed some, too lazy to check which ones.".

There's some irony in this story, however. It's safe to say that scalpers don't garner the same amount of love as puppies, and yet the 9,500 CAD he was asking for the cards is actually on par with or lower than commercial offerings. A commenter pointed out a Canadian Customs auction of an RTX 5090 that seemingly ended up selling for 8,300 CAD.

As of right now, an RTX 5090 at Memory Express will set you back around 10,000 CAD, and even the cheapest card at Newegg Canada is going for 9,300 CAD, though it's a pretty sweet combo deal (for these times), as you do get a motherboard, a case, and a power supply included in that price.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to a newly introduced report, Samsung’s next “Galaxy Watch 10” won’t be releasing in 2027 with the company moving to a bi-yearly release schedule for its smartwatches.

ETNews reports that Samsung will not have a latest Galaxy Watch model releasing in 2027, a series that would have likely been called “Galaxy Watch 10.” The reason, the report suggests, is that Samsung is “undertaking a structural overhaul to strengthen profitability” (translated) following two quarters in a row of losses in its mobile division.

Samsung has released a latest Galaxy Watch every year since 2018, with 2021’s Galaxy Watch 4 marking the switch to Wear OS.

The upcoming schedule will apparently see new Galaxy Watch releases every other year, pushing the next release into 2028. The report goes on to mention that Galaxy Watch is part of a “mature phase” of the smartwatch market, and that Galaxy Watch 9 sales “fell short of expectations” likely due in part to its higher price point.

Apparently, Samsung plans upcoming Galaxy Watch software updates next year as well as “enhancement of healthcare features.” The Galaxy Fit 4 fitness tracker is also expected in 2027, with Dealabs reporting that the tracker will be priced at €79.90 in Europe, a slight price hike over the previous release.
