💡 Key Takeaways
  • A homelabber has built a local AI system out of four used 32GB Nvidia V100s and a refurbished Lenovo M720q Tiny mini PC.
  • The user, who gives his name as Michael, details his “home AI box” in a YouTube video billed as a “full build guide.” The Australian builder describes the setup as “four docks, four datacentre cards, one little PC” in a “noise optimised build.”.
  • According to recent reports, the hardware for this particular build is based on a Lenovo M720q Tiny desktop, which has an i5-9400T CPU with 64GB of DDR4.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A homelabber has built a local AI system out of four used 32GB Nvidia V100s and a refurbished Lenovo M720q Tiny mini PC. Ok_Kaleidoscope9103’s construction, detailed on Reddit, relies on the GPUs going over four OCuLink cables from a PCIe switch card, with a solder bridge on the riser and coreboot getting past a BIOS that only booted two cards. The quiet-running build has the full 128GB of VRAM and can hit about 285 tokens per second in total running Qwen3.8-27B across its four cards.

The user, who gives his name as Michael, details his “home AI box” in a YouTube video billed as a “full build guide.” The Australian builder describes the setup as “four docks, four datacentre cards, one little PC” in a “noise optimised build.”.

According to recent reports, the hardware for this particular build is based on a Lenovo M720q Tiny desktop, which has an i5-9400T CPU with 64GB of DDR4. With a matching Lenovo 01AJ940 riser and a CEACENT CNOL4PE08 PCIe switch card — this has a 24-lane PEX8724 switch on board for an x8 link in and four x4 OCuLink ports out — each GPU card can run at PCIe Gen3 x4. OCuLink is an external PCIe cable connector often used with external GPUs (eGPU).

Recent findings suggest that on the software and firmware end, the Tiny had some roadblocks that had to be overcome. It “only powers its riser slot when the card pulls the presence pin,” which the switch card doesn’t, so a solder bridge was needed on the back of the riser. Then, “Lenovo’s BIOS only leaves a 128 GB window for 64-bit devices,” and each 32GB V100 needs 64GB, which limits the stock firmware to just two cards; a third “hangs at POST.”.

In a recent development, his workaround used coreboot 26.09 built for the board with an EDK2 payload and a config setting that allows above-4G allocation. This expands the window to about 486GB and, with three patches, more features were enabled: the riser slot is always on, there is a Wake-on-LAN override, and merged memory type range registers (MTRRs). Flashing it needed a CH341A programmer and SOIC8 clip for the BIOS chip.

It has been revealed that he then added four AOOSTAR AG01 eGPU docks, each with a built-in 800 W PSU, and assigned one V100 to each dock. Each dock’s PSU feeds its V100 through a dual PCIe 8-pin to CPU/EPS 8-pin adapter, because the card takes a CPU 8-pin. The Tesla V100s are otherwise passively cooled and rely on chassis or other external airflow.

Sources indicate that then there’s the matter of cooling without ear-bleeding. The V100s each get a 3D-printed 140 mm funnel — designed with the help of AI — with a Noctua NF-A14 iPPC-3000 fan, with all four driven on an ARCTIC 10-port USB fan controller. A separate ARCTIC P12 Silent is mounted in a Dremel-drilled hole in the Tiny’s lid to cool the switch card, as that does run hot. He measured the end result at about 62 dB at a distance of one meter.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Recent findings suggest that A script tracks the hottest card, stopping work at 83°C and powering the system off at 87°C. To keep temperatures in check, each card is also power-capped to 200 W, or 800 W total. A recent, separate dual-GPU build we detailed needs dual 12W fans to keep the Optane and system memory cool.

With this 4-card setup, 44.7 TFLOPS is doable with FP32 with a 71°C peak; this compares to Nvidia’s rating of 14 TFLOPS for each 250 W card. A single RTX 5090 is rated at 104.8 TFLOPS at 575 W, nearly double the 56 TFLOPS of four V100s. Qwen3.8-27B Q6 can chat at about 40 tokens per second with one card and about 285 per second with all four, each card running its own copy and handling four requests at once. A larger model, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-125B-A6B IQ4_XS, does about 43 tokens per second on chat over all four, or about 116 with eight requests.

The builder says that this cost him “~A$6.5k all-in,” a figure that includes local taxes; he puts it closer to $3,500 in U.S. dollars. Check the table for the cost breakdown. As noted in our coverage of other V100 builds, the cost of some of this hardware — SXM2 V100s, in particular — has climbed significantly this year; he says his PCIe cards “jumped in price” in recent months.

Although he calls using the full 128GB a “party trick,” he actually does use the build with Qwen3.8-27B, running separately on each card, to mine stock-announcement data dating back to the early 1990s for his business, which needs to read “millions of documents.” The build has been stable, running “pretty much 24/7 for a few weeks,” and with this setup he expects the system to pay itself back in about three months.

Sources indicate that some commenters wonder why he didn’t take the route of a fellow Redditor, a lawyer, who experimented with 32GB V100s as SXM2 modules on NVLink boards. His answer: noise, and that “the PCIe cards at the time were cheaper.” He also compares his four V100s to an RTX 5090, and says they have 4x the VRAM and about 2x the total memory bandwidth at “about half the price” of a 5090 in Australia. Next up is benchmarking SFNX and Infer-V100 to see how it compares to his llama.cpp setup.cpp setup, and possibly adding a second set of four V100s.

NVIDIA continues releasing permissive datasets in support of the open ecosystem with 6 Million Multilingual Reasoning Dataset.

Continuing the success of the recent Nemotron Post-Training Dataset v1 release used in Llama Nemotron Super model, and our Llama Nemotron Post-Training Dataset release earlier this year, we’re excited to release the reasoning dataset translated into five target languages: French, Spanish, German, Italian, and Japanese.

The newly released NVIDIA Nemotron Nano 2 9B brings these capabilities to the edge with leading accuracy and efficiency with a hybrid Transformer–Mamba architecture and a configurable thinking budget—so you can dial accuracy, throughput, and cost to match your real‑world needs.

Sources indicate that the release represents a significant step forward in our continued commitment to openness and transparency in model development and improvement. By releasing training data, in addition to the training tools and final model weights, NVIDIA supports continued improvement of open‑weight models.

It has been revealed that at a high level, the Nemotron Post-Training Dataset V2 takes our previously released English reasoning data and translates them into five target languages (French, German, Italian, Japanese, Spanish). To best take advantage of English knowledge instilled during pre‑training, we translate the user prompt and model response while preserving the original English reasoning chain.

AI App Builders are exploding in popularity, and for good reason. It’s never been easier to build real, functional apps and internal tools using app builders. To test them all, I built the same app on 10 of the most popular AI app builders and tested each across usability, cost, correctness, and ease of use. Most of them can turn a paragraph of description into something that looks like software within a single session. The differences show up around the tenth prompt, when you learn what each edit costs and who has to fix the code once something breaks. I took every price from the vendor's own pricing page on October 29, 2026.

TLDR: Of the best AI app builders I've used, Softr is the one I'd hand to a team that needs auth, data, user groups or integrations. The other nine I tested include code generators such as Lovable and Bolt and visual platforms such as Bubble and Glide, and each one carries a cost or upkeep trade-off worth seeing before you commit.

I looked at the same seven things in every tool, from the first prompt onward:.

It has been revealed that softr gets used a lot by operations and business teams as their AI app builder for secure client portals, internal tools and other business apps, none of which require code. Write a short brief in your own words, and the AI Co-Builder turns it into a database plus the core app that sits on it: tables, pages and layouts, the data connections behind them, plus user groups and permissions, so real customers can sign in from day one. Workflows come as the next step, either by prompting the Co-Builder again or by adding them in the visual editor.

The Free plan is $0 for unlimited apps, with room for 5 app users, 3 builders, 5,000 records and 5 AI credits each month. Basic runs $19 per month, Pro $99 and Business $329, all on annual billing. Enterprise pricing is custom and includes SSO and SCIM for organizations managing access at scale. The full plan table sits on Softr's pricing page.

Lovable builds full-stack web apps through conversation, writing React code while it takes care of hosting, SSL and the backend. It's designed to move a founder or product team from a prompt to a shareable prototype, and the preview updates as the agent works.

Base44 calls itself a no-code AI platform: you explain the app, and it generates the structure, design and logic while running the backend itself. Authentication, a database and analytics come on every blueprint, Free included.

Base44 is free for 25 message credits a month. Starter costs $16 per month and Builder $40 per month, both on annual billing, with Pro at $80 and Elite at $160.

Recent findings suggest that bolt is a coding agent that writes full-stack projects in the browser and runs them on Bolt Cloud, which supplies hosting, databases and integrations. It suits people who want to watch the code take shape and edit it themselves.

According to recent reports, bolt Free is $0 with 1M tokens a month and Bolt branding. Pro costs $25 per month with 10M tokens, and Teams runs $30 a month for each member on monthly billing.

Replit pairs its Agent with a cloud workspace, so a description turns into a running app whose sign-in, database, hosting and monitoring come wired up. The homepage pitches it to people who don't code, though the result underneath is a code project.

Core costs $20 per month ($18 with annual billing) and Pro costs $100 per month ($90 with annual billing). Enterprise is custom and adds SSO, SCIM and audit logs.

According to recent reports, glide starts internal business apps from whatever you hand it, whether a spreadsheet, a written prompt or a PDF, and its newer platform, GlideOS, reads a sheet's structure and relationships to draft screens and workflows. Its apps grew up on phones, and that heritage still shapes the product.

Industry observers note that glide Free is $0 with limited credits. Basic costs $25 per month, Plus $50 per month and Pro $125 per month; annual billing isn't offered yet, according to Glide.

According to recent reports, bubble is a visual builder that targets the browser as well as native iOS and Android, with an AI agent that drafts pages and logic before you refine them by hand. One editor covers the design, the database, the logic and the privacy rules behind each page.

In a recent development, bubble Free gives you 50K workload units and 500 AI credits each month. Web plans run $32 per month for Starter, $119 for Growth and $349 for Team, all on annual billing.

Retool is an internal tools engine aimed at engineering teams. You describe or assemble an app that connects straight to production databases, APIs and LLMs, with auth and access controls in place at deployment.

Industry observers note that v0 generates full-stack Next.js web apps from a prompt and deploys them to Vercel, with Design Mode for visual tweaks and GitHub sync for the code. It's designed around a developer's workflow.

It has been revealed that v0's Free blueprint gives new users $5 of one-time credits and caps messages at 7 per day. Plus runs $30 a month per user, and Business $100 a month per user.

Sources indicate that figma Make turns prompts and Figma design context into code-backed prototypes and web apps you can publish at a URL. It can also scaffold a Payload backend with a database, APIs, auth and an admin panel, or connect to Supabase for sign-in and stored data.

It has been revealed that figma's Starter initiative is free with up to 500 AI credits a month. Figma lists a Professional Full seat at $16 per month with 3,000 AI credits, and Organization Full seats cost $55 per month on annual billing.

Sources indicate that collins Dictionary named "vibe coding" its Word of the Year for 2025, and the phrase now covers any workflow where you describe software in plain language and an AI produces it. AI app builders package that workflow with hosting, data and sign-in, so a non-developer can get from idea to something clickable without installing anything.

The questions buyers ask have turned plainer since then: what each edit costs, who keeps the app running, and whether a client can sign in and see their own records alone. A generated front end makes a good demo, and a team using it every day needs permissions and a predictable bill for the next hundred edits.

Industry observers note that softr is now my default when recommending AI app builders. It handles teams, auth, and real organization data better than any other product. The AI Co-Builder drafts tables, pages and user groups, workflows follow as the next step, and the app keeps running on maintained platform components with no codebase to patch. App-user pricing and an editor that works without AI credits keep later changes from turning into a running meter.

Three situations call for a different tool. Glide makes a better mobile-first choice when the app spends its days on phones in the field. Bubble gives more front-end design freedom when a project calls for bespoke layouts, interactive animation or heavy brand styling. If your engineers want version control and audit logs and can handle a technical setup, Retool covers that need.

Agents are moving inside the apps these tools produce. Gartner expects task-specific AI agents inside 40% of enterprise applications by the close of 2026, against under 5% in 2025, so a 2027 app builder will need to host agents that respect the same permissions as human consumers.

According to recent reports, building is also leaving the builder's own window. The Model Context Protocol now sits under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation and reports more than 97 million SDK downloads a month, with client support in ChatGPT and Claude, among others. Softr's changelog dates its official Claude and ChatGPT connector to October 6, 2026, and I expect more teams to start an app from the chat assistant they already use.

Sources indicate that the caution comes from Gartner too: it predicts organizations will scrap upward of 40% of agentic AI projects before 2028, citing escalating costs, unclear business value and inadequate risk controls. Going into 2027, I'd judge any builder on whether it keeps agent costs and access rules visible to the team running the app.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The Borslon mouse, sharing a product and brand name, is a wired, “finger-worn gaming mouse,” as the brand describes it.
  • This product targets FPS gamers, and in the FPS gaming niche, there is an even smaller niche — aimers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that the Borslon wearable gaming mouse takes the concept of a gaming mouse to the extreme by making your finger the aiming device. The Kickstarter has already reached over $43,000 with more than 430 backers, beating its $5,000 goal — but is it truly innovative, or just a gimmick?

The Borslon mouse, sharing a product and brand name, is a wired, “finger-worn gaming mouse,” as the brand describes it. It has all the spec numbers you’d expect from a good gaming mouse: a PAW3395 sensor, an 8,000 Hz polling rate, 0.125 ms response time, programmable buttons, and weighs 36g. However, the specs are often only the base level for performance; how it performs in the real world could be a very different story.

This product targets FPS gamers, and in the FPS gaming niche, there is an even smaller niche — aimers. These aiming communities focus purely on the mechanical skill of precisely landing shots on targets, experimenting with techniques and devices to improve their aim. The community explores various aiming devices like tiny fingertip mice and even drawing tablets, with some brands directly marketing their mice in aiming Reddit groups.

The Borslon mouse isn’t the first extreme fingertip mouse; indie mice like the Precision Gaming Gear Titan-Ø and Titan-1 with their 3D-printed titanium construction and ruby joints introduced years ago and sold out extremely quickly due to their popularity in the aiming niche.

There is reason to be skeptical of the Borslon mouse, as the videos alone don’t show even remotely impressive aiming examples, only playing against bots in Counter-Strike 2 with the player showing sub-par aim, while the creator of the Titan series mice showed decent actual gameplay in Quake Champions and is active in the aiming community.

Conventionally, many Counter-Strike, Apex Legends, and Valorant players use the scroll wheel for jumping or bunny-hopping (or tap strafing in Apex Legends, a high-level movement mechanic), and most players use their index or middle finger to scroll. However, the Borslon places the mouse wheel at the thumb, including the five programmable buttons, leaving plenty of responsibility to the appendage. From the Kickstart promotional material, it doesn’t look like the index finger or the middle finger have any buttons to press — which means the thumb is responsible for your usual inputs like aiming down sights (ADS), firing, and jumping; actions that usually happen simultaneously or in quick succession.

Borslon aims to ship out by February of 2027, with mass production planned for December, leaving little to no time to drastically change the design of the product.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

There is also an unusual disconnect between the mouse and its supposedly intended market, as I have not found any discussions about the Borslon mouse in any of the top aiming circles, nor is there any mention of it in the Voltaic Discord, a popular aiming community with over 200,000 members.

Upon further research, the Borslon brand is made by Shenzhen Komodo Intelligent Technology Co., Ltd., with the Borslon website fully in Chinese, but neither the website nor the Kickstarter links to the other. A machine translation of the Borslon website of the tech giant timeline notes it released its first product in November 2025, while the Kickstarter says the concept initiation was in March 2026. The misalignments, combined with the heavy use of AI lifestyle images, don’t spark confidence in the project. If this is indeed real, it could potentially be a genuinely innovative mouse if the brand talked to the intended market and made proper changes.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Google’s Fitbit Air is a simple screenless fitness tracker, but it can do a bit more, and now someone has built an app that lets the Air buzz your wrist when phone notifications come through.

The era of vibe-coding has been very rapidly bringing ideas to reality, and these new Fitbit Air notification apps are a great example.

It has been revealed that “Air Relay” is the result of a developer managing to reverse-engineer a way to control haptics on the Fitbit Air via Bluetooth without affecting Google Health sync. “Cuff” uses the same method while also showing health stats if you don’t want to use Google Health.

The idea here is pretty simple. You can have apps on your phone ping your Fitbit Air as you choose. “Air Relay” lets you pick select apps and even change the vibration pattern or strength based on the app. You can set “Quiet hours” to prevent notifications while you’re sleeping, and there’s a WhatsApp-specific setting that lets you only get notifications from specific groups or people. A “Find My Air” setting uses Bluetooth strength you help you track down a lost tracker.

While a big part of the appeal of Fitbit Air is its screenless, disconnected nature, having the option to set up alerts for important apps or contacts is certainly a useful option.

“Air Relay” is free on Google Play, and Fitbit Air is available for $99.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, zeroGPU lets anyone spin up powerful Nvidia H200 hardware in Hugging Face Spaces without keeping a GPU locked for idle traffic. It’s efficient, flexible, and ideal for demos but it doesn’t always make full use of everything the GPU and CUDA stack can offer. Generating images or videos can take a significant amount of time. Being able to squeeze out more performance, taking advantage of the H200 hardware, does matter in this case.

Sources indicate that this is where PyTorch ahead-of-time (AoT) compilation comes in. Instead of compiling models on the fly (which doesn’t play nicely with ZeroGPU’s short-lived processes), AoT lets you optimize once and reload instantly.

The result: snappier demos and a smoother experience, with speedups ranging from 1.3×–1.8× on models like Flux, Wan, and LTX 🔥.

According to recent reports, in this post, we’ll show how to wire up Ahead-of-Time (AoT) compilation in ZeroGPU Spaces. We'll explore advanced tricks like FP8 quantization and dynamic shapes, and share working demos you can try right away. If you cannot wait, we invite you to check out some ZeroGPU-powered demos on the zerogpu-aoti organization.

Pro users and Team / Enterprise org members can create ZeroGPU Spaces, while anyone can freely use them (Pro, Team and Enterprise users get 8x more ZeroGPU quota).

Spaces is a platform powered by Hugging Face that allows ML practitioners to easily publish demo apps.

Typical demo apps on Spaces look like:.

This works great, but ends up reserving a GPU for the Space during its entire lifetime – even when it has no user activity.

When executing .to('cuda') on this line:.

Industry observers note that pyTorch initializes the NVIDIA driver, which sets up the process on CUDA forever. This is not very resource-efficient given that app traffic is not perfectly smooth, but is rather extremely sparse and spiky.

ZeroGPU takes a just-in-time approach to GPU initialization. Instead of setting up the main process on CUDA, it automatically forks the process, sets it up on CUDA, runs the GPU tasks, and finally kills the fork when the GPU needs to be released.

Thanks to the Python spaces package, the only code change needed to get this behaviour is as follows:.

By importing spaces and adding the @spaces.GPU decorator, we:.

It has been revealed that zeroGPU at the moment allocates an MIG slice of H200 (3g.71gb profile). Additional MIG sizes including full slice (7g.141gb profile) will come in late 2025.

Modern ML frameworks like PyTorch and JAX have the concept of compilation that can be used to optimize model latency or inference time. Behind the scenes, compilation applies a series of (often hardware-dependent) optimization steps such as operator fusion, constant folding, etc.

PyTorch (from 2.0 onwards) currently has two major interfaces for compilation:.

torch.compile works great in standard environments: it compiles your model the first time it runs, and reuses the optimized version for subsequent calls.

It has been revealed that however, on ZeroGPU, given that the process is freshly spun up for (almost) every GPU task, it means that torch.compile can’t efficiently re-use compilation and is thus forced to rely on its filesystem cache to restore compiled models. Depending on the model being compiled, this process takes from a few dozen seconds to a couple of minutes, which is way too much for practical GPU tasks in Spaces.

This is where ahead-of-time (AoT) compilation shines.

With AoT, we can export a compiled model once, save it, and later reload it instantly in any process, which is exactly what we need for ZeroGPU. This helps us reduce framework overhead and also eliminates cold-start timings typically incurred in just-in-time compilation.

But how can we do ahead-of-time compilation on ZeroGPU? Let’s dive in.

Let's go back to our ZeroGPU base example and unpack what we need to enable AoT compilation. For the purpose of this demo, we will use the black-forest-labs/FLUX.1-dev model:.

In the discussion below, we only compile the transformer component of pipe since, in these generative models, the transformer (or more generally, the denoiser) is the most computationally heavy component.

Compiling a model ahead-of-time with PyTorch involves multiple steps:.

Recall that we’re going to compile the model ahead of time. Therefore, we need to derive example inputs for the model. Note that these are the same kinds of inputs we expect to see during the actual runs. To capture those inputs, we will leverage the spaces.aoti_capture helper from the spaces package:.

When used as a context manager, aoti_capture intercepts the call to any callable (pipe.transformer in our case), prevents it from executing, captures the input arguments that would have been passed to it, and stores their values in call.args and call.kwargs.

Now that we have example args and kwargs for our transformer component, we can export it to a PyTorch ExportedProgram by using torch.export.export utility:.

An exported PyTorch program is a computation graph that represents the tensor computations along with the original model parameter values.

Once the model is exported, compiling it is pretty straightforward.

Recent findings suggest that A traditional AoT compilation in PyTorch often requires saving the model on disk so it can be later reloaded. In our case, we’ll leverage a helper function part of the spaces package: spaces.aoti_compile. It's a tiny wrapper around torch._inductor.aot_compile that manages saving and lazy-loading the model as needed. It's meant to be used like this:.

This compiled_transformer is now an AoT-compiled binary ready to be used for inference.

Now we need to bind our compiled transformer to our original pipeline, i.e., the pipeline.

A naive and almost working approach is to simply patch our pipeline like pipe.transformer = compiled_transformer. Unfortunately, this approach does not work because it deletes important attributes like dtype, config, etc. Only patching the forward method does not work well either because we are then keeping original model parameters in memory, often leading to OOM errors at runtime.

spaces package provides a utility for this, too -- spaces.aoti_apply:.

Industry observers note that et voilà! It will take care of patching pipe.transformer.forward with our compiled model, as well as cleaning old model parameters out of memory.

Industry observers note that to perform the first three steps (intercepting input examples, exporting the model, and compiling it with PyTorch inductor), we need a real GPU. CUDA emulation that you get outside of @spaces.GPU function is not enough because compilation is truly hardware-dependent, for instance, relying on micro-benchmark runs to tune the generated code. This is why we need to wrap it all inside a @spaces.GPU function and then get our compiled model back to the root of our app. Starting from our original demo code, this gives:.

With just a dozen lines of additional code, we’ve successfully made our demo quite faster (1.7x faster in the case of FLUX.1-dev).

If you want to learn more about AoT compilation, you can read PyTorch's AOTInductor tutorial.

Now that we have demonstrated the speedups one can realize under the constraints of operating with ZeroGPUs, we will discuss a few gotchas that came up while working with this setup.

AoT can be combined with quantization to deliver even greater speedups. For image and video generation, the FP8 post-training dynamic quantization schemes deliver good speed-quality trade-offs. However, FP8 requires a CUDA compute capability of at least 9.0 to work. Thankfully, for ZeroGPUs, since they’re based on H200s, we can already take advantage of the FP8 quantization schemes.

To enable FP8 quantization within our AoT compilation workflow, we can leverage the APIs provided by torchao like so:.

(You can find more details about TorchAO here.).

Sources indicate that and we can then proceed with the rest of the steps as outlined above. Using quantization provides another 1.2x of speedup.

Images and videos can come in different shapes and sizes. Hence, it’s important to also account for shape dynamism when performing AoT compilation. The primitives provided by torch.export.export make it easily configurable to provide what inputs should be treated accordingly for dynamic shapes, as shown below.

For the case of Flux.1-Dev transformer, changes in different image resolutions will affect two of its forward arguments:.

Recent findings suggest that we start by defining a range in which we want to let the (latent) image resolutions vary. To derive these value ranges, we inspected the shapes of hidden_states in the pipeline with respect to varied image resolutions. The exact values are model-dependent and require manual inspection and some intuition. For Flux.1-Dev, we ended up with:.

We then define a map of argument names and which dimensions in their input values we expect to be dynamic:.

In a recent development, then we need to make our dynamic shapes object replicate the structure of our example inputs. The inputs that do not need dynamic shapes must be set to None. This can be done very easily with PyTorch tree_map utility:.

Now, when performing the export step, we simply supply transformer_dynamic_shapes to torch.export.export:.

Check out this Space that reveals how to use both quantization and dynamic shapes during the export step.

Dynamic shapes is sometimes not enough when dynamism is too vital.

According to recent reports, this is, for instance, the case with the Wan family of video generation models if you want your compiled model to generate different resolutions. One thing can be done in this case: compile one model per resolution while keeping the model parameters shared and dispatching the right one at runtime.

Here is a minimal example of this approach: zerogpu-aoti-multi.py. You can also see a fully working implementation of this paradigm in the Wan 2.2 Space.

According to recent reports, since the ZeroGPU hardware and CUDA drivers are perfectly compatible with Flash-Attention 3 (FA3), we can use it in our ZeroGPU Spaces to speed things up even further. FA3 works with ahead-of-time compilation. So, this is ideal for our case.

According to recent reports, compiling and building FA3 from source can take several minutes, and this process is hardware-dependent. As consumers, we wouldn’t want to lose precious ZeroGPU compute hours. This is where Hugging Face kernels library comes to the rescue. It provides access to pre-built kernels that are compatible for a given hardware. For example, when we try to run:.

It tries to load a kernel from the kernels-community/vllm-flash-attn3 repository, which is compatible with the current setup. Otherwise, it will error out due to incompatibility concerns. Luckily for us, this works seamlessly on the ZeroGPU Spaces. This means we can leverage the power of FA3 on ZeroGPU, using the kernels library.

Here is a fully working example of an FA3 attention processor for the Qwen-Image model.

Recent findings suggest that so far, we have been compiling the full model. Depending on the model, full model compilation can lead to significantly long cold start times. Long cold start times make the development experience unpleasant.

In a recent development, we can also choose to compile regions within a model, significantly reducing the cold start times, while retaining almost all the benefits of full model compilation. Regional compilation becomes promising when a model has repeated blocks of computation. A standard language model, for example, has a number of identically structured Transformer blocks.

In our example, we can compile the repeated blocks of the Flux transformer ahead of time, and propagate the compiled graph to the remaining repeated blocks. The Flux Transformer has two kinds of repeated blocks: FluxTransformerBlock and FluxSingleTransformerBlock.

You can check out this Space for a complete example.

💡 For Flux.1-Dev, switching to regional compilation reduces the compilation time from 6 minutes to just 30 seconds while delivering identical speedups.

Once a model (or even a model block) is compiled ahead of time, we can serialize the compiled graph module as an artifact and reuse later. In the context of a ZeroGPU-powered demo on Spaces, this will significantly cut down the demo startup time by skipping the compilation time.

To keep the storage light, we can just save the compiled model graph without including any model parameters inside the artifact.

Check out this collection that reveals a full workflow of obtaining compiled model graph, pushing it to the Hub, and then using it to build a demo.

ZeroGPU within Hugging Face Spaces is a powerful feature that enables AI builders by providing access to powerful compute. In this post, we showed how people can benefit from PyTorch’s ahead-of-time compilation techniques to speed up their applications that leverage ZeroGPU.

Industry observers note that we demonstrate speedups with Flux.1-Dev, but these techniques are not limited to just this model. Therefore, we encourage you to give these techniques a try and provide us with feedback in this community discussion.

#149367. SAIR: Accelerating Pharma R&D with AI-Powered Structural Intelligence

📅 02 Sep 2025 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1231 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

SAIR: Accelerating Pharma R&D with AI-Powered Structural Intelligence

📅 02 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1231 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This summer, SandboxAQ released the Structurally Augmented IC50 Repository (SAIR), the largest dataset of co-folded 3D protein-ligand structures paired with experimentally measured IC₅₀ labels, directly linking molecular structure to drug potency and overcoming a longstanding scarcity in training data.
  • SAIR is an open-sourced dataset and is publicly available for free under a permissive CC BY 4.0 license, making it immediately actionable for commercial and non-commercial R&D pipelines.
  • AI and computer-aided design have great potential in dramatically accelerating the development of fresh drugs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This summer, SandboxAQ released the Structurally Augmented IC50 Repository (SAIR), the largest dataset of co-folded 3D protein-ligand structures paired with experimentally measured IC₅₀ labels, directly linking molecular structure to drug potency and overcoming a longstanding scarcity in training data. This dataset is now available on Hugging Face, and for the first time, researchers have open access to more than 5 million AI‑generated, high‑accuracy protein-ligand 3D structures, each paired with validated empirical binding potency data.

SAIR is an open-sourced dataset and is publicly available for free under a permissive CC BY 4.0 license, making it immediately actionable for commercial and non-commercial R&D pipelines. More than just a dataset, SAIR is a strategic asset that bridges the long-standing data gap in AI-powered drug design. It empowers pharmaceutical, biotech, and tech‑bio leaders to accelerate R&D, expand target horizons, and supercharge AI models – moving more of the costly, lengthy drug design and optimization from the wet lab to in silico. This means shorter hit‑to‑lead timelines, more efficient lead optimization, fewer dead‑end projects, and a more predictable path from initial idea to clinical candidate.

AI and computer-aided design have great potential in dramatically accelerating the development of fresh drugs. For decades, scientists have dreamed about AI that could identify or design a potent, non-toxic, and efficacious compound from a prompt describing the disease pathway, practically compressing years of drug R&D into a few minutes on a computer. However, this vision is bottlenecked by AI's ability to predict critical drug properties like potency, toxicity, etc., based solely on its molecular structure.

Industry observers note that furthermore, traditional structure‑based discovery is often slowed early by the determination of reliable 3D structures. Three‑dimensional molecular structure dictates a molecule’s functionality, dynamics and interactions, which is especially important when a potential drug candidate is expected to bind to a human protein target.

It has been revealed that experimental methods, such as X-ray crystallography and cryo-EM, require extensive time and investment, and many promising disease targets still lack experimentally validated structural information. Computer simulations have helped lower the barrier of getting 3D structures and predicting binding affinity. However, earlier generations of algorithms for protein folding and docking (like AlphaFold and Vina respectively) only predict static snapshots of molecules and proteins (which, in reality, are inherently dynamic and shape-changing).

Recent findings suggest that SAIR solves that constraint by compiling over 1 million unique computationally co-folded protein–ligand pairs, ultimately yielding 5.24 million distinct 3D complexes (five different co-folded structures per pair). Each structure is paired with a curated IC₅₀ measurement from ChEMBL or BindingDB, providing for the first time a scalable link between high-quality 3D structures and drug potency, and bridging the historic data gap that has hindered AI-driven discovery. Deep-learned affinity models such as Boltz-2, trained on similar data, have been shown to yield up to a 1,000x speed-up over the traditional, first-principle approach.

Sources indicate that creating SAIR was a major feat of high-performance AI computing. It took more than 130,000 GPU hours to compute the SAIR dataset using Boltz1, a cofolding AI model, on a cluster of 760 NVIDIA H100 processors, leveraging the NVIDIA DGX Cloud through Google Cloud Platform.

Capturing highly granular node, operator, scheduler, and GPU metrics, as well as a close collaboration on both infrastructure and workload optimization, helped NVIDIA AI Accelerator and SandboxAQ engineering teams identify bottlenecks and optimize configurations to achieve the highest workload throughput.

Consequently, the two teams were able to achieve > 95% GPU compute utilization for generating the SAIR dataset. This enabled us to create SAIR in three weeks – as opposed to the original estimate of three months (more than a 4X speed up) – and resulted in a highly optimized, GPU-native computational workflow that seamlessly integrates with today’s cutting-edge enterprise compute environments.

Sources indicate that generating such a massive volume of data is only half the story. Equally vital is confidence in its quality, which is why every predicted complex underwent rigorous validation with PoseBusters, an industry-standard, open-source tool for benchmarking structure-related AI in drug discovery. This tool checks chemical sanity and physical plausibility.

Industry observers note that the end result was that 97 percent of SAIR’s structures passed all checks. In addition to PoseBusters validation, we benchmarked leading affinity prediction methods, such as empirical scoring functions, 3D CNNs, and graph neural networks, across SAIR’s synthetic structures and experimental IC₅₀ values. The detailed results of these studies are available in our scientific manuscript on bioRxiv.

SAIR data is a reliable foundation for benchmarking newly introduced models as well as downstream modelling, screening, and design.

Industry observers note that A persistent challenge in drug discovery is the “dark proteome,” or disease‑relevant proteins for which experimental structures simply do not exist. SAIR illuminates these uncharted regions by providing credible, AI‑predicted complexes wherever experimental data is scarce. For example, more than 40 percent of the proteins in the SAIR dataset have no available structures in the Protein Data Bank (PDB) whatsoever, with or without a ligand. SAIR addresses one of the biggest challenges with existing AI models, low generalizability due to data scarcity. With SAIR, scientists can now explore targets that were previously deemed undruggable, armed with structural hypotheses to guide virtual screening and lead optimization using trustworthy model predictions.

Moreover, SAIR’s cross‑target breadth uncovers polypharmacology patterns and elucidates how a single molecule might interact with multiple proteins. Leveraging this rich tapestry of interactions, you can train AI models to predict off‑target effects or identify upcoming repurposing opportunities, equipping your organization with a deeper understanding of compound profiles before any lab work begins.

SAIR is freely available on Hugging Face. Here’s a quick guide to pull SAIR from Hugging Face, peek at the main table, and (optionally) download a few structure archives.

We use the Hub to fetch files and pandas+pyarrow to read the Parquet.

This grabs the file from the Hub and loads it into a DataFrame.

In a recent development, structure files are shipped as many .tar.gz archives under structures_compressed/. List them and pick what you need.

Each archive can be large (≈10 GB). Download only the ones you need and extract them locally.

AI writing tools are now part of everyday work for students, marketers, developers and editors, and a parallel category of tools has appeared to answer one question: was this text written by a person or a model? Teachers, publishers, hiring teams and content managers use these detectors to screen submissions, but the technology is probabilistic, its accuracy claims vary, and the cost of a wrong call can be high.

This guide compares six AI detector tools, CudekAI, GPTZero, Copyleaks, Originality.ai, Turnitin and Sapling, on what their own pages state. It then explains how detectors work, summarizes the research on their limits, and ends with a short script you can use to test any detector on your own samples. The tools are listed in no ranking order. Feature details, limits and prices change often, so confirm current information on each vendor’s site before you commit.

According to recent reports, • A detector gives a probability, not proof. Every vendor in this list warns that results can be wrong, and several advise against using a score alone.

• Limits differ widely. Character limits, supported languages, models detected and free allowances vary between tools and even between pages of the same tool.

It has been revealed that • Bias and short text are known weak spots. Research has found detectors misclassify some non-native English writing, and most vendors say accuracy improves with longer text.

Recent findings suggest that • Vendor accuracy claims are not comparable. Figures come from different datasets, thresholds and models, so test on your own material.

• Use detection as one signal. Combine it with drafts, version history, interviews or other evidence before acting on a result.

CudekAI’s AI detector returns an AI percentage and a human percentage for pasted text, with paragraph, sentence and word-level analysis for mixed documents. According to its page, it also accepts PDF and Word files with per-page scores and downloadable reports, and offers separate code and image detectors. The page lists models it says it detects, including ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Llama, DeepSeek and Grok, and says it supports more than 100 languages.

Strengths: sentence-level highlighting, file uploads with reports, and extra detectors for code and images in the same product.

In a recent development, limitations and gaps: the page shows different character limits in different places, including 1,000, 5,000 and 15,000, so check the limit that applies to your initiative. It says to start free but does not state a free allowance, and it lists detection as costing one credit. A headline accuracy figure of 99 percent appears in its page metadata, while the body refers to independent benchmarking without naming sources, and its FAQ says accuracy may vary for mixed or paraphrased text and that false positives can occur. API access is listed under an enterprise plan.

Fits: writers and teams who want a quick check with sentence-level detail and file reports, and who will verify results rather than rely on a single percentage.

According to recent reports, GPTZero gives an overall score and highlights flagged sentences, and adds a Writing Replay feature that records the writing process, including typing patterns and paste events. It also lists a plagiarism checker and integrations with Google Docs, Google Classroom, Canvas, Zapier and a Chrome extension, plus an API.

Strengths: process-based evidence through Writing Replay, strong education integrations and published benchmark figures. On the RAID benchmark, the page reports 95.7 percent of AI text detected and 1 percent of human text wrongly flagged.

Limitations and gaps: it claims full support for five languages (English, German, Portuguese, French and Spanish) and indicates other languages lack stated accuracy levels. The company’s own page says no detector is 100 percent accurate, that results should not be the final verdict, and that accuracy is higher on longer English text. The free scan box has a 10,000-character limit, and proposal prices are not listed on the page.

Fits: educators and editors who want writing-process evidence as well as a score.

Copyleaks describes an AI detector covering more than 30 languages and models including ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, DeepSeek and Llama. Its AI Logic feature explains why text was flagged, and it says it can detect AI-generated code. It offers a browser extension, a Google Docs add-on, learning-management-system integrations and an enterprise API.

Strengths: explanation of flagged text, code detection, broad integrations and published per-language accuracy figures, which range from 93.08 percent for Portuguese to 99.20 percent for English on AI text, according to the page.

It has been revealed that limitations and gaps: the figures are the vendor’s own. It claims a 0.03 percent false-positive rate and cites a 2023 study, so treat the number as a claim to verify on your data. Free scans cover up to 25,000 characters, but paid proposal prices sit on a separate pricing page.

Fits: organizations that need multilingual coverage, code detection or integrations.

According to recent reports, originality.ai combines AI detection with a plagiarism checker and a fact and hallucination checker. It lists sentence-level highlights, a mixed AI and human category in its newer detection models, a Chrome extension with a writing replay feature and an AI detection API.

Industry observers note that strengths: several checks in one product, an API with documentation and a clear statement of limits. The page acknowledges false positives, says very short text under a 100-word minimum and AI rewriting tools can affect results, and advises against using the score alone.

Industry observers note that limitations and gaps: it is credit-based, free scans are capped at 100 credits per account and credits expire two years after purchase. Its accuracy claims cite third-party studies and internal benchmarks that you should review yourself.

Fits: publishers, agencies and SEO teams that want detection, plagiarism and fact checks in one workflow.

Sources indicate that turnitin is built for educators and institutions. Its AI writing detection estimates how much of a submission is human-written versus likely AI-generated, including likely AI-paraphrased content, and works inside learning-management systems alongside similarity checking.

Industry observers note that strengths: deep institutional integration and unusually explicit framing of results as probabilities. For documents above its 300-word minimum, the page reports false-positive rates of 0.014 for English language learners and 0.013 for native English writers and concludes there is no statistically significant bias. It also links guidance on handling suspected false positives.

Limitations and gaps: it is aimed at institutions rather than individual freelancers, the page does not give an overall false-positive figure, and it describes detection as just one piece of a broader challenge. Mention of language support is limited, with a linked post about Arabic.

Fits: schools and universities that already use Turnitin and want detection within the same workflow.

It has been revealed that sapling offers an AI content detector with a free check of the first 2,000 characters, and Pro and Enterprise accounts can check up to 100,000 characters. It provides a free API key and documentation, and it publishes unusually candid guidance on limits.

In a recent development, strengths: transparent caveats and a developer-friendly API. The page claims false positives and negatives may occur, that accuracy varies with dataset, text length and threshold, and advises measuring results on your own examples. It also warns that some tools claiming to be undetectable falsely say they passed its detector.

Limitations and gaps: accuracy improves after about 50 words, non-English text is scored by the English model for unsupported languages and is described as less reliable, and prices are not listed on the page. A reported 60 percent drop in false positives comes from internal evaluations that the page does not publish.

Fits: developers and teams that want to integrate detection and test it on their own data.

The table summarizes what each page states. It is not a benchmark, and “not stated” means the page did not say, not that the feature is absent.

It has been revealed that • False positives. Human writing can be flagged, especially when it is short, formulaic or highly predictable.

Industry observers note that • Bias risk. A research paper titled GPT detectors are biased against non-native English writers found that the detectors it tested consistently misclassified non-native English writing as AI-generated, and warned against using such detectors in educational settings. Turnitin’s page reports the opposite for its own tool, which is a reason to test on your population.

• Evasion. Paraphrasing or editing AI text can lower scores. The same research found that simple prompting strategies could both reduce bias and get text past detectors.

• Mixed authorship. A document that is partly AI-assisted can get a low overall score while individual sentences score high, as Sapling’s page points out.

• Moving targets. New models change the text distribution, so a tool trained on older models can lose accuracy.

In a recent development, • Shifting benchmarks. Vendors report different datasets and thresholds, so numbers are not comparable.

According to recent reports, openAI’s own experience is a useful reminder. Its AI text classifier correctly flagged 26 percent of AI-written text on a challenge set while mislabeling 9 percent of human text, and the page states that the classifier was withdrawn on July 20, 2023 due to its low rate of accuracy. Detection has improved since, but the underlying difficulty has not gone away.

Industry observers note that most detectors are classifiers trained on large collections of human-written and machine-generated text. They look for statistical patterns, such as how predictable the word choices are or how uniform the sentence structure is, and output a probability. Some systems add features such as sentence-level scoring, writing-process data, or checks for hidden provenance signals.

Industry observers note that • Statistical signals. Text that a language model finds highly predictable tends to look machine-like, which is why formulaic human writing can be misflagged.

According to recent reports, • Trained classifiers. Detectors learn from labeled examples and revision as new models appear.

• Writing-process evidence. Tools such as Writing Replay record how a document was typed or pasted, which is stronger evidence than a style score.

According to recent reports, • Provenance. Standards such as C2PA Content Credentials aim to record the origin and edits of content when the creating tool supports them, which is different from guessing after the fact.

Which Tool Fits Which Situation?

It has been revealed that because vendor figures are not comparable, the most reliable approach is to measure. Build a small labeled set that reflects your real content, including human writing from different groups of authors, and calculate false-positive and false-negative rates by group. The script below wraps any detector behind a single function. The stub is a placeholder, so replace it with a call to the tool you are evaluating and follow that vendor’s API documentation.

from dataclasses import dataclass.

is_ai: bool        # ground truth you control.

Industry observers note that group: str = "all" # e.g. "native", "non-native", "technical".

def evaluate(detect, samples, threshold=0.5):.

"""detect(text) -> probability the text is AI-generated (0..1).

Wrap any vendor API or tool export in this function.""".

flagged = detect(s.text) >= threshold.

g = stats.setdefault(s.group, {"fp": 0, "human": 0, "fn": 0, "ai": 0}).

g["fn"] += not flagged          # AI text that slipped through.

g["fp"] += flagged              # human text wrongly flagged.

fpr = g["fp"] / g["human"] if g["human"] else float("nan").

fnr = g["fn"] / g["ai"] if g["ai"] else float("nan").

print(f"{group:12} false positive rate {fpr:.1%}  false negative rate {fnr:.1%}").

return 0.9 if "delve" in text.lower() else 0.2.

Sample("Let us delve into the topic.", True, "native"),.

Sample("I wrote this note by hand.", False, "native"),.

Sample("We delve into methods used here.", False, "non-native"),.

Sample("The results were reviewed twice.", True, "non-native"),.

With only a handful of samples the numbers mean little, so use a larger, representative set and report results per group, because an acceptable overall rate can hide a high rate for one group.

According to recent reports, • Never treat a score as proof. Use it to start a conversation, not end one.

It has been revealed that • Gather corroborating evidence. Drafts, version history, writing-process data and discussion with the author carry more weight than a percentage.

• Tell people how detection is used. Publish a policy so authors know what to expect and how to appeal.

• Check for bias. Test on writers like those you evaluate, including non-native speakers.

It has been revealed that • Protect privacy. Do not paste confidential or personal text into a tool unless you have checked how it handles data.

A tool that estimates how likely a piece of text is to have been generated by an AI model, usually as a percentage, often with sentence-level highlighting.

They can be useful, but accuracy depends on the text, length, language and threshold, and every vendor in this guide states that errors can occur. Test on your own samples.

It has been revealed that yes. False positives are acknowledged by vendors and documented in research, particularly for short or formulaic text and some non-native English writing.

Free tiers are fine for a quick check, but they have limits on length and features, and the result should not be the sole basis for a decision.

Sometimes. Paraphrasing and editing can lower scores, and partly AI-generated documents can produce mixed results.

Industry observers note that A plagiarism checker looks for matches with existing sources. An AI detector estimates whether text resembles machine-generated writing, which is a different and less certain task.

It has been revealed that AI detectors are useful screening tools, but none is a verdict. The six reviewed here differ in language coverage, limits, integrations, explainability and how candidly their pages describe error, and their accuracy figures come from different tests. Compare them on the factors that matter for your content, measure false positives on your own samples, and combine any score with other evidence before acting on it.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI changed the game at Chess.com, helping it expand to 11 other classics this year.﻿.

AI changed the game at Chess.com, helping it expand to 11 other classics this year.﻿.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Chess.com is ready to go a lot bigger than chess. After launching Gambit, a gambling-free poker site, earlier this year, the company is now adding 10 more games: backgammon, checkers, go, hearts, mahjong, shogi, sudoku, solitaire, xiangqi, and a Scrabble alternative called word. They’re all part of Chess’s new Classic Games platform, which is launching its public beta on Saturday on the web and through a new app for iOS and Android.

“Our cofounders have had many people come up to them and say, ‘Hey, I run a mahjong night on Wednesdays’ or ‘I go to this local bar in Chicago with like five people, and we love playing go, but we lack a Chess.com,’” chief growth officer Albert Cheng indicates in an interview with The Verge. “The way that Chess.com has grown this community of almost 300 million members has not really happened for a lot of these other types of classic games.”.

Sources indicate that classic Games is aimed at filling that gap. Some of the new games, like shoji or xiangqi, are strategy games similar to chess while others are further afield, like sudoku, solitaire, and word. The Classic team chose the new games through “a mix of community feedback, market research, and then just our own confidence in our ability to serve that game well,” Cheng claims. It’s focused on classics that “have some sort of lifelong journey of learning and a community.”.

Industry observers note that classic Games will feel familiar if you’ve ever played a match on Chess.com. Each game has lessons, leaderboards, and a rating system. Multiplayer games like checkers or mahjong have options for matches against other players or bots, and they use the same bot characters that Chess.com has. (Martin remains the lowest-rated bot across the board, whether it’s on Chess, Gambit, or Classic.) Not all of the games have the same play modes — word and mahjong have puzzles like chess, while sudoku has a set of daily grids and solitaire has daily deals.

The expansion hasn’t put Chess.com itself on the back burner, according to Cheng. If anything, it’s never been better. “Chess is more and more so in the public zeitgeist than I’ve ever seen it, frankly, during my time here,” Cheng says. “Our daily active customers are higher than they’ve ever been during the company’s history.” He declined to share exactly how many daily users Chess.com at the moment has but mentioned the site is “doing amazingly well.”.

So, while the firm is expanding beyond its domain name, chess remains its primary focus. “The amount of folks that are fully dedicated toward building upcoming games is less than 1 percent of the company,” according to Cheng.

It has been revealed that AI played a key role in helping Chess.com launch 11 latest games in a matter of months with a team of only a few people. Earlier this year, Cheng told The Verge his team built Gambit with the help of AI, mainly for coding tasks. He claims they used “almost entirely the same approach” for Classic, with AI helping to speed up the coding process again.

Industry observers note that “Because these games are built on top of the Chess.com code base and design system and bot characters and rating systems, it’s a huge advantage and allows us to move very quickly alongside AI to bring these types of games to market with a very small team,” Cheng states. “As we create more and more games, the adjacent games that can be created to it just happen much faster because the infrastructure is there, as opposed to standing everything up from scratch.”.

AI wasn’t used for Classic Games’ art and design, Cheng indicates. “The look and feel of it is very carefully crafted by humans, and we’re proud of that,” he says. “The truth is, it really is a blend. It’s a small team of really talented folks that have good product and design judgment, and they’re leveraging AI.”.

“We are fortunate in some ways that AI and chess have been intermixed for 30-ish years.”.

It has been revealed that chess.com’s comfort with AI may come from the fact that human chess players have now spent decades playing and learning alongside machines. “We are fortunate in some ways that AI and chess have been intermixed for 30-ish years,” Cheng says, calling back to Garry Kasparov’s 1996 chess match against IBM’s Deep Blue supercomputer. “Even before the company was founded 20 years ago, the idea that AI was super powerful at the game of chess was embedded in how the cofounders thought about the company.”.

Sources indicate that elsewhere in the games industry, there’s been increasing tension over the use of AI. Cheng says that while Chess.com may be using AI to “accelerate” coding tasks, the creative side of things has become more notable. “On the art and the design side, the ratios are shifting a decent amount, where we’re hiring more of those folks,” he says, adding that the tech giant has “shipped a lot more major features in Chess.com than in previous years” using what they’ve learned from Classic Games’ faster development process.

Chess.com might not be done growing its library of games, either. Cheng mentioned it will likely expand to “a lot more” games in the future.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AirTag-like trackers for Android and iPhone are everywhere nowadays, but Kodak’s new SlideTag steps it up with a built-in E-Ink display that can show off your photos, widgets, and more along with being able to track down your items.

Compatible with both the Android Find Hub and Apple Find My networks, the Kodak SlideTag is a tracker inspired by the golden era of Kodak photography. The tracker is built by Reto, the same firm that built the Kodak Chamera keychain digital camera.

SlideTag’s premise is relatively simple. You get a tracker with an E-Ink display and a frame in one of eight styles inspired by classic 35mm slides. Those styles are sold in a blind box format, meaning you don’t know what you’re getting until you open the box (unless you buy the full set). There’s also a ninth style that only shows up in one out of every 64 boxes.

The E-Ink display can show six-color versions of your photos, or it can display things like lists, calendars, and more. There’s enough storage on the tracker for a 12-photo slideshow, synced through the Kodak Memory Link app on Android and iOS.

Sources indicate that connect instantly via Bluetooth to the KODAK Memory Link App. From live slideshows and custom QR codes to countdowns and dual-network tracking with Apple Find My and Google’s Find Hub, the KODAK SlideTag seamlessly integrates retro aesthetics into your everyday carry.

Kodak SlideTag is available today from Amazon.

In a recent development, I’ve created a new little tool to help run and manage scripts in a folder tree, called scriptura. It is based on the idea behind sd and is made for fish owners.

Industry observers note that if I type in scriptura run os update linde, it will run the script at ~/scripts/os/update/linde, whilst providing tab completion for each element. Pressing tab after a script has been resolved will first add -- to clearly show the end of the script part of the command line, then use the default shell filename completion.

The usage information gives more detail on what can be done.

To reduce the amount of typing required, I have set the following aliases.

The fish completion system handles these well: sf will show me scripts to be run, whereas sfm will show me the subcommands of the tool.

To aid documentation, scriptura will look in a couple of places:.

Whilst scriptura is written in fish, scripts don’t have to be; it’s just the default. scriptura new will create scripts with a fish shebang, which can be freely edited. I also initiative to add a command-line option to set a different interpreter.

The blog post version of sd and the version published to Github already differ in that the blog post version uses subcommands like sd upcoming, whereas the Github version uses flags for actions that don’t involve running a script (e.g. sd --new). I prefer the subcommand style, at least when there is a short alias to the run subcommand.

Additionally, I’ve added some fresh features.

The latest subcommand invokes the underlying command’s tab-completion after a script name is given:.

will run the tree command with the working directory set to $SCRIPTURA_ROOT.

One thing that I thought would be useful is a tree subcommand. However, I don’t want to force that on any other potential consumers. Whilst I could have settled with the cmd subcommand mentioned in the previous section, I decided I wanted it to be even easier. Scripts under the special scriptura subdirectory are exposed as subcommands, which pass flags to the underlying command and interpret positional arguments as script path components:.

Recently, I found sd, which is designed to help run and manage scripts under a specific directory tree.

There are two reasons I’m not using this tool directly:.

Also, I expected a fish implementation to be easier to read and write, as well as not requiring so many external command calls.

Recent findings suggest that in the introductory blog post, Ian writes It’s not really a thing. It’s more of an idea. You can implement it yourself in one sitting, if you want..

It took me more than one sitting, but I enjoyed it.

Visit the repository for installation instructions, including a home-manager module:.

Welcome EmbeddingGemma, Google's new efficient embedding model

📅 04 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2741 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that today, Google releases EmbeddingGemma, a state-of-the-art multilingual embedding model perfect for on-device use cases.
  • Industry observers note that text embeddings have become the backbone of modern natural‑language applications, turning words, sentences, and documents into dense vectors that capture meaning, sentiment, and intent.
  • It has been revealed that building on this foundation, Google DeepMind’s EmbeddingGemma arrives as the newest, most capable small multilingual embedding model yet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that today, Google releases EmbeddingGemma, a state-of-the-art multilingual embedding model perfect for on-device use cases. Designed for speed and efficiency, the model features a compact size of 308M parameters and a 2K context window, unlocking new possibilities for mobile RAG pipelines, agents, and more. EmbeddingGemma is trained to support over 100 languages and is the highest-ranking text-only multilingual embedding model under 500M on the Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (MTEB) at the time of writing.

Industry observers note that text embeddings have become the backbone of modern natural‑language applications, turning words, sentences, and documents into dense vectors that capture meaning, sentiment, and intent. These vectors enable fast similarity search, clustering, classification, and retrieval across massive corpora, powering everything from recommendation engines and semantic search to retrieval-augmented generation and code‑search tools. Embedding models that calculate these embeddings are widely used, with well over 200 million monthly downloads on Hugging Face.

It has been revealed that building on this foundation, Google DeepMind’s EmbeddingGemma arrives as the newest, most capable small multilingual embedding model yet. With just 308M parameters, a 2k‑token context window, and support for over 100 languages, EmbeddingGemma delivers state‑of‑the‑art performance on the Massive Multilingual Text Embedding Benchmark (MMTEB) while staying under 200 MB of RAM when quantized.

The various design choices result in a very practical, open-source tool for computing high-quality multilingual embeddings on everyday devices.

In this blogpost, we describe the EmbeddingGemma architecture and training, and show you how to use the model with various frameworks like Sentence Transformers, LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack, txtai, Transformers.js, Text Embedding Inference, and ONNX.

Industry observers note that afterwards, we demonstrate how to finetune EmbeddingGemma on your domain for even stronger performance. In our example, we finetune EmbeddingGemma on the Medical Instruction and Retrieval Dataset (MIRIAD). The resulting model, sentence-transformers/embeddinggemma-300m-medical, achieves state-of-the-art performance on our task: retrieving passages of scientific medical papers in response to detailed medical questions. It even outperforms models twice as big on this task.

EmbeddingGemma builds on the Gemma3 transformers backbone, but modified to use bi-directional attention instead of causal (one-way) attention. This means that earlier tokens in the sequence can attend to later tokens, effectively turning the architecture from a decoder into an encoder. Encoder models can outperform LLMs, which are decoders, on embedding tasks like retrieval (Weller et al., 2025). With this backbone, the model can process a sizable 2048 tokens at once, sufficient for typical retrieval inputs, especially given that larger inputs often result in information loss in the text embeddings.

Beyond the newly introduced Gemma3-based encoder backbone, which produces token embeddings, a mean pooling layer converts these token embeddings into text embeddings. Lastly, two dense layers transform the text embeddings into their final form, a 768-dimensional vector.

The EmbeddingGemma model has been trained with Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL), allowing you to truncate the 768‑dimensional output to 512, 256, or 128 dimensions on demand. This results in faster downstream processing and lower memory and disk space utilization. See the Sentence Transformers usage for a snippet showing how to perform this truncation.

Sources indicate that the model has been trained using a carefully curated, multilingual corpus totalling approximately 320 billion tokens. The proprietary dataset is a blend of publicly available web text, code and technical documentation, and synthetic task‑specific examples. It has been filtered to avoid Child Sexual Abuse Material (CSAM), sensitive data, and low-quality or unsafe content.

Industry observers note that embeddingGemma was benchmarked on the MMTEB (Multilingual, v2) and MTEB (English, v2) suites, which span a wide range of tasks, domains, and languages. Despite its modest 308M‑parameter size, the model consistently beats comparable baselines while keeping a very small memory footprint.

The results will be listed on the official MTEB Leaderboard. We exclude any model that has been trained on more than 20% of the MTEB data, to mitigate potential over‑fitting.

The demo can also be experienced in full screen.

Experience the demo yourself on a Desktop device.

In a recent development, embeddingGemma is integrated with many popular tools, making it easy to incorporate into your existing workflows and applications. The model has been integrated in Sentence Transformers, and thus also in projects that use Sentence Transformers behind the scenes, such as LangChain, LlamaIndex, Haystack, and txtai. See the examples below to get started with your preferred framework.

For production deployments, you can use Text Embeddings Inference (TEI) to serve the model efficiently on various hardware configurations, and you can use Transformers.js for use in web applications.

Recent findings suggest that regardless of your framework choice, you should be mindful of the prompts. For embedding models, prompts are prepended to the input text to allow the model to distinguish between different tasks. Industry observers note that because google/embeddinggemma-300m was trained with MRL, the embeddings generated by this model can be truncated to lower dimensionalities without considerably hurting the evaluation performance. Embeddings with lower dimensionalities are both cheaper to store on disk and in memory, as well as faster for downstream tasks like retrieval, clustering, or classification.

In Sentence Transformers, you can set a lower dimensionality using the truncate_dim parameter on either the SentenceTransformer initialization or when calling model.encode/model.encode_query/model.encode_document:.

Note that the ranking is preserved despite using 3x smaller embeddings compared to the full-sized embeddings.

You can easily deploy EmbeddingGemma for both development and production using Text Embeddings Inference (TEI) version 1.8.1 or later.

If you run the Docker container with the cuda-1.8.1 tag, it includes support for multiple GPU architectures: Turing, Ampere, Ada Lovelace, and Hopper. For a lighter image tailored to just your GPU, you can instead use a specific tag such as turing-1.8.1, 1.8.1 and 86-1.8.1 (Ampere), 89-1.8.1 (Ada Lovelace), or hopper-1.8.1.

Once deployed, regardless of the device or runtime, you can leverage the /v1/embeddings endpoint based on the OpenAI Embeddings API Specification to generate embeddings.

Alternatively, you can also leverage the /embed endpoint from the Text Embeddings Inference Embeddings API, which supports the prompt_name parameter, meaning there’s no need to manually prepend the prompt to the inputs but select it via prompt_name instead.

Additionally, note that since google/embeddinggemma-300m was trained with Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL), you can also leverage the dimensions parameter, on both /v1/embeddings and /embed, to truncate the embeddings to lower dimensionalities (512, 256, and 128) without hurting the evaluation performance.

In a recent development, you can also run the model directly with ONNX Runtime, making it highly portable and cross-platform compatible. The example below reveals usage in Python, but the same approach can be applied in other languages (Java, C#, C++, etc.) as well.

Sources indicate that as with all models compatible with the Sentence Transformers library, EmbeddingGemma can be easily fine-tuned on your specific dataset. To showcase this, we'll be finetuning google/embeddinggemma-300m on the Medical Instruction and RetrIeval Dataset (MIRIAD) dataset, such that our finetuned model becomes particularly adept at finding passages up to 1000 tokens from scientific medical papers given detailed medical questions. These passages can be used as crucial context for a generative model to answer questions more effectively.

Below, you can explore each key component of the finetuning process using expandable tabs. Each tab contains the relevant code and a detailed explanation.

This code loads the EmbeddingGemma model from Hugging Face, with optional model card metadata for documentation and sharing. The SentenceTransformer class loads the model weights and configuration, while the model_card_data argument attaches metadata useful for inclusion in the automatically generated model card.

Recent findings suggest that this code loads the MIRIAD dataset, or rather, a copy that has been divided into train, eval, and test splits. Using a large, high-quality dataset ensures the model learns meaningful representations, while subsetting allows for faster experimentation. The load_dataset function fetches the dataset from Hugging Face Datasets, and the .select() method limits the number of samples for each split.

Sources indicate that this code defines the loss function for training, using Cached Multiple Negatives Ranking Loss (CMNRL). CMNRL is effective for retrieval tasks, as it uses in-batch negatives to efficiently train the model to distinguish between correct and incorrect pairs. The loss takes question-answer pairs and treats other answers in the batch as negatives, maximizing the distance between unrelated pairs in the embedding space. The mini_batch_size parameter controls the memory usage, but does not affect the training dynamics.

Industry observers note that it's recommended to use this loss with a large per_device_train_batch_size in SentenceTransformerTrainingArguments and a low mini_batch_size in CachedMultipleNegativesRankingLoss for a strong training signal with low memory usage. Additionally, the NO_DUPLICATES batch sampler is recommended to avoid accidental false negatives.

Recent findings suggest that this code sets up all hyperparameters and configuration for training, evaluation, and logging. Proper training arguments are crucial for efficient, stable, and reproducible training. The arguments control batch sizes, learning rate, mixed precision, evaluation and saving frequency, and more. Notably, the prompts dictionary maps dataset columns to prompts used by the model to distinguish queries from documents.

Recent findings suggest that this code sets up an evaluator for information retrieval, using queries and a corpus to measure model performance. Evaluation during training helps monitor progress and avoid overfitting. The evaluator computes retrieval metrics (NDCG, MRR, Recall, Precision, MAP, etc.) by checking if the model retrieves the correct passages for each query. It can be run before, during, and after training, and the results will be logged and incorporated in the automatically generated model card.

In a recent development, note that this snippet in particular uses all (1k) evaluation questions against a corpus of all (1k) evaluation passages and 30k training passages, for a total of 31k documents. Evaluating only against evaluation passages is too simple for the model.

This code initializes and runs the training loop, coordinating all components.

If desired, you can further reduce the memory footprint by reducing mini_batch_size on the CachedMultipleNegativesRankingLoss and batch_size on the InformationRetrievalEvaluator instances. The performance of the base model was already excellent, with a strong 0.8340 NDCG@10 on our MIRIAD test set. Despite that, we were able to increase it considerably on this domain-specific dataset.

Our fine-tuning process achieved a significant improvement of +0.0522 NDCG@10 on the test set, resulting in a model that comfortably outperforms any existing general-purpose embedding model on our specific task, at this model size. Additional time and compute investment would allow for even stronger results, such as hard negatives mining or training with more than 100k data pairs.
