Dynamic tone mapping for HDR10 content.

Matte anti-glare screen is very effective.

Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

If you’re shopping for one of the best OLED gaming monitors, the 240 Hz QHD category offers the most choices and the best bang for the buck. But 4K at 240 Hz is creeping downward in price and only represents a small upcharge. It also means that you can go to 32 inches and maintain good pixel density. If you have enough video card horsepower to push frame rates over 180fps, the quality is unmatched.

It has been revealed that samsung slides into the neither-expensive-nor-inexpensive position with its Odyssey G8 G80SH. This 32-inch Quantum Dot OLED runs 240 Hz at 4K resolution with Adaptive-Sync, HDR10, HDR10+, wide gamut color, factory calibration, and high brightness for HDR content. Let’s take a look.

Quantum Dot Organic Light Emitting Diode.

Max Resolution and Refresh Rate.

First, I want to clear up any potential confusion with another recently reviewed Samsung display, the G80HS. That is a 6K resolution dual-refresh mode model that currently costs around $1,600. The G80SH I’m covering here is a 4K screen with a single 240 Hz mode, and it’s currently selling for $900.

Industry observers note that the G80SH delivers the best of everything in the premium OLED category. It’s 4K with a Quantum Dot layer that delivers a measured 106% coverage of DCI-P3. That’s about average among the QD-OLEDs I’ve tested, which range from 104 to 108%. The visual difference there is extremely small, not enough to affect a purchase decision. The G80SH also offers excellent out-of-the-box accuracy courtesy of a factory calibration. Though my sample didn’t need any tweaking, it benefited from a few adjustments. And that capability extends to HDR content, where you have full control of color temp, brightness, and luminance tracking.

It has been revealed that speaking of HDR, you get the requisite HDR10 support that all monitors have, plus Samsung’s answer to Dolby Vision, HDR10+. This extension of HDR10 includes dynamic tone mapping where the content matches its luminance curve to whatever display it’s shown on. Since HDR is mastered to a specific peak luminance, usually 1,000 nits but sometimes as high as 10,000, it’s beneficial when the screen can adapt to the incoming metadata to accommodate a lower or higher limit. You’ll see the same fine detail and nuance that the content creator did.

Gaming benefits from the aforementioned 240 Hz refresh rate plus a flawless implementation of Adaptive-Sync. The G80SH works with equal precision on G-Sync and FreeSync platforms, as well as the VRR output from gaming consoles. To help with your aim, there are reticles available in different colors and shapes, with a dynamic mode that keeps them in contrast with the background.

Sources indicate that like every Samsung monitor I’ve experienced, the G80SH delivers high style and solid build quality. The main color is silver, which you can see everywhere except the front, keeping the screen and surrounding bezel all black. There’s a matte anti-glare coating too, effectively eliminating all ambient light reflections. If you have a sunny room, this monitor can handle it without a degradation in image quality. You also get the latest video interfaces, four in total, plus USB and a headphone jack. LED lighting is featured on the back and can be controlled from the OSD.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

According to recent reports, so, just to recap before we jump into the tests, this is the Odyssey G8 G80SH, a 4K 240 Hz OLED that sells for $900. If you’re interested in learning more about the 6K model, my review from a few months ago is here.

Recent findings suggest that samsung still uses crumbly foam to ship its monitors, and my G80SH sample arrived safe and sound. The base, upright, and stand assemble with a captive bolt and a snap-on to create a solid package. To keep the panel thin, the power supply is external. It’s quite large, so consider that when fitting it into your space. The accessory bundle includes right-angle power cables plus one each of DisplayPort, HDMI, and USB-C.

The G80SH’s silver trim is visible from the front in the base and a thin border around the screen that wraps around from the back. The actual bezel is very narrow and flush, so you can’t see it when the power’s off. A small protrusion in the bottom center says Samsung in tiny letters and houses an equally tiny power LED that can’t be seen from the front. Samsung is one of the few manufacturers to offer matte-screened OLEDs, and this implementation is excellent. Even a bright flashlight can’t throw a reflection onto the screen. Sunny office dwellers, this is your monitor.

In the back, it’s all silver all the time with a smooth finish and minimalist styling. There’s a thin ventilation grill on top, a small logo on one side, and hooray, inputs that face backward. You get two HDMI 2.1, a DisplayPort 2.1, USB-C with 98 watts, and two USB-A downstream ports. There are no internal speakers, but there is a 3.5mm headphone jack. On one side of the I/O panel is a joystick, the G80SH’s sole control key. Around the stand’s attachment point is an LED ring with colors and effects available in the OSD. If you remove the stand, a 100mm VESA mount is revealed should you prefer an aftermarket solution. Fasteners are not included.

That large external power supply keeps the panel thin at just under two inches. The stand is solid and wobble-free and offers 2/25 degrees tilt, 30 degrees swivel, a 90-degree portrait mode and a 4.7-inch height range. Movements are firm and smooth, in keeping with the G80SH’s premium status.

The G80SH’s OSD keeps Samsung’s traditional gaming monitor styling with its control panel appearance. Up top are portholes that deliver information about game-related settings. No refresh rate info, though. It would be nice to have that.

Sources indicate that in the Game menu, you get an Adaptive-Sync toggle, aiming points, a black equalizer to enhance shadow detail, and the LED lighting control. The reticles come in two shapes and three colors. Or you can use AI Mode, which changes the color to maintain contrast with the background. You can also position the aiming point somewhere other than the center of the screen. The lighting has multiple effects or can remain a single static color. One miss here is a frame counter. There’s no way to monitor the refresh rate.

In the Picture menu are all the G80SH’s calibration controls. You get five color temps, all adjustable, and seven gamma presets. The Contrast Enhancer is a field dimming control. True variable brightness is only active in HDR mode. You can choose between static and active tone mapping for HDR, which is handy for HDR10 content because it helps bring out highlights without clipping fine shadow detail.

Recent findings suggest that you won’t find an sRGB mode among the color space choices, but if you pick Auto, the G80SH will render sRGB for SDR content. This is an approach that I like, and almost no other manufacturers do it that way. If you’d rather see the full gamut for all content, just leave it on Native. Peak Brightness does just what it notes for HDR content; it raises the peak output. In my HDR tests, I saw 530 nits from a 25% window pattern.

Remaining menu items include port version control, an off timer, DSC toggle, and USB-C control. You also get two panel care options: logo brightness (dimming, actually) and pixel refresh. You can pause the incoming video signal while this is running if you wish.

The G80SH includes a factory calibration with a report saved in the monitor’s firmware. I found visually perfect color and grayscale tracking, but gamma was a little light. Two clicks of the gamma slider made that much better. I noted that though the default picture mode is called Eco, it is just as bright as the other presets, so that you can use it for all content. In HDR mode, you get Display HDR, which has excellent tone mapping and color accuracy. Suppose you want sRGB; just set Color Space to Auto. Then the G80SH will automatically render sRGB for SDR and the full gamut for HDR, which covers 106% of DCI-P3. If you want full color for SDR, set it to Native. My recommended settings are below.

It has been revealed that the G80SH’s color quality and accuracy make it well suited for duty as a post-production monitor or perhaps an on-site display for location shoots. Only a slight gamma anomaly separates it from perfection. It nails grayscale and gamut tracking, which you can read about on pages four and five. And it’s bright enough for any indoor space. I noted that there was no variable brightness option for SDR, but you can turn on a dynamic contrast option, which equates to field dimming. In HDR mode, dimming occurs at the pixel level, and you can choose between Active and Static tone mapping. The former delivers more punch to HDR10 content.

I also noted the G80SH’s excellent color balance. SDR lets you choose between Native and Auto. Native shows the full gamut, which covers 106% of DCI-P3 and is very colorful. It will be the likely choice for most owners. If you prefer sRGB for SDR, set the color space to Auto. Then, it will switch automatically. This is something very few monitors offer. I also noted that the HDR mode allows calibration of grayscale and gamma, another thing I rarely see.

With the image dialed in, I turned to a few afternoons of gaming where the G80SH provided the addictive quality that all premium OLEDs have. It doesn’t have a frame counter, so I had to use FRAPS to monitor the refresh rate, which stayed around 200fps at the max detail settings in Doom Eternal. This was fast enough to provide blur-free motion and input lag low enough to keep up with my most frenetic movements. You’ll see on the next page that it offers response typical of other 4K 240 Hz OLEDs. That means you’ll be able to aim and shoot with speed and precision. I got extra credit in hoard mode for jump shots where I was able to land grenades on target while flying through the air. Turn and shoot became second nature as I mowed through my opponents.

Recent findings suggest that detail in close encounters made me stop and admire the picture more than a few times. Tiny highlights like sweat and other bodily fluids popped right out, making the characters look three-dimensional. Other textures like stone and metal looked better thanks to strong reflections. These highlights moved smoothly over objects like the player’s weapon, which further enhanced realism. The G80SH has some of the best-looking HDR I’ve seen of late.

It makes a great workday monitor too, with understated styling that stands out but doesn’t scream for attention. The LED lighting is just a ring in the back with smoothly playing effects or static colors available, or you can shut it off. The stand is rock solid with comfortable and usable ergonomics. The joystick navigates the OSD intuitively and efficiently. I really appreciated the rear-facing ports, which were easy to see and access. You get two USB-A downstream ports, which can accommodate peripherals once you make a connection to the USB-C input, which doubles as a charger with 98 watts of power. There are no internal speakers, but headphones plug into the 3.5mm jack.

Sources indicate that takeaway: If Samsung keeps the G80SH’s price below $1,000, it will sell a lot of them. It’s a super versatile display for any form of productivity or entertainment. It’s addictive for gaming, with smooth operation and quick response. The image looks stunning in every respect, whether moving or static. Color accuracy is good enough that calibration isn’t required. It has unique but understated styling and excellent ergonomics with a solid stand and rear-facing ports. Aside from a lack of internal speakers, there is nothing missing here.

Tech Report: Tricks from OpenAI gpt-oss YOU 🫵 can use with transformers

📅 11 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2556 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

💡 Key Takeaways
  • OpenAI recently released their GPT-OSS series of models.
  • In this blog post, we talk about all the upgrades in-depth, and how they become part of the transformers toolkit so other models (current and future) can benefit from them.
  • Best part: Most of these features should work across all major models within transformers!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

OpenAI recently released their GPT-OSS series of models. The models feature some novel techniques like MXFP4 quantization, efficient kernels, a brand latest chat format, and more. To enable the release of gpt-oss through transformers, we have upgraded the library considerably. The updates make it very efficient to load, run, and fine-tune the models.

In this blog post, we talk about all the upgrades in-depth, and how they become part of the transformers toolkit so other models (current and future) can benefit from them. Providing clean implementations of upcoming methods in transformers also allows the community to quickly understand and adopt them. Frameworks such as MLX, llama.cpp or vLLM can use the transformers code as a reference to build their own implementations.

For this release, we worked on:.

Best part: Most of these features should work across all major models within transformers!

In a recent development, A kernel is a specialized, compact program that runs on accelerators to execute tasks like matrix multiplications, activations, or normalizations. In eager PyTorch, operations trigger individual kernels sequentially, which is straightforward but can incur extra memory transfers and launch overheads. PyTorch 2.0's torch.compile with backends like TorchInductor addresses this by automatically fusing and optimizing kernels, delivering 2–10× performance gains.

It has been revealed that in addition, the community has created custom kernels for frequent combinations of operations, not just individual PyTorch ops like matmul. For example, Flash Attention was created to optimize the critical attention block that defines the transformers architecture, and is present in many models including most LLMs. By carefully combining all the attention operations inside a single kernel, memory transfers are minimized, memory use is reduced, and speedups can be achieved.

Industry observers note that the problem is that all these various kernels are available in separate libraries, which creates a dependency bloat if they were to be added to the transformers library. Furthermore, these kernels are not just Python code, they consist of low-level cuda code, glued together with C++ and exposed through a Python layer. This means they have to be compiled in the target system, which in turn requires whatever build system is required by each kernel library.

It has been revealed that the kernels package solves this problem by downloading pre-built binaries of supported kernels from the Hub. You just indicate the kernel you want to use, and kernels will look for a version compatible with your system and download it on first use.

Industry observers note that GPT-OSS, a Mixture of Experts (MoE) model, is a substantial user of Kernels from the Hub. It leverages several custom kernels:.

Let's take a look at the first two ones.

Behind the scenes, the decorators (1 and 2) simply point to community-contributed kernels. For example, RMSNorm comes from liger_kernels, while the MegaBlocksMoeMLP kernel comes from megablocks. Depending on your device (CUDA or ROCm) and whether you’re training or running inference, the right kernel is pulled in automatically.

This design is both specific and general: the RMSNorm liger kernels are already being reused across multiple models, and the MoE kernel could be applied to future MoEs as well.

Because kernels pulls code from the Hub, you have to opt-in to this feature by passing use_kernels=True in your model instantiation, as shown below. We enable INFO logging in the example so you can easily verify that downloadable kernels are in use.

Industry observers note that these kernels are not compatible with mxfp4, so inference will happen in bfloat16 if you use them. Please, benchmark your system for the best combination in memory and throughput that suits your project!

Running a quick generation yields log messages like.

Figure 1 highlights that, in the system we tested, these kernels work best for larger batch sizes. We always recommend to benchmark any performance-related changes as closely to your production conditions as possible.

You can explore and play with the benchmarking script here.

Sources indicate that openAI gpt-oss models use attention sinks, which improves quality and facilitates the use of longer contexts. The vLLM team added this feature to the latest version of Flash Attention (Flash Attention 3), and the resulting custom kernel is available on the Hub. At the moment, this kernel is compatible with the Hopper architecture. If you have one, this is the way to enable it:.

Large language models are memory-hungry. Quantization reduces memory footprint by storing weights (and sometimes activations) in lower-precision formats. For reference, FP32 uses 32 bits per number and BF16 uses 16. By reducing bit width, we trade some precision for smaller models and faster memory movement.

If you want a visual primer on quantization trade-offs, Maarten Grootendorst’s article is excellent: A Visual Guide to Quantization.

Industry observers note that MXFP4 is a 4-bit floating format with E2M1 layout: 1 sign bit, 2 exponent bits, and 1 mantissa bit, as shown in Figure 2. On its own, E2M1 is very coarse. MXFP4 compensates with blockwise scaling:.

This blockwise scheme lets MXFP4 keep range while using very few bits. In practice, GPT-OSS 20B fits in roughly 16 GB of VRAM and GPT-OSS 120B fits in roughly 80 GB when MXFP4 is active, which is the difference between “cannot load” and “can run on a single GPU.” The catch is that matrix multiplies now have to respect block scales. Doing this efficiently at scale requires dedicated kernels.

Recent findings suggest that transformers now includes native support for MXFP4, leveraging optimized triton (MXFP4) kernels for enhanced performance. This builds on the community-driven kernel distribution discussed earlier, utilizing pre-compiled kernels from the Hub to simplify deployment.

To check if a model supports MXFP4, inspect its configuration:.

If 'quant_method': 'mxfp4' is present, the model will automatically use the MXFP4 pathway with Triton kernels when supported.

Thanks to this pull request, you can fine-tune gpt-oss models and save them directly to the Hub in MXFP4 format, streamlining deployment with optimized performance.

If these constraints are not met, transformers falls back to a higher-precision path (bfloat16 is used by default), which requires about 4× the memory of MXFP4.

Recent findings suggest that the snippet loads GPT-OSS twice on CUDA: once with Mxfp4Config(dequantize=True) (memory intensive) and once in the default quantized path (memory efficient). Figure 3 highlights the amount of used VRAM after each load so you can visualize the savings.

Efficient MXFP4 requires kernels that understand 32-element blocks and their scales during GEMMs and fused ops. This is where Kernels from the Hub comes in again. transformers automatically pulls in the MXFP4-aware Triton kernels from the community repository when you load a model that needs them. The repository will appear in your local cache and will be used during the forward pass. For the MXFP4 kernels one does not need to use the use_kernels=True parameter like before, it is set to default in transformers.

Quick sanity check with the Hugging Face cache CLI, after running gpt-oss-20b on a GPU compatible with the triton MXFP4 kernels:.

This indicates the MXFP4 kernels were fetched and are available for execution.

It has been revealed that let's run some benchmarks and see how well the MXFP4 kernels perform. In Figure 4, we see that the MXFP4 kernels are even better than the custom MoE and RMSNorm kernels for larger batches.

You can explore and play with the benchmarking script here.

Tensor Parallelism (TP) splits tensors inside a layer across multiple GPUs (as shown in Figure 5). Each GPU multiplies its shard in parallel, and then partial results are collected using all-gather or all-reduce operations. This reduces per-GPU memory and keeps all GPUs working on the same layer, which improves throughput as sequence length or batch size grow. TP is communication-intensive and generally works best on a single machine with fast intra-node links.

Recent findings suggest that transformers implements TP directly in from_pretrained. You can start with the predefined initiative:.

If you don’t have the infrastructure to run the above, you can just spawn a process on our GPUs using Hugging Face Jobs!

hf jobs is available for all Hugging Face PRO & Enterprise consumers.

Under the hood, tp_plan="auto" selects a predefined sharding recipe for each layer and wires the necessary collectives. You can inspect the active plan with print(model._tp_plan) if you want to verify what is being sharded.

Use TP when the model is too large for one GPU and you want parallel compute, not only memory placement. TP tends to scale throughput with more GPUs, especially for long sequences or larger batches.

If you are curious about how TP differs from device_map="auto" (memory placement), this short Stack Overflow answer explains the distinction and when to use each.

To learn more about TP, here are two must-read resources:.

Industry observers note that expert Parallelism (EP) shards experts inside MoE layers across GPUs. Each token is routed to one or a few experts, so only those experts run their feed-forward pass. Since experts are independent MLPs, we can place different experts on different ranks and exchange only the hidden states for the routed tokens. This keeps the matrix multiplies intact on each rank and replaces tensor slicing with routing and collectives.

Run with multiple processes using torchrun. EP is enabled via the distributed configuration and works with GPT-OSS MoE layers out of the box in transformers.

Here is how you would run using hf jobs.

When you enable Expert Parallelism, Tensor Parallelism is also activated. This means you enjoy the best of both worlds!

Many recent LLMs use sliding window attention, or a combination of sliding and global attention layers, as a means to save memory and reduce those expensive quadratic matmuls that grow with sequence length. However, the dynamic KV cache implementation in transformers used to continue to allocate space according to sequence length, without looking at the individual attention layers. You could always optimize memory using compilation (meaning, fixed shapes), but that's a separate scenario altogether.

transformers now has a DynamicSlidingWindowLayer and a config‑aware DynamicCache. If the model config declares sliding‑window or hybrid attention (both sliding and global attention layers are used), the cache stops growing past the window for the sliding layers. If you don’t pass the config, behavior stays as before (full, ever‑growing KV as sequence length grows).

For models that only use sliding window layers, such as Mistral 7B, cache memory stops growing when the sequence reaches the window size (4096, in this case). This makes sense, because the sliding layers can't look past the previous 4K tokens anyway.

OpenAI gpt-oss alternates between sliding and global attention layers, which results in total KV cache memory being halved, as we'll see, as sequence length increases. This provides us with:.

The optimized cache is set by default, that means you don't have to make any changes to your existing code. If you want to create the DynamicCache explicitly here is how you would do it:.

Figure 6 showcases how much of a difference it makes for us to use the Dynamic KV Cache with sliding window attention.

Sources indicate that A typical autoregressive generation process looks like Figure 7. You input the prefill tokens, and the model predicts each new token one after the other until it predicts the EOS (End of Sequence) token.

Let’s see what the generation process looks like when we pass a batch of inputs. In Figure 8 you notice that some generations finish off earlier than the others. This mismatch of length underutilizes the GPUs.

This type of batching sequences is called static batching. While this is simple and easy to understand, it inherently comes with inefficiencies. Only after each sentence is completely generated can we move on to the next batch.

Recent findings suggest that to bypass this issue, we use dynamic batching (also known as continuous batching). Instead of waiting for all the generation to finish, we schedule incoming requests to the completed generations. That way, as soon as a generation in a batch is complete, we prefill the batch with the next request. The process looks like Figure 9.

Recent findings suggest that transformers supports continuous batching with the generate_batch API. This is not meant for production-grade model serving –frameworks like vLLM and SGLang are great at that–, but can be very helpful for evaluation and experimentation. Here is an example script that runs CB end to end on Qwen/Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507.

We have also performed a benchmark between Continuous Batching and Static Batching with 100 samples. In Figure 9, we note that CB is quite faster than SB.

You can play around with the benchmark here: SB, CB.

When you load a large model into your GPU, PyTorch needs to reserve GPU memory for each layer’s weights. Each of these requests (per layer) takes time, and for multi-billion-parameter models it can mean thousands of tiny memory allocations, adding up to a long wait before the model is ready. Instead of asking the GPU for newly introduced memory every single time, it can hold on to a massive chunk once and then hand out slices from it promptly.

PyTorch allocators can do exactly this. The catch is that the allocator only gets fast after you’ve given it some memory to work with. If you don’t “stock the pantry” first, you still end up doing many slow trips to the market. This PR (🎉 #36380) taught transformers to pre-stock the pantry before it starts copying model weights.

It has been revealed that you have to make no changes to your existing code, as this is default behaviour in transformers. If you use device_map="auto" or provide your own device map, your model will now load faster automatically. If you’re running with Tensor Parallel (tp_plan="auto") and torchrun you also benefit from companion changes that make multi-GPU loading smarter.

transformers moves rapidly and it is community-first. The library evolves at the pace of the field because contributors shape it in the open. Pieces added for upcoming models become part of the toolkit and are reused in future integrations.

This velocity enables day-zero integrations like the GPT-OSS series. As the stack becomes increasingly PyTorch-first, it trims bloat and doubles down on the PyTorch paths that matter in practice. The result is a cleaner core that unlocks new capabilities through community kernels, quantization, and parallelism looks, while also standardizing model definitions so that architectures supported in transformers are a reference and extend across the wider ecosystem.

This post is a one-time snapshot of a process we repeatedly iterate on towards the same direction: serve the needs of the community. To be up to date with the latest additions to transformers, check the docs and release notes. And please, keep sharing your feedback and releasing your models in transformers for the community to enjoy 🤗.

Sources indicate that online payments are an essential part of modern web applications. E-commerce platforms, subscription services, and online marketplaces all depend on payment gateways to process transactions and manage customer orders.

However, integrating a payment gateway involves more than adding a payment button or displaying a checkout form. Developers must ensure that payment requests are sent to legitimate providers, transaction information is validated correctly, and payment confirmations cannot be manipulated.

Fake payment gateways introduce another challenge. They can imitate legitimate payment interfaces, use copied checkout templates, and redirect customers to fraudulent websites. Even when a checkout page looks professional, its underlying implementation may not be trustworthy.

Industry observers note that for developers, understanding these risks is important when designing payment workflows. This article explores common payment integration vulnerabilities and practical techniques for building secure checkout systems using JavaScript and Node.js.

A payment gateway connects an application with a payment processing service. It handles transaction requests and communicates payment results to the merchant's application.

A typical checkout process involves several components:.

A frontend checkout interface where customers review their orders.

A backend application that creates payment requests.

A payment provider that processes transactions.

A webhook endpoint that receives payment notifications.

A database that stores order and transaction information.

Attackers can target different parts of this process.

For example, a fraudulent website may copy the appearance of a legitimate checkout page while sending submitted information to an unauthorized server. Another approach involves manipulating payment requests or creating fake confirmation pages that make an unsuccessful transaction appear complete.

These techniques are also relevant to marketplace fraud. An eBay scam can involve fraudulent payment requests and misleading transaction links, illustrating why developers need to consider payment security beyond the appearance of a checkout page.

The important distinction is that a legitimate-looking interface does not establish that the payment request is reaching an authorized provider.

One of the first steps in reviewing a payment integration is checking where the application sends its payment requests.

Developers should inspect network requests using browser developer tools. The Network tab can reveal which domains receive requests when a customer opens the checkout page or submits a payment form.

Look for unexpected requests, unfamiliar domains, and scripts loaded from sources that are not part of the approved integration.

For example, a checkout application might load a payment script like this:.

The URL above is illustrative, not an actual payment provider.

Developers should compare the script URL and integration method with the provider's official documentation rather than trusting a URL simply because it appears familiar.

Reviewing external JavaScript dependencies.

Checking whether payment forms submit data to approved endpoints.

Inspecting redirects during checkout.

Confirming that HTTPS is used throughout the payment process.

Reviewing changes to payment-related scripts during development.

A Content Security Policy (CSP) can also restrict which domains are allowed to load scripts and receive certain types of requests.

These example domains must be replaced with the actual domains documented by the selected payment provider.

A carefully configured policy can reduce the risk of unauthorized scripts and unexpected form submissions.

A common mistake in payment development is trusting values submitted directly from the browser.

Consider an application where the frontend sends an order ID and payment amount to the backend.

An attacker could modify the amount before submitting the request. If the backend accepts that value without checking the original order, the application may create a payment session for an incorrect amount.

The safer approach is to retrieve the order from the database and calculate the amount on the server.

Here is a simplified Node.js example:.

Here, payment Gateway create Checkout Session() represents a provider-specific server-side SDK method.

The important part is that the backend retrieves the amount from its own database rather than accepting a price supplied by the customer.

Developers should also validate product IDs, quantities, discounts, currency, and order ownership before creating a payment session.

This prevents frontend manipulation from directly determining the final transaction amount.

Developers should avoid building payment processing around unverified scripts, copied templates, or unknown third-party services.

Instead, use official APIs and SDKs provided by established payment processors.

According to recent reports, A hosted checkout integration is one common option. The merchant's backend creates a payment session through the provider's API, and the customer is redirected to the provider's hosted checkout page.

This approach can reduce the amount of sensitive card information handled by the merchant's application.

However, developers still need to configure the integration correctly.

Store secret API keys in server-side environment variables or a secrets manager.

Never expose private credentials in frontend JavaScript.

Use the provider's official SDK where available.

Validate checkout session creation on the backend.

Restrict success and cancellation URLs to approved destinations.

Use HTTPS for application and payment communication.

Recent findings suggest that developers should also understand the difference between public and secret API credentials. Public keys may be designed for browser use, while secret keys must remain on the server.

The OWASP Third-Party Payment Gateway Integration Cheat Sheet provides additional guidance on securing payment requests, validating transaction details, and handling payment callbacks.

Payment providers often use webhooks to notify applications when transactions are completed, failed, or refunded.

However, webhook endpoints are publicly accessible URLs in many integrations. Without proper verification, an attacker may send a fabricated HTTP request that looks like a successful payment notification.

Developers should verify webhook signatures using the payment provider's official SDK.

Consider this simplified Node.js example:.

It has been revealed that the verify Webhook() method represents the signature verification functionality of a payment provider's SDK. It is not a universal Node.js method.

According to recent reports, the example also assumes that the provider's event contains the relevant order and transaction details. Developers should follow the provider's actual event schema and retrieve the authoritative payment status when required.

The application should never mark an order as paid simply because a customer has reached a success URL.

Instead, payment confirmation should depend on an authenticated provider notification or a server-side verification request.

Another notable glitch in payment development is duplicate processing.

Imagine a customer clicks the payment button twice because the first request takes too long. The application may create two payment sessions or attempt to charge the customer more than once.

Network interruptions and automatic retries can create similar situations.

Idempotency helps prevent these problems by ensuring that repeated requests with the same idempotency key do not create duplicate operations.

A simplified example using Node.js might look like this:.

Recent findings suggest that the example uses a provider-specific idempotency option. Actual SDK syntax and key requirements vary between providers.

In a production application, developers should also store payment attempts in the database and enforce appropriate uniqueness constraints.

This helps maintain consistent transaction records even when requests are repeated or interrupted.

A payment integration should be tested beyond the normal successful checkout process.

Most established payment providers offer sandbox environments that allow developers to simulate transactions without charging real customers.

These environments are useful for testing different transaction scenarios.

A practical testing checklist includes:.

Missing or invalid webhook signatures.

Duplicate webhook notifications.

Network interruptions during checkout.

Incorrect order and transaction IDs.

Developers should also test whether the application handles provider downtime correctly.

For example, if the payment provider becomes temporarily unavailable, the application should not mark an order as completed or assume that the transaction succeeded.

Automated integration tests can help verify these scenarios before deployment. Monitoring payment failures, unexpected status changes, and repeated webhook errors can also help developers identify problems after release.

Security does not end when a payment integration goes live.

Developers should implement monitoring to identify unusual transaction patterns and unexpected changes in payment behavior.

Useful monitoring activities include:.

Recording payment attempts and transaction IDs.

Tracking failed payment requests.

Monitoring webhook signature verification failures.

Detecting repeated requests for the same order.

Alerting on unexpected order status changes.

Reviewing payment provider API errors.

However, logging must be implemented carefully.

Applications should never store card verification codes or expose secret API keys in application logs. Sensitive information should be excluded from debugging output, and access to transaction records should be restricted.

Developers should also follow the payment provider's security requirements and applicable PCI DSS obligations when handling payment data.

Detecting fake payment gateways and building secure checkout integrations requires more than checking whether a payment page looks legitimate.

Developers need to examine the complete transaction flow, validate payment information on the server, use official payment APIs, verify webhook signatures, and prevent duplicate transactions.

JavaScript and Node.js provide useful tools for implementing these security controls, but the reliability of a payment system ultimately depends on how its frontend, backend, database, and payment provider communicate.

A well-designed checkout integration should verify every notable transaction before fulfilling an order. By following these development practices, teams can build payment systems that are easier to maintain, more reliable, and better protected against common payment manipulation techniques.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the Co Print Quadro is an Independent Quad Extrusion (IQEX) bedslinger 3D printer, carrying four fully functional printheads on one gantry. The 3D printer accessory organization’s first 3D printer aims to bring IQEX technology to the masses at a budget price, with an SRP of only $899. It has already raised over $500,000, crushing its goal of only $9,820.

Recent findings suggest that independent Quad Extrusion, or IQEX, is unlike tool-changer 3D printers. Instead of one print head swapping assemblies, it has four individual print heads. This allows for increased productivity by printing with all four heads at once, or reducing waste by not going through any purging steps.

In a recent development, the Co Print Quadro is a non-enclosed bedslinger, and its design is quite similar to the Bambu Lab A1, albeit much beefier. The four print heads line up on one gantry, with space for three extruders on either side so they can get out of the way while either of the extruders on the edges can print. It has a large build volume of 300mm3, while the unit itself takes up a massive 780 x 620 mm footprint (2.5 x 2 feet).

Industry observers note that co print claims the Quadro can switch colors in one second, beating out tool changers that still need to park, grab, and home each tool, possibly with some priming as well. The Quadro’s demonstration video still used a prime tower, but it’s likely optional, meaning it can achieve zero color-change waste. What’s even more impressive is the copy printing technology, allowing multiple or even all print heads to print the same objects at once, potentially increasing productivity fourfold. Of course, it also has its own slicer for added IQEX functions, and it’s based on OrcaSlicer, so we’ll likely see community mods that make it do even crazier things.

According to recent reports, the Co Print Quadro is not without competition, however, as another IQEX printer finished its Kickstarter campaign earlier this year: the LightMake L4, raising $3 million in backing over its $50,000 goal. The L4 is an enclosed Core-XY printer with an even bigger print volume of 354 x 370 x 386mm in a smaller 610 x 620 mm footprint while still able to let each print head reach every corner of the build plate. The L4 has the size and enclosure advantage, but Co Print does plan to sell an enclosure for the Quadro as well for more demanding filaments. The L4 has two gantries and can also print four objects at once, but it has a much higher SRP of $2,400 compared to the Quadro’s $899.

The Quadro is Co Print’s first 3D printer, but the tech giant is no stranger to 3D printing, providing multi-color upgrade kits for Creality, Elegoo, and Flashforge printers, including open-source printer brands like Sovol, Voron, and QIDI. While the products are mostly viewed positively, many forums complain about Co Print’s customer service and support. If Co Print wants to sell a whole 3D printer, it should be prepared to deal with issues and take feedback.

  • GGUF and MLX quantizations are also available for your convenience:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The team at WRITER is thrilled to announce the release of three latest open models in the Palmyra-mini family. These models are designed to be powerful, lightweight, and highly performant for their size (1.5B to 1.7B), making them ideal for a wide range of applications with efficient inference.

In a recent development, the "thinking" models have been trained with a Chain of Thought (CoT) approach, which improves their reasoning abilities. We're excited to see what the community will build with these fresh models!

GGUF and MLX quantizations are also available for your convenience:.

palmyra-mini-thinking-a-MLX-BF16.

palmyra-mini-thinking-b-MLX-BF16.

palmyra-mini: Our non-reasoning improved base model, delivering a score of 52.6% on Massive Bench Hard (get-answer)(exact_match), making it a fantastic all-rounder for a wide variety of generative tasks.

palmyra-mini-thinking-a: This variant is your go-to for complex logical challenges. Trained with a Chain of Thought (CoT) approach, it achieves an impressive 82.87% on GSM8K (strict match), demonstrating its powerful reasoning capabilities. It has the highest overall average score on benchmarks relative to other models in the release.

Recent findings suggest that palmyra-mini-thinking-b: Pushing the boundaries of problem-solving, this model scores a solid 92.5% on AMC23. It's a great choice when you need a model that can "think" its way through demanding tasks. This has the highest average benchmark scores in the benchmarks AIME24,AIME25, GPQA, HMMT25, HLE, MMLU_PRO,MATH500, LCB relative to the other models in the release.

It has been revealed that we're releasing both pass@1(avg-of-1) and pass@1(avg-of-64) results. Benchmarking methodology (sampling parameters: temperature 0.6, top_p 0.95): Pass@1(avg-of-1) scores:.

GSM8K through MBPP: collected using lm_eval framework. AIME24 through HMMT25: collected using lighteval framework.

Pass@1(avg-of-64) scores: collected using nemoskills framework.

Since all the base models are Qwen architecture the inference should be runnable on popular inference frameworks such as vLLM, SGLang, TRTLLM, TGI.

For palmyra-thinking-b the base model was https://huggingface.co/nvidia/OpenReasoning-Nemotron-1.5B. We ran RL fine tuning and observed that it's capable of improving performance. While Reinforcement learning improved single-shot accuracy (pass@1), it reduced sampling diversity, leading to a drop in majority@64 performance compared to the SFT base model. This highlights a trade-off between accuracy and diversity, and we believe transparency around these findings will spark further research along mode collapse, small model performance and other areas.

Through this work, we've tried to push the boundaries of what's achievable with small parameter models, and we're excited to see how the community will continue advancing inference efficiency without sacrificing performance quality.

Industry observers note that the Ryzen 7 9850X3D needs no introduction. It's the best CPU for gaming, without question, leveraging AMD's latest Zen 5 architecture alongside its 3D V-Cache to accelerate frame rates as much as 30% above the competition. It's down to its lowest price ever in the run-up to Black Friday, dropping to $399 after an instant coupon on Amazon.

If you're after the ultimate in gaming performance, there's no better option than the Ryzen 7 9850X3D. Thanks to its 93MB of L3 cache, this 8-core/16-thread processor can push out class-leading frame rates in every game out there. With only a 120W TDP, it even stays cooler than the competition, saving you a few extra bucks on that expensive AIO purchase.

It has been revealed that as you can see from our CPU benchmark hierarchy, the Ryzen 7 9850X3D is the fastest gaming processor money can buy. The Ryzen 7 9850X3D is identical to the Ryzen 7 9800X3D outside of a slight boost in clock speed. We found that the base Ryzen 7 9800X3D can reach the same performance level with AMD's Precision Boost Overdrive (PBO), and it usually remains the cheaper of the two CPUs. The Ryzen 7 9850X3D remains the gold standard for gaming performance. The closest chip without 3D V-Cache is Intel's Core i9-14900K, which itself only provided 78.2% of the 1080p gaming performance of the 9800X3D. That's despite the fact that the chip often runs below 100W in games, and it has access to only eight cores and 16 threads.

Those eight cores can pose some limitations in heavily threaded apps, particularly compared to the Intel competition. If you're less focused on gaming, a CPU like the Core Ultra 7 270K Plus remains our recommendation. If you just dabble in non-gaming applications, however, the Ryzen 7 9850X3D is a great option.

Intel may have superior core counts, but the Ryzen 7 9850X3D comes with eight full, fat Zen 5 cores, and it can clock up to 5.6 GHz, giving you plenty of grunt for content creation applications alongside games. It slots into existing AM5 motherboards with a 600- or 800-series chipset, though you may need a BIOS update.

It has been revealed that this chip comes with AMD's second-gen 3D V-Cache, which places the extra SRAM under the compute die. This gives the cores direct access to the Integrated Heat Spreader (IHS), meaning the chip can boost as well as its non-X3D counterpart without the SRAM acting as an insulating layer.

Last year, we shared a blogpost on watermarking, explaining what it means to watermark generative AI content, and why it's notable. The need for watermarking has become even more critical as people all over the world have begun to generate and share AI-generated images, video, audio, and text. Images and video have become so realistic that they’re nearly impossible to distinguish from what you’d see captured by a real camera. Addressing this matter is multi-faceted, but there is one, clear, low-hanging fruit 🍇:.

To help out, we at Hugging Face have made visible watermarking trivially easy: Whenever you create a Space like an app or a demo, you can use our in-house app-building library Gradio to display watermarks with a single command.

For images and video, simply add the watermark parameter, like so:.

Watermarks can be specified as filenames, and for images we additionally support open images or even numpy arrays, to work best with how you want to set up your interface. One option I particularly like is QR watermarks, which can be used to get much more information about the content, and can even be matched to the style of your image or video.

You can also add custom visible watermarks for AI-generated text, so that whenever it is copied, the watermark will appear. Like so:.

This automatically adds attribution when users copy text from AI responses, further aiding in AI transparency and disclosure for text generation.

Try it all out today, build your own watermark, have fun!

Acknowledgements: Abubakar Abid and Yuvraj Sharma collaborated on this work and blog post.

In a recent development, very cool, good step towards transparency! 🤗.

I encourage the development community to adopt watermarks and a comprehensive policy related to identifying AI-generated images and video. If not, I believe there will be legislation and legal "incentives" enforcing such a policy. We must take initiative instead of waiting to respond to a negative event.

A very useful article! Indeed, it is becoming increasingly difficult to distinguish generated content from reality, and visible watermarks in Gradio are an excellent solution for transparency. However, sometimes you get tired of this digital race and just want to experience real luck and emotions. If you're looking for a way to switch gears after coding, I recommend checking out VegasHero — there's no need for watermarks there, just pure excitement.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that TL;DR Today we release LeRobotDataset:v3!
  • Sources indicate that leRobotDataset is a standardized dataset format designed to address the specific needs of robot learning, and it provides unified and convenient access to robotics data across modalities, including sensorimotor readings, multiple camera feeds and teleoperation status.
  • Within lerobot, the robotics library we are developing at Hugging Face, LeRobotDataset provides a unified interface for working with multi-modal, time-series data, and it seamlessly integrates both with the Hugging Face and Pytorch ecosystems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that TL;DR Today we release LeRobotDataset:v3! In our previous LeRobotDataset:v2 release, we stored one episode per file, hitting file-system limitations when scaling datasets to millions of episodes. LeRobotDataset:v3 packs multiple episodes in a single file, using relational metadata to retrieve information at the individual episode level from multi-episode files. The newly introduced format also natively supports accessing datasets in streaming mode, allowing to process large datasets on the fly.We provide a one-liner util to convert all datasets in the LeRobotDataset format to the new format, and are very excited to share this milestone with the community ahead of our next stable release!

Sources indicate that leRobotDataset is a standardized dataset format designed to address the specific needs of robot learning, and it provides unified and convenient access to robotics data across modalities, including sensorimotor readings, multiple camera feeds and teleoperation status. Our dataset format also stores general information regarding the way the data is being collected (metadata), including a textual description of the task being performed, the kind of robot used and measurement details like the frames per second at which both image and robot state streams are sampled. Metadata are useful to index and search across robotics datasets on the Hugging Face Hub!

Within lerobot, the robotics library we are developing at Hugging Face, LeRobotDataset provides a unified interface for working with multi-modal, time-series data, and it seamlessly integrates both with the Hugging Face and Pytorch ecosystems. The dataset format is designed to be easily extensible and customizable, and already supports openly available datasets from a wide range of embodiments—including manipulator platforms such as the SO-100 arms and ALOHA-2 setup, real-world humanoid data, simulation datasets, and even self-driving car data! You can explore the current datasets contributed by the community using the dataset visualizer! 🔗.

Besides scale, this new release of LeRobotDataset also enables support for a streaming functionality, allowing to process batches of data from large datasets on the fly, without having to download prohibitively large collections of data onto disk. You can access and use any dataset in v3.0 in streaming mode by using the dedicated StreamingLeRobotDataset interface! Streaming datasets is a key milestone towards more accessible robot learning, and we are excited about sharing it with the community 🤗.

lerobot is the end-to-end robotics library developed at Hugging Face, supporting real-world robotics as well as state of the art robot learning algorithms. The library allows to record datasets locally directly on real-world robots, and to store datasets on the Hugging Face Hub. You can read more about the robots we currently support here!

Sources indicate that leRobotDataset:v3 is going to be a part of the lerobot library starting from lerobot-v0.4.0, and we are very excited about sharing it early with the community. You can install the latest lerobot-v0.3.x supporting this new dataset format directly from PyPI using:.

Follow the community's progress towards a stable release of the library here 🤗.

Once you have installed a version of lerobot which supports the upcoming dataset format, you can record a dataset with our signature robot arm, the SO-101, by using teleoperation alongside the following instructions:.

Head to the official documentation to see how to record a dataset for your use case.

A core design choice behind LeRobotDataset is separating the underlying data storage from the user-facing API. This allows for efficient serialization and storage while presenting the data in an intuitive, ready-to-use format. Datasets are organized into three main components:.

In a recent development, to support datasets with potentially millions of episodes (resulting in hundreds of millions/billions of individual frames), we merge data from different episodes into the same high-level structure. Concretely, this means that any given tabular collection and video will not contain information about one episode only, but a concatenation of the information available in multiple episodes. This keeps the pressure on the file system manageable, both locally and on remote storage providers like Hugging Face. We can then leverage metadata to gather episode-specific information, e.g. the timestamp a given episode starts or ends in a certain video.

Datasets are organized as repositories containing:.

LeRobotDataset:v3.0 will be released with lerobot-v0.4.0, together with the possibility to easily convert any dataset presently hosted on the Hugging Face Hub to the new v3.0 using:.

It has been revealed that we are very excited about sharing this newly introduced format early with the community! While we develop lerobot-v0.4.0, you can still convert your dataset to the newly updated version by using the latest lerobot-v0.3.x supporting this new dataset format directly from PyPI using:.

Note that this is a pre-release, and generally unstable version. You can follow the status of the development of our next stable release here!

Industry observers note that the conversion script convert_dataset_v21_to_v30.py aggregates the multiple episodes episode-0000.mp4, episode-0001.mp4, episode-0002.mp4, .../episode-0000.parquet, episode-0001.parquet, episode-0002.parquet, episode-0003.parquet, ... into single files file-0000.mp4/file-0000.parquet, and updates the metadata accordingly, to be able to retrieve episode-specific information from higher-level files.

Every dataset on the Hugging Face Hub containing the three main pillars presented above (Tabular and Visual Data, as well as relational Metadata), and can be accessed with a single line.

Sources indicate that most robot learning algorithms, based on reinforcement learning (RL) or behavioral cloning (BC), tend to operate on a stack of observations and actions. For instance, RL algorithms typically use a history of previous observations o_{t-H_o:t}, and BC algorithms are instead typically trained to regress chunks of multiple actions. To accommodate for the specifics of robot learning training, LeRobotDataset provides a native windowing operation, whereby we can use the seconds before and after any given observation using a delta_timestamps argument.

Conveniently, by using LeRobotDataset with a PyTorch DataLoader one can automatically collate the individual sample dictionaries from the dataset into a single dictionary of batched tensors.

You can also use any dataset in v3.0 format in streaming mode, without the need to download it locally, by using the StreamingLeRobotDataset class.

In a recent development, leRobotDataset v3.0 is a stepping stone towards scaling up robotics datasets supported in LeRobot. By providing a format to store and access large collections of robot data we are making progress towards democratizing robotics, allowing the community to train on possibly millions of episodes without even downloading the data itself!

You can try the new dataset format by installing the latest lerobot-v0.3.x, and share any feedback on GitHub or on our Discord server! 🤗.

We thank the fantastic yaak.ai team for their precious support and feedback while developing LeRobotDataset:v3. Go ahead and follow their organization on the Hugging Face Hub! We are always looking to collaborate with the community and share early features. Reach out if you would like to collaborate 😊.

We are still polishing it up a bit before releasing, but if you're interested you can checkout this PR to read more: https://github.com/huggingface/blog/pull/3084.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It said that the board voted unanimously in favor of reinstatement despite its recent statement that it had no intention of doing so ….
  • Huang’s affair with a woman suspected to be a Chinese spy became the main headline news in the tech press after coming to light at the end of last month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that nvidia has announced that disgraced CEO Jensen Huang has been reinstated to the role, effective immediately. The company’s share price jumped more than 30% in response, with the rest of the market also making significant gains.

It said that the board voted unanimously in favor of reinstatement despite its recent statement that it had no intention of doing so ….

Huang’s affair with a woman suspected to be a Chinese spy became the main headline news in the tech press after coming to light at the end of last month. The New York Times broke the story on October 29, citing it then as “a close relationship.” Nvidia initially denied that the relationship was anything out of the ordinary.

Industry observers note that that changed on November 8 when Huang publicly admitted to the affair. Nvidia’s shares dropped 5%, and the manufacturer’s board of directors opened an independent investigation. Further details emerged over the following days. Things got even worse when the same paper reported that Huang had also had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reports to him.

That led to Huang being fired resigning on November 12.

He won’t make that mistake again!

Despite putting the tech giant at enormous risk and initially lying to its board of directors, there were calls in some quarters for Huang to be reinstated. He responded by saying that he would be “honored” to return if asked to do so.

The board of directors, however, said that it had no intention of inviting him back.

Nvidia’s chair Harvey Jones noted: “The board does not intend to reinstate him.”.

That changed today, with the organization making the announcement in a press release.

According to recent reports, nvidia today announced that effective immediately, Jensen Huang has been reinstated as President and Chief Executive Officer and as a member of the Board. The Board of Directors voted unanimously to reinstate Mr. Huang following a series of discussions and meetings with Mr. Huang, after which the Board was satisfied with respect to Mr. Huang’s candor and ability to lead NVIDIA. In the process of reaching its decision, the Board received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the Board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.

Industry observers note that “The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” stated Harvey C. Jones, Chair of the Board. “We have every confidence in Jensen and look forward to working with him as he resumes his leadership of the Firm. We are grateful to Colette Kress for her outstanding service as interim CEO, in addition to her continuing responsibilities as NVIDIA’s Chief Financial Officer.” Harvey Jones will remain as Board chair.

“I am honored to return to NVIDIA and lead one of the most consequential technology companies in the world at the beginning of a fresh industrial revolution,” said Jensen Huang. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment. I want to thank the NVIDIA Board for its confidence and deliberation through this process. I am especially grateful to Harvey Jones for his leadership as Chair, and to Colette Kress and our executive staff for leading NVIDIA during this period. DRAMA is an AI facial changer from SyncMonster. In the web app, owners upload a video or image (MP4, MOV, JPG, PNG), pick a face, choose an emotion, and set intensity on a slider from subtle to strong. The app offers four core emotions (Happy, Sad, Angry, Excited) plus presets such as Surprised, Serious, Evil and Intimidating, with the extra presets on paid prepares. It supports emotion blending and editing one face in a group shot without touching the others. SyncMonster states that edits keep the original resolution, lighting and details such as glasses and beards, which is a vendor claim you should test on your own footage.

Democratizing AI Safety with RiskRubric.ai

📅 18 Sep 2025 | ⏱️ 5 min read (909 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Building trust in the open model ecosystem through standardized risk assessment.
  • More than 500,000 models can be found on the Hugging Face hub, but it’s not always clear to users how to choose the best model for them, notably on the security aspects.
  • As models become more powerful and adoption accelerates, we need equally rapid progress in AI safety and security reporting.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Building trust in the open model ecosystem through standardized risk assessment.

More than 500,000 models can be found on the Hugging Face hub, but it’s not always clear to users how to choose the best model for them, notably on the security aspects. Developers might find a model that perfectly fits their use case, but have no systematic way to evaluate its security posture, privacy implications, or potential failure modes.

As models become more powerful and adoption accelerates, we need equally rapid progress in AI safety and security reporting. We're therefore excited to announce RiskRubric.ai, a novel initiative led by Cloud Security Alliance and Noma Security, with contributions by Haize Labs and Harmonic Security, for standardized and transparent risk assessment in the AI model ecosystem.

RiskRubric.ai provides consistent, comparable risk scores across the entire model landscape, by evaluating models across six pillars: transparency, reliability, security, privacy, safety, and reputation.

The platform's approach aligns perfectly with open-source values: rigorous, transparent, and reproducible. Using Noma Security capabilities to automate the effort, each model undergoes:.

According to recent reports, these assessments produce 0-100 scores for each risk pillar, rolling up to clear A-F letter grades. Each evaluation also includes specific vulnerabilities found, recommended mitigations, and suggestions for improvements.

RiskRubric also comes with filters to help developers and organizations make deployment decisions based on what’s important for them. Need a model with strong privacy guarantees for healthcare applications? Filter by privacy scores. Building a customer-facing application requiring consistent outputs? Prioritize reliability ratings.

Evaluating both open and closed models with the exact same standards highlighted some interesting results: many open models actually outperform their closed counterparts in specific risk dimensions (particularly transparency, where open development practices shine).

Risk distribution is polarized – most models are strong, but mid-tier scores show elevated exposure.

The total risk scores range from 47 to 94, with a median of 81 (on a 100 points). Most models cluster in the “safer” range (54% are A or B level), but a long tail of underperformers drags the average down. That split indicates a polarization: models tend to be either well-protected or in the middle-score range, with fewer in between.

Industry observers note that the models concentrated in the 50–67 band (C/D range) are not outright broken, but they do provide only medium to low overall protection. This band represents the most practical area of concern, where security gaps are material enough to warrant prioritization.

According to recent reports, what this means: Don’t assume the “average” model is safe. The tail of weak performers is real – and that’s where attackers will focus. Teams can use composite scores to set a minimum threshold (e.g. 75) for procurement or deployment, ensuring outliers don’t slip into production.

Safety risk is the “swing factor” – but it tracks closely with security posture.

The Safety & Societal pillar (e.g. harmful output prevention) demonstrates the widest variation across models. Importantly, models that invest in security hardening (prompt injection defenses, policy enforcement) almost always score better on safety as well.

What this means: Strengthening core security controls goes beyond preventing jailbreaks, but also directly reduces downstream harms! Safety seems like it is a byproduct of robust security posture.

Guardrails can erode transparency – unless you design for it.

Stricter protections often make models less transparent to end customers (e.g. refusals without explanations, hidden boundaries). This can create a trust gap: users may perceive the system as “opaque” even while it’s secure.

Recent findings suggest that what this means: Security shouldn’t come at the cost of trust. To balance both, pair strong safeguards with explanatory refusals, provenance signals, and auditability. This preserves transparency without loosening defenses.

An updating results sheet can be accessed here.

Industry observers note that when risk assessments are public and standardized, the entire community can work together to improve model safety. Developers can see exactly where their models need strengthening, and the community can contribute fixes, patches, and safer fine-tuned variants. This creates a virtuous cycle of transparent improvement that's impossible with closed systems. It also helps the community at large understand what works and does not, safety wise, by studying best models.

If you want to take part in this initiative, you can submit your model for evaluation (or suggest existing models!) to understand their risk profile!

We also welcome all feedback on the assessment methodology and scoring framework.

Really insightful breakdown, Gal, the level of depth and transparency RiskRubric brings is impressive, especially given how fast the open model ecosystem is growing. At Openforge.io we’ve worked with teams navigating healthcare and finance compliance, and the lack of clear security benchmarks for AI models is often a blocker for adoption.

The six-pillar framework feels like a solid step toward building that missing trust layer. Curious, do you see RiskRubric evolving into something that could be integrated into CI/CD pipelines for real-time scoring during development?

Thanks a lot for the thoughtful comment!Yes, RiskRubric can absolutely be integrated into CI/CD or model approval workflows. Several companies that have adopted RiskRubric already use it that way: models that achieve a risk score above a defined threshold can be automatically fast-tracked for deployment, while others trigger additional reviews, compensating controls, or specific-use restrictions.We are also working on additional integrations that would make this easier and more extensible for that use!

We also have an AMA session to connect with the community and answer any further questions - feel free to register and attend!https://noma.security/behind-the-riskrubric-ai-algorithm-an-ama-on-transparent-ai-model-risk/.

Recent findings suggest that pose detection in the browser is a solved problem. You can load a model, point it at a webcam, and get a skeleton tracking a human body in real time, on a laptop, with no server involved.

And then you have a skeleton that follows someone around the screen, which is a toy.

Recent findings suggest that the gap between that toy and a feature someone would pay for is smaller than most developers expect, and it isn't made of machine learning. It's made of trigonometry you already know. This article builds a working bicep-curl rep counter to show exactly where that line falls — and more importantly, which side of it your bugs live on.

It has been revealed that I'm using MediaPipe Pose Landmarker from Google AI Edge, which is Apache-2.0 licensed and runs entirely in the tab. Here's the whole setup:.

Point that at a element carrying a camera stream and call detectForVideo. What comes back, per frame, is this:.

It has been revealed that thirty-three points. Each one is a normalised coordinate — x and y run 0 to 1 across the frame, z is a relative depth estimate — plus a visibility score saying how confident the model is that it can actually see that joint.

That's the entire output. Coordinates and confidences.

The model has no concept of exercise. It doesn't know what an arm is for. It has never heard of a bicep curl. It reports where it thinks your joints are, thirty-odd times a second, and stops.

Everything that turns that into a product is yours, and it's ordinary code.

A bicep curl is a change in the angle at the elbow. The elbow angle is defined by three of those 33 points: shoulder, elbow, wrist. In MediaPipe's pose topology those are indices 11, 13 and 15 on the left side, 12, 14 and 16 on the right.

Getting the angle is two vectors and a dot product:.

Industry observers note that this is the same maths you'd use to point a game character in a direction. Nothing about it is machine learning, and that matters for a reason I'll come back to.

One thing to notice: I'm ignoring z entirely. The depth estimate is relative, not metric — it's good enough for working out which parts of a body are nearer the camera, and not good enough to measure anything. For a 2D elbow angle, using it adds noise and buys nothing.

Here's where almost everyone's first attempt breaks.

The naive version looks at the angle and counts whenever the arm is up:.

Run that at 30 frames a second and one slow curl gives you about twenty reps. You haven't counted repetitions. You've counted frames in which the arm happened to be bent.

A rep isn't a state. It's a transition between states:.

It has been revealed that fifteen lines, and that's the feature. The counter increments exactly once per cycle, on the edge, because the guard on phase makes every other frame in that cycle a no-op.

If you used a single threshold — say, 100 degrees — you'd get a counter that fires repeatedly whenever someone holds their arm near 100 degrees and the estimate jitters by a degree either side. Every tiny fluctuation across the line is a transition, and every transition is a rep.

Two widely separated thresholds give you hysteresis. Once the arm is "up," it has to travel all the way past 150 degrees before the counter will consider another rep. Noise of a few degrees can't produce a count because no amount of jitter near 55 crosses 150.

This is the same trick a thermostat uses to avoid switching the heating on and off every few seconds, and it's the single most useful pattern in this whole category of work. Any time you turn a continuous signal into discrete events, you want two thresholds, not one.

visibility is the field people skip, and skipping it is how you get phantom reps.

When a joint goes out of frame or gets occluded, the model still returns a coordinate for it. It is obliged to return 33 points. What it does is return a guess, with a low visibility score attached — and a guessed wrist position can swing wildly between frames, which looks exactly like a very fast curl.

According to recent reports, returning null and having update bail out means an occluded frame holds the current state rather than corrupting it. The arm stays "up" until the model can actually see it come down.

In a recent development, if you want to be stricter, smooth the angle over the last three or four frames with a rolling median before it reaches the state machine. A median rejects single-frame outliers in a way a mean doesn't.

Once you've written one of these, you start recognising the shape everywhere:.

None of those require a different model. They're the same 33 coordinates with different geometry sitting on top, and the geometry is a few dozen lines each.

Here's why I keep insisting on the distinction between coordinates and meaning.

In a recent development, when my rep counter miscounts, I don't retrain anything. I don't collect a dataset, I don't label examples, I don't spin up a training job. I look at two things: my thresholds, and my state machine. One of them is wrong.

Industry observers note that that's a normal bug in normal code, and you already know how to find it. You can log the angle. You can set a breakpoint on the transition. You can write a unit test that feeds a synthetic sequence of angles through upgrade and asserts the count — no camera, no model, no fixtures:.

In a recent development, the hard part of this problem — turning pixels into joint positions — was solved by a research team and shipped to you as a file you can download. The part that's left is the part you're already good at.

You are not blocked on machine learning knowledge. You were blocked on nobody telling you this was available.

I set delegate: 'GPU' above without comment, and it deserves one. MediaPipe Tasks lets you choose between a CPU path and a GPU path, and availability of the GPU path varies by browser, platform and graphics driver.

Sources indicate that the practical consequence is that you have to test the CPU path, because for some meaningful share of your owners it isn't a fallback — it's the only path they will ever take. If you develop on a machine where the GPU delegate works and never exercise the CPU one, you have shipped something you've never run.

In a recent development, that, and the question of how often you should run the model at all, is a bigger subject than this article. It's the next one.

Jay holds a Master of Science in Information Systems from Northeastern University and a Bachelor of Engineering in Computer Engineering from the University of Mumbai.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, two days before earnings, an employee asks their coworker agent to send the preliminary quarterly results to an investor who says they're under NDA, and to copy the employee's personal Gmail so they can review the numbers tonight. The agent can read the file and send email, so it fulfills the user request. Semantic governance policies, available in Preview in Gemini platform, enable enterprises to govern their agents and provide guardrails to stop that call before it runs. They check each tool call an agent proposes against what the user asked for and against rules you write in plain language.

According to recent reports, permissions alone can't catch this. They say what an agent can do, not whether a particular call follows your rules. A model can also be talked out of the rules in its system instructions, by a user with a good reason, or by a document telling it to do something nobody asked for, a technique called indirect prompt injection. So the check has to sit outside the agent. Semantic governance policies are enforced through a policy enforcement point, such as Agent Gateway, alongside the agent governance controls we expanded in October, so policies stay separate from your agent's code.

Semantic governance policies check each tool call your agent's model proposes, before it runs, against two things:.

A call has to pass both checks to run.

Today, the policy enforcement point that Semantic governance policies support is Agent Gateway. You need to configure your agent so all your agent egress traffic goes through Agent Gateway, facilitating traffic between your agent and its model. When the model responds with a tool call, Agent Gateway sends the proposed call to the Semantic governance policy engine for evaluation before the response reaches your agent.

In the policy engine, an LLM judge evaluates the proposed call against the conversation so far, the agent's system instructions and tool descriptions, and your policies.

If the call passes, the response reaches your agent unchanged. If it doesn't, the engine replaces the response's content, tool calls included, with a configurable denial message, so the call never runs. Either way, the verdict and the judge's rationale go to Cloud Logging in your project. Responses that contain only text, such as an answer, a blueprint, or a question back to the user, aren't evaluated, because they take no action.

📅 22 Sep 2025 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1596 w)
