📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CrowdStrike and Zscaler announced a definitive acquisition agreement on November 23, 2026, under which CrowdStrike would acquire Zscaler in an all-stock transaction valuing Zscaler at an enterprise value of approximately $43.9 billion. The deal would add network controls and AI-agent connection security to CrowdStrike’s Falcon platform.

Each outstanding Zscaler share would be exchanged for 1.135 CrowdStrike shares, implying approximately $260.41 per Zscaler share based on CrowdStrike’s November 20, 2026 closing price and a roughly 34% premium to Zscaler’s closing price on that date. Both companies’ boards unanimously approved the agreement. Existing CrowdStrike and Zscaler shareholders are expected to own approximately 84.1% and 15.9%, respectively, of the combined firm after completion.

The acquisition would take CrowdStrike into network security, reflecting a model in which people, applications, and AI agents connect directly to cloud services and their traffic does not return through the data center. Firewalls and VPNs built to guard data centers cannot see, inspect, or stop that traffic. Zscaler’s Zero Trust Exchange sits inline between users, agents, and applications to enforce zero-trust controls on every connection.

It has been revealed that that position would complement CrowdStrike’s controls over endpoints, cloud workloads, identities, and data. After closing, Falcon would add Zscaler’s Zero Trust SASE, Security for AI, and Data Protection offerings, placing controls both where an agent runs and where its connections travel. CrowdStrike CEO and founder George Kurtz summarized the change: “The network used to connect people to places. Now it connects agents to data.”.

Recent findings suggest that the plan also joins the companies’ telemetry. Falcon Next-Gen SIEM would unify device and network data in one security dataset, while Falcon Flex would let customers add either manufacturer’s products under a single contract. CrowdStrike says Falcon generates trillions of endpoint and cloud-workload events daily, Zscaler processes more than 750 billion transactions per day, and the combined data would let its SafeMind frontier security models train on the adversary’s full attack path.

The companies report that their existing technology alliance spans more than 2,000 shared customers and 16 integrations, while approximately 8,000 Zscaler customers remain outside CrowdStrike’s customer base. That gap creates a cross-selling base for Falcon. Zscaler protects half of the Fortune 500 and operates its distributed inline security cloud across more than 200 service locations.

The companies project more than $10 billion in combined annual recurring revenue at closing, including Zscaler’s $3.9 billion as of its fiscal first quarter of 2027.

Industry observers note that crowdStrike estimates that the acquisition will expand its total addressable market by more than $185 billion in calendar year 2029. That figure describes potential demand rather than current revenue.

CrowdStrike targets approximately $1 billion in annualized run-rate revenue synergies by the end of the first 30 months after closing and $500 million in annualized run-rate cost synergies within 18 to 24 months. The revenue benefits would come from deeper customer relationships, cross-selling and upselling, and integration with Falcon Flex; cost savings would primarily come from optimizing data-center infrastructure, vendors, and broader operations.

Recent findings suggest that the transaction is expected to close in the second half of CrowdStrike’s fiscal year 2028, subject to Zscaler shareholder approval, required regulatory approvals, and other customary conditions. Both companies will operate independently until closing. Zscaler founder, chairman, and CEO Jay Chaudhry and his affiliates, representing approximately 34% of Zscaler’s outstanding shares, have signed voting agreements supporting the transaction.

After closing, Chaudhry is expected to continue leading the Zscaler business and join CrowdStrike’s board of directors.

The proposed combination would move customers from integrations between separate products toward one data layer and one contract. Its security value rests on whether that shared dataset can give CrowdStrike a broader view of AI-agent connections and attack paths, turning the companies’ complementary control points into more effective protection.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Planemaker's 2-to-3-year blueprint to ditch Redmond's suite stops short of the 22% who can't go near the cloud.
  • Airbus has a strategy to phase out Microsoft Office, but about 22 percent of its roughly 165,000 employees will stay on it because their sensitive data must remain on-premise.
  • In March 2018, Airbus signed a contract with Google to move its workforce - 130,000 strong at that time - onto the cloud-based Workspace suite.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Planemaker's 2-to-3-year blueprint to ditch Redmond's suite stops short of the 22% who can't go near the cloud.

Airbus has a strategy to phase out Microsoft Office, but about 22 percent of its roughly 165,000 employees will stay on it because their sensitive data must remain on-premise.

In March 2018, Airbus signed a contract with Google to move its workforce - 130,000 strong at that time - onto the cloud-based Workspace suite. Years later, compatibility challenges mean some owners still need Excel.

Catherine Jestin, Airbus's executive vice president of digital, told The Register that Google is still working to resolve software interface conflicts between departments and improve features.

Last year, for example, Google tripled the number of cells available in Sheets, which let Airbus "reduce significantly the number of users on Microsoft." This year, Google improved the compatibility of document watermarking. Contracts, for instance, are often exported from Excel to Sheets by one department, edited by another, and sent back.

"Sometimes we had compatibility complications when you were commenting, the comments were lost, or they were not transferable in one way or the other," she said.

"Now they [Google] have made it totally compatible, which means that it makes it much easier for us to decommission people working on contracts… the legal department, the sales department, purchasing department, making it much easier to have that internal collaboration.".

Airbus and Google have a roadmap to eliminate Microsoft Office. Jestin expects the migration to finish in "another two to three years.".

Recent findings suggest that not every part of the organization will switch. The Defence division, which accounts for the 22 percent (more than 36,000 people), will keep using classic Microsoft Office.

In a recent development, "We will not get 100 percent out of Microsoft because again, for the defense industry people, they cannot [use] Microsoft Office 365 or Google Workspace, they have to stay on-premise, and the only solution that is available on-premise is Microsoft. So Microsoft Office will remain for colleagues who are working in the defense and space programs.".

Industry observers note that as we pointed out a year ago, kicking the Microsoft habit is no easy feat. ®.

Recent findings suggest that if you run your own mail server, Microsoft's consumer email is terrible to deal with. You can do every thing right (SPF, DKIM, DMARC all correct and tight) and have zero problems with your IP reputation, and NEVER having sent bulk email (never mind spam/uce), and Microsoft's servers can _still_ do one of two things:.

- (bad) 550 your message, w/ no explanation. "its your problem to figure out why we rejected your mail", more or less- (worse): Accept your message, but not actually deliver it.

This latter point is especially bad. A mail server shouldn't accept a mail it can't (or won't) deliver.

Meanwhile, I put a 550 block in place on all Microsoft email servers from India, since they were hitting me with business spam _constantly_. These were validish looking O365/M365 tenants that Microsoft was apparently fine w/ sending outbound spam.

I concluded pretty promptly that I will never want to receive an email from an Indian server purporting to be an American business.

Industry observers note that it's important that people not use Microsoft or Google email hosting just as a matter of principle, at this point. Email is supposed to be distributed, not concentrated in the hands of the worlds worst actors.

The protocols powering email were written in a time of complete trust, and are horribly "broken" today (they technically transport mail, but that's only 5% of the modern email situation). There are bandaids on top of bandaids on top of bandaids which all make it a black box for any given provider. If they told you their magic sauce then others can work around it, and people running their own mail servers are such a tiny part of the internet now that it's not worth working directly with you.

According to recent reports, I'm not really sure what you mean. Sure, SMTP is ancient and designed for a better, vanished time. But the status codes all have very well documented meanings, and the "bandaids on top of bandaids" are largely within the post-SMTP (or inter-SMTP) pieces, where one company (in this case Microsoft) controls the inputs, outputs, and intermediate states. Those bandaids are not at the SMTP layer, so blaming them on SMTP is odd. This recent problem was all due to Microsoft, which either noted via SMTP "yes I a.

The reason attempts at other protocols has been abandoned is the same reason ultimately telcos can't really build a system that gets rid of all crank and marketing calls; the systems are supposed to create effectively anonymous frictionless connections between two end points. You're supposed to be able to access these networks from anywhere and connect with another end point, while the protocols find the most reliable path for the data.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that today, we are announcing that Sentence Transformers is transitioning from Iryna Gurevych’s Ubiquitous Knowledge Processing (UKP) Lab at the TU Darmstadt to Hugging Face. Hugging Face's Tom Aarsen has already been maintaining the library since late 2023 and will continue to lead the project. At its new home, Sentence Transformers will benefit from Hugging Face's robust infrastructure, including continuous integration and testing, ensuring that it stays up-to-date with the latest advancements in Information Retrieval and Natural Language Processing.

Sentence Transformers (a.k.a. SentenceBERT or SBERT) is a popular open-source library for generating high-quality embeddings that capture semantic meaning. Since its inception by Nils Reimers in 2019, Sentence Transformers has been widely adopted by researchers and practitioners for various natural language processing (NLP) tasks, including semantic search, semantic textual similarity, clustering, and paraphrase mining. After years of development and training by and for the community, over 16,000 Sentence Transformers models are publicly available on the Hugging Face Hub, serving more than a million monthly unique owners.

In a recent development, "Sentence Transformers has been a huge success story and a culmination of our long-standing research on computing semantic similarities for the whole lab. Nils Reimers has made a very timely discovery and has produced not only outstanding research outcomes, but also a highly usable tool. This continues to impact generations of students and practitioners in natural language processing and AI. I would also like to thank all the owners and especially the contributors, without whom this project would not be what it is today. And finally, I would like to thank Tom and Hugging Face for taking the project into the future.".

Industry observers note that "We're thrilled to officially welcome Sentence Transformers into the Hugging Face family! Over the past two years, it’s been amazing to see this project grow to massive global adoption, thanks to the incredible foundation from the UKP Lab and the amazing community around it. This is just the beginning: we’ll keep doubling down on supporting its growth and innovation, while staying true to the open, collaborative spirit that made it thrive in the first place.".

According to recent reports, sentence Transformers will remain a community-driven, open-source project, with the same open-source license (Apache 2.0) as before. Contributions from researchers, developers, and enthusiasts are welcome and encouraged. The project will continue to prioritize transparency, collaboration, and broad accessibility.

Recent findings suggest that the Sentence Transformers library was introduced in 2019 by Dr. Nils Reimers at the Ubiquitous Knowledge Processing (UKP) Lab at Technische Universität Darmstadt, under the supervision of Prof. Dr. Iryna Gurevych. Motivated by the limitations of standard BERT embeddings for sentence-level semantic tasks, Sentence-BERT used a Siamese network architecture to produce semantically meaningful sentence embeddings that could be efficiently compared using cosine similarity. Thanks to its modular, open-source design and strong empirical performance on tasks such as semantic textual similarity, clustering, and information retrieval, the library rapidly became a staple in the NLP research toolkit, spawning a range of follow-up work and real-world applications that rely on high-quality sentence representations.

Sources indicate that in 2020, multilingual support was added to the library, extending sentence embeddings to more than 400 languages. In 2021, with contributions from Nandan Thakur and Dr. Johannes Daxenberger, the library expanded to support pair-wise sentence scoring using Cross Encoder and Sentence Transformer models. Sentence Transformers was also integrated with the Hugging Face Hub (v2.0). For over four years, the UKP Lab team maintained the library as a community-driven open-source project and provided continued research-driven innovation. During this period, the project's development was supported by grants to Prof. Gurevych by the German Research Foundation (DFG), German Federal Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF), and Hessen State Ministry for Higher Education, Research and the Arts (HMWK).

In late 2023, Tom Aarsen from Hugging Face took over maintainership of the library, introducing modernized training for Sentence Transformer models (v3.0), as well as improvements of Cross Encoder (v4.0) and Sparse Encoder (v5.0) models.

Sources indicate that the Ubiquitous Knowledge Processing (UKP) Lab at Technische Universität Darmstadt, led by Prof. Dr. Iryna Gurevych, is internationally recognized for its research in natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning. The lab has a long track record of pioneering work in representation learning, large language models, and information retrieval, with numerous publications at leading conferences and journals. Beyond Sentence Transformers, the UKP Lab has developed a number of widely used datasets, benchmarks, and open-source tools that support both academic research and real-world applications.

Hugging Face would like to thank the UKP Lab and all past and present contributors, especially Dr. Nils Reimers and Prof. Dr. Iryna Gurevych, for their dedication to the project and for entrusting us with its maintenance and now stewardship. We also extend our gratitude to the community of researchers, developers, and practitioners who have contributed to the library's success through model contributions, bug reports, feature requests, documentation improvements, and real-world applications. We are excited to continue building on the strong foundation laid by the UKP Lab and to work with the community to further advance the capabilities of Sentence Transformers.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mach7 Technologies and Rad AI declared a partnership on November 23, 2026, to connect Mach7’s Flamingo Worklist and eUnity enterprise viewer with Rad AI Reporting, aiming to move measurements and case context between image interpretation and radiology reporting without manual re-entry.

The companies are addressing a handoff that can persist even when imaging, AI and reporting systems are connected: measurements and other clinical data do not always transfer. They framed the problem against growing imaging volumes, increasingly complex studies and a radiologist workforce struggling to keep pace. The integration is in development, with availability to be confirmed later and features and timing subject to change.

Recent findings suggest that the companies strategy to demonstrate two capabilities at RSNA 2026. Bidirectional synchronization would allow the Mach7 applications and Rad AI Reporting to share patient, study and provider context, with updates flowing from either application as a radiologist moves through cases. Dynamic measurement exchange is designed to make lengths, areas and other measurements taken in eUnity available in real time for inclusion in the report, removing the need to retype those values.

Mach7’s eUnity product documentation describes a zero-footprint diagnostic viewer, meaning it runs in a supported browser without client software or a plug-in. It works across existing imaging systems and archives and includes tools for measuring distances, angles and selected regions. The viewer can also display third-party AI and computer-aided detection results beside the original study, including the algorithm name and version. The new partnership concerns the next step: getting measurements and case context into the report.

Rad AI’s reporting documentation describes a workflow that begins with natural dictation; its Omni Report feature then generates the report and its concluding impressions, personalized to the radiologist’s style. Real-time quality checks and radiologist review precede finalization. The proposed integration would supply shared context and measurements to a workflow that still leaves verification and sign-off with the radiologist.

Recent findings suggest that the products involved are at different commercial stages. Mach7’s Flamingo product page states that the platform is not yet for sale and describes its first release as designed. Its Worklist module uses customer-set priorities and rules, turnaround targets, per-study countdowns and early alerts as studies approach their targets. Mach7 does not analyze images or clinical content to rank studies, separating that worklist logic from diagnostic image analysis. eUnity and Mach7’s vendor-neutral archive, by contrast, are already available.

Mach7’s RSNA 2026 page distinguishes those current-release products from a designated forward-looking station for forthcoming capabilities. The Rad AI integration is scheduled for demonstration at booth 4116 in Chicago’s McCormick Place during technical exhibits from November 29 to December 2, 2026.

It has been revealed that mach7 CEO Teri Thomas described the demonstration as an initial step. “Radiologists should be able to pick the best reporting tool for their reading room and have it work smoothly with their viewer from day one,” she said.

In a recent development, the companies initiative to extend the integration over time and shape its roadmap with input from mutual customers. For radiology groups combining separate viewer and reporting suppliers, the announcement establishes a specific interoperability path. Its practical significance depends on delivery: the companies still need to confirm availability, while mutual customers will help determine which extensions follow the initial synchronization and measurement exchange.

Old-school Linux desktops find fresh routes to Wayland

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1025 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Xfce lines up 4.22 for 2027, while MATE gains an Ubuntu-based distro and a compositor of its own.
  • Xfce's next release is taking shape for 2027, while MATE consumers have fresh options for moving their familiar desktop onto Wayland.
  • One of the oldest surviving Linux desktops has a relatively slow release schedule: newly introduced stable releases of Xfce tend to appear every two years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Xfce lines up 4.22 for 2027, while MATE gains an Ubuntu-based distro and a compositor of its own.

Xfce's next release is taking shape for 2027, while MATE consumers have fresh options for moving their familiar desktop onto Wayland.

One of the oldest surviving Linux desktops has a relatively slow release schedule: newly introduced stable releases of Xfce tend to appear every two years. The project just updated its release engineering roadmap for the forthcoming Xfce 4.22, and it looks like the next version won't arrive until early next year.

Sources indicate that we covered the release of Xfce 4.20 in December 2024, but 4.22 is still incubating. The roadmap schedules its first prerelease and feature freeze for December 15, 2026, followed by a second prerelease on January 15, 2027. A third prerelease is optional, and neither that nor the final release has a date. February or March might be plausible, but that's our guess, not the project's promise. The Xfce developers tend not to rush into things.

According to recent reports, wayland development continues in 4.22, building on the preliminary support in 4.20. The team is also working on its own compositor, xfwl4, although the roadmap doesn't promise feature parity with X11. (In Wayland terminology, the "compositor" is the combined display server and window manager.) The compositor has its own development roadmap. The name is a nod to the current Xfce X11 window manager, which is called xfwm4.

The main developer of the fresh xfwl4 compositor is Brian Tarricone, who has been working on other parts of Xfce since 2004. Back in July, he shared a blog post about his use of generative-AI coding assistants called LLMs and xfwl4.

He notes: "So yes, I use Claude quite a bit while developing xfwl4. I don't vibe-code, ever, and I probably use the LLM to generate less code than most people do. After all, building things with code is my hobby and passion (and I'm lucky I got to do it professionally for a quarter century), and driving an LLM is kinda boring.".

We find this somewhat reassuring, but any really passionate anti-LLM Xfce consumers reading this may be glad that the release schedules of Ubuntu LTS versions and Xfce stable releases are so far out of sync – sticking with Xubuntu 26.04 means there's no immediate need to adopt the new LLM-assisted compositor. Or, of course, simply keep using X11 instead of Wayland – although that might eventually mean choosing a distro that maintains X11 support, perhaps through XLibre, which has other drawbacks for some.

It has been revealed that there are other options, too. We've also seen an independent fork of xfwm4 called xfwm4-gl. It's in active development and uses OpenGL to perform window compositing directly, while the current version uses the now rather old Xrender extension.

Last year, when we looked at the release candidate of openSUSE Leap 16.0, we found that it ran Xfce on Wayland by replacing Xfwm4 with the labwc compositor that we first saw in PiOS 5.2. This worked well – about the only difference we could find was the absence of some window-management shortcuts.

(Saying that, this vulture is still happy with X11. There is only one Wayland feature we want: the ability to set different dots-per-inch ratios on different screens. We can approximate that on X11 by scaling individual outputs. This works well enough – it just makes one of the screens look a little fuzzy.).

Labwc is one of the more flexible, and X11-like, compositors out there, and can be found in other projects. Scott Sturrock recently wrote to us to tell us about his newly introduced MATE Wayland Desktop project. This is an independent distro, combining an Ubuntu 26.04 base, the latest MATE 1.29, and version 0.9 of the labwc compositor. (That's from labwc's older 0.9 series; the latest release is 0.20.3. The numbering jumped to align with the version of wlroots it uses, while 0.9 remains a maintenance branch.).

MATE is a continuing fork of GNOME 2.32, the final release of GNOME 2. GNOME 2 used the Metacity X11 window manager – indeed, the Windows-like GNOME Flashback session still uses Metacity, which is at the moment at version 3.56.0. MATE's fork of Metacity is called Marco.

In a recent development, there is already a way to run MATE using Wayland: the MATE Wayland Session uses the Wayfire compositor. Wayfire was inspired by Compiz, the 3D compositing window manager remembered for its "wobbly windows" effect, and Wayfire has lots of its own special effects, as the Wayfire wiki's tutorial demonstrates with a lot of animated images. Wayfire is quite a capable environment in its own right – so, arguably, somewhat overkill for the traditional-style MATE environment.

Industry observers note that as yet another alternative, developer Kerem Söke recently declared a latest MATE-specific compositor called Polo. Polo is intended as a direct replacement for Marco. The Polo 1.0 release notes tell some of the story. Polo aims to be as similar as it can to the familiar Marco window manager: it picks up existing configuration, keystrokes, Alt-Tab behaviour, and so on. It's already at version 1.0.2. It can do wobbly windows and so on as well, it has its own polo-tweaks program, and a roadmap for improving MATE's integration with Wayland.

In a recent development, both projects went public around the same time, but MATE Wayland Desktop is already packaged up and ready to install. We suspect that if Polo is successful, it will find its way into the Ubuntu repositories, and perhaps the two projects will eventually come together.

Sources indicate that xfce is about a year older than KDE – however, the early releases of Xfce weren't open source. So, KDE is the oldest Linux desktop that has been open source from the start.

According to recent reports, xfce isn't the oldest Linux desktop of all, though. There were some proprietary commercial desktop environments around before either Xfce or KDE existed, such as IXI's X.desktop [PDF]. Most originally ran on commercial Unixes and were later ported to Linux – but they didn't stick around into the modern FOSS era. ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we’re excited to announce a newly introduced collaboration between Hugging Face and VirusTotal, the world’s leading threat-intelligence and malware analysis platform. This collaboration enhances the security of files shared across the Hugging Face Hub, helping protect the machine learning community from malicious or compromised assets.

TL;DR - Starting today, every one of the 2.2M+ public model and datasets repositories on the Hugging Face Hub is being continuously scanned with VirusTotal.

Industry observers note that AI models are powerful but they’re also complex digital artifacts that can include large binary files, serialized data, and dependencies that sometimes carry hidden risks. As of today HF Hub hosts 2.2 Million Public model artifacts. As we continue to grow into the world’s largest open platform for Machine Learning models and datasets, ensuring that shared assets remain safe is essential.

By collaborating with VirusTotal, we’re adding an extra layer of protection and visibility by enabling files shared through Hugging Face to be checked against one of the largest and most trusted malware intelligence databases in the world.

In a recent development, whenever you visit a repository page or a file or directory page, the Hub will automatically retrieve VirusTotal information about the corresponding files. Example.

This provides valuable context to customers and organizations before they download or integrate files from the Hub.

If you’d like to learn more about this integration or explore ways to contribute to a safer open-source AI ecosystem, reach out to security@huggingface.co.

Together, we can make AI collaboration not just open but secure by design.

Sierra Raises $1.75B in Series F Funding at $30B Valuation

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (626 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sierra confirmed on November 23, 2026 that it is raising $1.75 billion in Series F funding at a $30 billion valuation, in a round led by Greenoaks and Lightspeed Venture Partners.
  • Sources indicate that the terms follow Sierra’s May 4, 2026 announcement that it was raising $950 million, led by Tiger Global and GV, at a valuation above $15 billion.
  • Sierra reported on October 30, 2026 that annual recurring revenue (ARR) had passed $400 million, including more than $150 million added in the third quarter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sierra confirmed on November 23, 2026 that it is raising $1.75 billion in Series F funding at a $30 billion valuation, in a round led by Greenoaks and Lightspeed Venture Partners. The organization builds AI agents that handle customer interactions and carry out business tasks for large enterprises.

Sources indicate that the terms follow Sierra’s May 4, 2026 announcement that it was raising $950 million, led by Tiger Global and GV, at a valuation above $15 billion. Benchmark, Sequoia, Greenoaks, GV and Tiger Global are participating again after previously serving as lead investors.

Sierra reported on October 30, 2026 that annual recurring revenue (ARR) had passed $400 million, including more than $150 million added in the third quarter. That quarterly addition exceeded the ARR it added during the entire prior year.

The manufacturer stated ARR took six months to double from $100 million to $200 million, then five months to double from $200 million to $400 million.

Customer adoption has accompanied that growth. Sierra reported working with more than 40% of the Fortune 50 in May and almost 50% by the October enhancement. The latter disclosure also described a large US retailer with more than $40 billion in revenue going from its first meeting with Sierra to a live agent in 27 days.

The May announcement supplied further deployment measures: Nordstrom introduced its Nora voice agent in five weeks; Singtel launched in 10 weeks with resolution rates above 70%; and Cigna entered production in eight weeks while reducing patient-authentication time by 80%.

Sierra also describes the approach as more complex operationally, contractually and for accounting than seat- or consumption-based pricing. Ghostwriter sits above that pricing model. Sierra states teams define goals and guardrails, and the system builds, tests and deploys agents. A September 28, 2026 update made Ghostwriter proactive inside Slack and Teams: it can review customer conversations, recommend changes and experiments, monitor results and identify when those results are statistically significant.

Sierra says its constellation-of-models architecture assembles agents from 15 or more frontier, open-weight and proprietary models, selecting different models for tasks such as low-latency tool calling, classification, long-context reasoning and tone. Its Agent OS orchestrates those tasks, applies supervisors for guardrails and quality checks, and tracks provider latency, errors and timeouts so traffic can fail over to healthier models when a provider degrades.

The financing ultimately ties Sierra’s growth story to execution: rapid deployments supply the customer base, while its pricing model requires agents to operate autonomously and produce clearly attributable results.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Shares plunge around 70% as outsourcer cuts profit expectations and plans £190M cash call.
  • Capita CEO Adolfo Hernandez has stepped down with immediate effect as the outsourcer warned of sharply lower profits next year, nearly a year after its troubled takeover of administration of the UK's Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS).
  • In a statement, Capita said CFO Pablo Andres had become CEO, with group financial controller Gemma Bate-Williams succeeding him as finance chief.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Shares plunge around 70% as outsourcer cuts profit expectations and plans £190M cash call.

Capita CEO Adolfo Hernandez has stepped down with immediate effect as the outsourcer warned of sharply lower profits next year, nearly a year after its troubled takeover of administration of the UK's Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS).

In a statement, Capita said CFO Pablo Andres had become CEO, with group financial controller Gemma Bate-Williams succeeding him as finance chief.

Industry observers note that capita now expects adjusted operating profit for 2027 to be £85 million to £95 million below previous expectations. That includes £15 million to £25 million in additional costs under a pensions recovery plan agreed with the Cabinet Office, alongside pressure from contract exits and other trading headwinds.

Shares fell around 70 percent following the announcement.

Industry observers note that the tech giant – which is also coming under fire for its £370 million contract with the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) – mentioned it had made significant progress in its transformation and strategic simplification. It also prepares to raise around £190 million through a share issue in the first half of 2027 to reduce borrowing and to "allow the business to move forward from a more stable foundation," subject to support from its financial creditors.

James Preece, principal analyst at UK tech research firm Megabuyte, noted: "Slow motion car crash comes to mind. It has been a turnaround job for coming up to four years now, with long-suffering shareholders watching dozens of disposals and business exits fail to arrest a structural decline in both margins and growth.

According to recent reports, "Today's update suggests that management's underlying forecast assumptions alongside other more transient factors were still too punchy, and the leverage situation now calls for action. The share price reaction suggests confidence in this being a one-and-done raise is limited," he noted.

Capita took over administration of the scheme in December 2025 under a seven-year, £239 million contract, after which The Register exclusively revealed problems with its online systems. The vendor promised AI and automation, but the takeover brought a glitchy online portal, while some members struggled to receive pension payments. By January, it was clear the service was seriously failing, leaving some retired civil servants struggling to make ends meet.

Industry observers note that capita missed its deadline to restore normal service by the end of June. It subsequently told MPs that all but the most complex cases would return to normal service by September.

The pensions scheme serves around 1.7 million members. Media reports and MPs have described members feeling upset, frustrated, and ignored, with some waiting months for payments.

Industry observers note that the government said it had withheld £10 million in payments over Capita's performance during the transition of the pensions service and was negotiating further penalties. It also appointed an auditor to assess the case for further penalties for Capita's performance on the contract.

Industry observers note that last month, the National Audit Office launched an investigation into the CSPS contract. Responding to the investigation, Capita said it "accepts that performance remains below the standards that scheme members and the Government rightly expect" and that fixing the problems was its top priority.

Industry observers note that the Public and Commercial Services Union is campaigning to get the government to scrap a separate Capita contract, the Synergy shared services deal, which Capita values at £370 million. The deal covers HR, payroll, finance, and other back-office services across four government departments and nearly 100 arm's-length bodies. Rival bidder Sopra Steria, which owns incumbent provider SSCL, has also released a legal challenge alleging Capita's bid was abnormally low. Capita and the DWP – which leads on the contract – have denied the allegations. ®.

According to recent reports, with tools like TRL, TorchForge and verl, the open-source community has shown how to scale AI across complex compute infrastructure. But compute is only one side of the coin. The other side is the developer community; the people and tools that make agentic systems possible. That’s why Meta and Hugging Face are partnering to launch the OpenEnv Hub: a shared and open community hub for agentic environments.

Recent findings suggest that agentic environments define everything an agent needs to perform a task: the tools, APIs, credentials, execution context, and nothing else. They bring clarity, safety, and sandboxed control to agent behavior.

These environments can be used for both training and deployment, and serve as the foundation for scalable agentic development.

Industry observers note that modern AI agents can act autonomously across thousands of tasks. However, a large language model isn’t enough to get those tasks to actually run — it needs access to the right tools. Exposing millions of tools directly to a model isn’t reasonable (or safe). Instead, we need agentic environments: secure, semantically clear sandboxes that define exactly what’s required for a task, and nothing more. These environments handle the critical details:.

To supercharge this next wave of agentic development, Meta-PyTorch and Hugging Face are partnering to launch a Hub for Environments: a shared space where developers can build, share, and explore OpenEnv-compatible environments for both training and deployment. The figure below shows how OpenEnv fits in the new post-training stack being developed by Meta, with integrations for other libraries like TRL, SkyRL, and Unsloth underway:.

Alongside this, we’re releasing the OpenEnv 0.1 Spec (RFC) to gather community feedback and help shape the standard.

Recent findings suggest that in the current state of the repository, environment creators can create environments using step(), reset(), close() APIs (part of RFCs below). A few examples on how to create such environments can be seen here. Environment users can play with local Docker based environments for all environments already available in the repo. Following RFCs are under review:.

In a recent development, this is just the beginning. We’re integrating the OpenEnv Hub with Meta’s new TorchForge RL library, and collaborating with other open-source RL projects such as verl, TRL, and SkyRL to expand compatibility. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Payments platform hasn't disclosed how the data was captured or the scale of the breach.
  • Software e-commerce platform Cleverbridge has admitted that hackers stole customers' card numbers and CVV security codes, raising questions about how the attackers captured data that payment security rules prohibit retaining after authorization.
  • Recent findings suggest that the Germany-headquartered firm, which handles software sales and subscriptions on behalf of other businesses, detected unauthorized activity on its platform on November 4.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Payments platform hasn't disclosed how the data was captured or the scale of the breach.

Software e-commerce platform Cleverbridge has admitted that hackers stole customers' card numbers and CVV security codes, raising questions about how the attackers captured data that payment security rules prohibit retaining after authorization.

Recent findings suggest that the Germany-headquartered firm, which handles software sales and subscriptions on behalf of other businesses, detected unauthorized activity on its platform on November 4. In an incident update, Cleverbridge stated it had cut off the intruders' access and released an investigation that later established payment card information had been copied from its systems.

The public notice doesn't spell out exactly what was stolen, but an email sent to affected customers, seen by The Register, fills in some rather key blanks.

"Based on our investigation to date, the information involved includes payment card details you used to make a purchase through Cleverbridge, notably your card number, expiry date, card security code (CVV/CVC), and contact details," the company told customers.

Email addresses, billing addresses, and phone numbers were also among the information potentially exposed, although Cleverbridge reckons account passwords escaped the breach.

Industry observers note that more concerning are the stolen CVV codes. PCI DSS rules prohibit retaining card verification codes after authorization, even in encrypted form.

It has been revealed that cleverbridge hasn't explained how the attackers obtained the codes, whether they were retained after transactions, or whether the criminals intercepted them during payment processing. The company didn't respond to The Register's questions about the breach.

Cleverbridge handles the business of selling software online, from taking payments to managing subscriptions, and its client roster includes some familiar names in enterprise IT, such as Red Hat, SUSE, Tenable, Veeam, Jamf, Parallels, and Plesk.

In a recent development, that doesn't mean customers of all those companies had their card details stolen. Cleverbridge hasn't named the vendors affected by the intrusion, nor has it disclosed how many people were caught up in the breach or how long the hackers were poking around its systems.

Recent findings suggest that in its notification to customers, the manufacturer mentioned it had contacted data protection authorities, payment card schemes, and its payment partners, and was working with a specialist police cybercrime unit. It began notifying affected individuals on November 20, more than two weeks after discovering the intrusion.

Recent findings suggest that affected customers are being offered 24 months of free credit monitoring and fraud assistance. That may help detect identity misuse, but it won't stop a crook armed with their card number, expiration date, and CVV from attempting a fraudulent purchase.

Recent findings suggest that two years of credit monitoring is a nice gesture, but customers whose card numbers and CVVs are now in criminal hands might prefer a new bit of plastic. ®.

From revamped datasets to versatile editing tools, latest simulation environments, and a groundbreaking plugin system for hardware, LeRobot is continuously evolving to meet the demands of cutting-edge embodied AI.

LeRobot v0.4.0 delivers a major upgrade for open-source robotics, introducing scalable Datasets v3.0, powerful newly introduced VLA models like PI0.5 and GR00T N1.5, and a new plugin system for easier hardware integration. The release also adds support for LIBERO and Meta-World simulations, simplified multi-GPU training, and a new Hugging Face Robot Learning Course.

Industry observers note that we've completely overhauled our dataset infrastructure with LeRobotDataset v3.0, featuring a newly introduced chunked episode format and streaming capabilities. This is a game-changer for handling massive datasets like OXE (Open X Embodiment) and Droid, bringing unparalleled efficiency and scalability.

We've also provided a conversion script to easily migrate your existing v2.1 datasets to the new v3.0 format, ensuring a smooth transition. Read more about it in our previous blog post. Open-source robotics keeps leveling up!

Working with LeRobot datasets just got a whole lot easier! We've introduced a powerful set of utilities for flexible dataset editing.

With our latest lerobot-edit-dataset CLI, you can now:.

These tools streamline your workflow, allowing you to curate and optimize your robot datasets like never before. Check out the docs for more details!

We're continuously expanding LeRobot's simulation capabilities to provide richer and more diverse training environments for your robotic policies.

LeRobot now officially supports LIBERO, one of the largest open benchmarks for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies, boasting over 130 tasks! This is a huge step toward building the go-to evaluation hub for VLAs, enabling easy integration and a unified setup for evaluating any VLA policy.

Check out the LIBERO dataset and our docs to get started!

Industry observers note that we've integrated Meta-World, a premier benchmark for testing multi-task and generalization abilities in robotic manipulation, featuring over 50 diverse manipulation tasks. This integration, along with our standardized use of gymnasium ≥ 1.0.0 and mujoco ≥ 3.0.0, ensures deterministic seeding and a robust simulation foundation.

Train your policies with the Meta-World dataset today!

We're making robot control more flexible and accessible, enabling fresh possibilities for data collection and model training.

Getting data from a robot to a model (and back!) is tricky. Raw sensor data, joint positions, and language instructions don't match what AI models expect. Models need normalized, batched tensors on the right device, while your robot hardware needs specific action commands.

Recent findings suggest that we're excited to introduce Processors: a new, modular pipeline that acts as a universal translator for your data. Think of it as an assembly line where each ProcessorStep handles one specific job—like normalizing, tokenizing text, or moving data to the GPU.

It has been revealed that you can chain these steps together into a powerful pipeline to perfectly manage your data flow. We've even created two distinct types to make life easier:.

According to recent reports, this system makes it simple to connect any policy to any robot, ensuring your data is always in the perfect format for every step of the way. Learn more about it in our Introduction to Processors documentation.

It has been revealed that training large robot policies just got a lot faster! We've integrated Accelerate directly into our training pipeline, making it incredibly simple to scale your experiments across multiple GPUs with just one command:.

According to recent reports, whether you're fine-tuning a policy or running large-scale experiments, LeRobot now handles all the complexities of distributed training for you. This means you can drastically reduce training time, cutting it in half with 2 GPUs, down to a third with 3 GPUs, and beyond.

Check out the documentation to accelerate your robot learning!

According to recent reports, you can find the models on the Hugging Face Hub: pi0.5_base, pi0_base, and their Libero-tuned counterparts. For more details, checkout the Physical Intelligence Reasearch.

This open foundation model is a powerhouse for generalized robot reasoning and skills. But what makes GR00T N1.5 a game-changer?

Now, connecting any robot, camera, or teleoperator is as simple as a pip install, eliminating the need to modify the core library.

Learn how to create your own plugin in our documentation.

Thanks to our fresh plugin system, we've also added Reachy 2 from Pollen Robotics to LeRobot! Reachy 2 is available for both real robot control and simulation, enabling you to experiment with teleoperation and autonomous demos right away.

Thanks to our powerful new pipeline system, you can now teleoperate your follower arm right from your phone (iOS/Android). The phone acts as a teleoperator device, and our RobotProcessor pipeline handles all the transformations, allowing you to drive robots in different action spaces (like end-effector space) with ease. Check out the examples!

Sources indicate that we're launching a comprehensive, self-paced, and entirely open-source course designed to make robot learning accessible to everyone! If you're curious about how real-world robots learn, this is the perfect place to start.

Join the Hugging Face Robotics organization to follow along and start your journey!

This guide provides self-contained explanations, re-derives modern techniques from first principles, and includes ready-to-use code examples using LeRobot and Hugging Face.

Sources indicate that the tutorial itself is hosted in a Space and it features practical examples using LeRobot, with all models and datasets on the Hugging Hub. You can also check out our paper for a detailed overview.

Beyond these major features, this release is packed with numerous bug fixes, documentation improvements, updated dependencies, more examples and better infrastructure to make your experience with LeRobot smoother and more reliable.

We want to extend a huge thank you to everyone in the community for your invaluable contributions, feedback, and support. We're incredibly excited about the future of open-source robotics and can't wait to work with you on what's next!

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Microsoft has issued a critical vulnerability advisory after attackers were caught raiding Azure API Management (APIM) instances for secrets and performing admin operations.
  • According to a nonpublic advisory, seen by The Register, Microsoft stated the attacks, which have already affected two major energy companies, only impact customers on Azure API Management Classic tiers, not Azure API Management v2.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft claims mitigation is in place, but admins must investigate possible compromise and rotate secrets.

Microsoft has issued a critical vulnerability advisory after attackers were caught raiding Azure API Management (APIM) instances for secrets and performing admin operations.

According to a nonpublic advisory, seen by The Register, Microsoft stated the attacks, which have already affected two major energy companies, only impact customers on Azure API Management Classic tiers, not Azure API Management v2.

It noted of the now-patched vuln: "Our investigation found that customers were exposed and an unauthorized party could have used the problem to access secrets stored in Azure API Management Classic instances before Microsoft identified the security issue.".

Microsoft linked exposure to Classic-tier configurations that did not follow its network security guidance or stored secrets directly in APIM rather than referencing them from Azure Key Vault.

Microsoft directs customers to its security guidance for the recommended configuration.

The advisory lists potentially exposed secrets, including named values, client secrets associated with identity providers and OpenID Connect providers, subscription keys, and tokens used to call direct management APIs.

Security expert Anders Kristiansen warned that stolen credentials could also give attackers access to services behind APIM.

"If someone obtains a credential from that configuration, they may be able to use it directly against the service it protects, outside APIM," he wrote. "What they can reach depends on the credential's permissions and whether it is still valid.".

Norway's National Security Authority (NSM) urged organizations using APIM to assume their secrets and named values had been exposed and rotate all tokens and secrets.

The agency also advised mapping the information accessible through each APIM instance to assess the potential scope of any compromise.

In a recent development, NSM credited Norway's energy sector with first detecting the vulnerability last week. It named gas giant Equinor and hydropower company Skagerak Energi among the affected organizations.

The authority commended Equinor for its early detection and rapid information-sharing, and warned that growing use of AI increased the risk of further exploitation.

Sources indicate that "The vulnerability affects several sectors in Norway and also beyond Norway's borders," it said. "NSM has close dialogue and cooperation with national and international partners and businesses about the situation.

"When a vulnerability becomes known, multiple actors will be able to attempt to exploit it. Rapid escalation in the use of artificial intelligence is affecting the situation. This poses a risk to Norwegian businesses.".

Sources indicate that customers who spoke to The Register warned that forgotten development and test instances could leave more organizations exposed. The extent of exploitation remains unclear.

Microsoft mentioned it identified the security problem on November 18 and automatically applied a mitigation to close the access path the following day.

The Windows giant stated customers still needed to investigate whether their instances had been compromised before the mitigation was applied.

NSM nevertheless advised organizations to check their instance's runtime version against its published patch thresholds and contact their provider if it remained unpatched.

Microsoft did not immediately respond to our request for comment. ®.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Marlowe confirmed on November 23, 2026 that it had raised $277 million in seed funding and detailed its plan to build and operate AI factories designed for inference workloads across multiple types of chips.

According to recent reports, the institutional investors named include Accel, Bessemer, Altimeter, Atreides and Eclipse, alongside other venture firms and angel investors. Dan Lewis and Kutta Srinivasan founded Marlowe in May 2026 in collaboration with Lior Susan, Ido Susan and Chris Ré. Lewis is chief executive and Srinivasan is chief technology officer.

Marlowe says inference usage is growing faster than supply, increasing costs and throttling use. Existing clusters are not optimized for inference, while financing, construction, permitting, regulation and power constraints are making upcoming capacity harder to bring online. Data-center construction costs have risen 40% since 2020, intensifying the focus on getting more output from available power.

Marlowe positions its approach against the NVIDIA-centered AI factory, which integrated GPUs, CPUs, networking and software as the industry built larger training clusters. Its strategy addresses two limitations of general-purpose infrastructure: a single system cannot serve every training and inference workload efficiently, and dependence on one chipmaker concentrates supply-chain risk.

AMD, Amazon, Arm, Broadcom, Cerebras, Etched, Google and Meta are among the companies Marlowe identifies as developing chips intended to reduce inference costs or improve performance. Its premise is that a chip alone cannot produce tokens; facilities, networking and software are necessary for upcoming silicon to reach its design potential.

Industry observers note that marlowe intends to design, build and operate compute for specific inference workloads rather than supply identical configurations for every customer. Its variables include response time, CPU-to-GPU ratio, model size and architecture, input-to-output ratio, security and price sensitivity. A coding agent, a voice assistant that must respond in under a second and long-document analysis therefore present different infrastructure requirements.

Industry observers note that marlowe says optimizing data-center and inference layers independently can strand power and underutilize compute. Its alternative is to co-design the stack for each major workload class. The published design extends from chip selection and facility design to the software that manages servers, executes models and routes tokens.

The company projects that gains in networking, power management, AI-driven fleet operations and workload-specific inference optimization can compound into a 2–3x overall advantage in performance, availability, resiliency and cost. Its operating measures are tokens per watt, tokens per dollar and GPU uptime, tying that objective to energy use, customer economics and utilization.

Marlowe expects its first site to go live in December 2026 as it develops sites and works with several chipmakers. AMD senior vice president of AI Vamsi Boppana noted AMD expects to deploy its Helios system with Marlowe in 2027, and highlighted Marlowe’s contributions to AMD’s software ecosystem.

Etched co-founder and president Rob Wachen mentioned Etched expects to deploy its first inference clusters with Marlowe during 2026. Marlowe’s team also embeds with AI application companies to optimize their workloads for alternative silicon. Its target customers are AI application and platform companies seeking greater compute capacity at lower cost, and the organization is hiring in data-center engineering, infrastructure software and hardware-software co-design.

Those deployments will test whether Marlowe’s coordinated design can make alternative silicon practical for customers while delivering the efficiency gains it has projected.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • TL;DR: After five years of development, huggingface_hub has reached v1.0 - a milestone that marks the library's maturity as the Python package powering 200,000 dependent libraries and providing core functionality for accessing over 2 million public models, 0.5 million public datasets, and 1 million public Spaces.
  • 🚀 We highly recommend upgrading to v1.0 to benefit from major performance improvements and fresh capabilities.
  • In a recent development, major changes in this release include the migration to httpx as the backend library, a completely redesigned hf CLI (which replaces the deprecated huggingface-cli) featuring a Typer-based interface with a significantly expanded feature set, and full adoption of hf_xet for file transfers, replacing the legacy hf_transfer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TL;DR: After five years of development, huggingface_hub has reached v1.0 - a milestone that marks the library's maturity as the Python package powering 200,000 dependent libraries and providing core functionality for accessing over 2 million public models, 0.5 million public datasets, and 1 million public Spaces. This release introduces breaking changes designed to support the next decade of open machine learning, driven by a global community of almost 300 contributors and millions of consumers.

🚀 We highly recommend upgrading to v1.0 to benefit from major performance improvements and fresh capabilities.

In a recent development, major changes in this release include the migration to httpx as the backend library, a completely redesigned hf CLI (which replaces the deprecated huggingface-cli) featuring a Typer-based interface with a significantly expanded feature set, and full adoption of hf_xet for file transfers, replacing the legacy hf_transfer. You can find the full release notes here.

We’ve worked hard to ensure that huggingface_hub v1.0.0 remains backward compatible. In practice, most ML libraries should work seamlessly with both v0.x and v1.x versions. The main exception is transformers, which explicitly requires huggingface_hub v0.x in its v4 releases and v1.x in its upcoming v5 release. For a detailed compatibility overview across libraries, refer to the table in this issue.

Every major library has a story. For huggingface_hub, it began with a simple idea: what if sharing machine learning models could be as easy as sharing code on GitHub?

In a recent development, in the early days of the Hugging Face Hub, researchers and practitioners faced a common frustration. Training a state-of-the-art model required significant compute resources and expertise. Once trained, these models often lived in isolation, stored on local machines and shared via (broken) Google Drive links. The AI community was duplicating work, wasting resources, and missing opportunities for collaboration.

The Hugging Face Hub emerged as the answer to this challenge. Initially, it was primarily used to share checkpoints compatible with the transformers library. All the Python code for interacting with the Hub lived within this library, making it inaccessible for other libraries to reuse.

In late 2020, we shipped huggingface_hub v0.0.1 with a simple mission: extract the internal logic from transformers and create a dedicated library that would unify how to access and share machine learning models and datasets on the Hugging Face Hub. Initially, the library was as straightforward as a Git wrapper for downloading files and managing repositories. Five years and 35+ releases later, huggingface_hub has evolved far beyond its origins.

According to recent reports, the early releases established the basics. Version 0.0.8 introduced our first APIs, wrapping Git commands to interact with repositories. Version 0.0.17 brought token-based authentication, enabling secure access to private repositories and uploads. These were humble beginnings, but they laid the groundwork for everything that followed.

Industry observers note that in June 2022, version 0.8.1 marked a pivotal moment: we introduced the HTTP Commit API. Instead of requiring Git and Git LFS installations, users could now upload files directly through HTTP requests. The new create_commit() API simplified workflows dramatically, especially for large model files that are cumbersome to use with Git LFS. In addition, a git-aware cache file layout was introduced. All libraries (not only transformers, but third party ones as well) would now share the same cache, with explicit versioning and file deduplication.

In a recent development, this wasn't just a technical improvement. It was a philosophical shift. We were no longer building a Git wrapper for transformers; we were building purpose-built infrastructure for machine learning artifacts that could power any library in the ML ecosystem.

According to recent reports, as the Hub grew from a model repository into a full platform, huggingface_hub kept pace with an expanding API surface. Core repository primitives matured: listing trees, browsing refs and commits, reading files or syncing folders, managing tags, branches, and release cycles. Repository metadata and webhooks rounded up the offering so teams could react to changes in real time.

It has been revealed that in parallel, Spaces emerged as a simple yet powerful way to host and share interactive ML demos directly on the Hub. Over time, huggingface_hub gained full programmatic control to deploy and manage Spaces (hardware requests, secrets, environment configuration, uploads). To deploy models on production-scale infrastructure, Inference Endpoints were integrated as well. Finally, the Jobs API came later (Q3 2025) to complete our compute offering.

The social and community layers became first-class citizens too: from APIs for pull requests and comments, to user and organization info, repository likes, following and followers, all the way through Collections to curate and share sets of related resources. Everyday ergonomics improved too: seamless authentication in Colab, resumable downloads, reliable uploads of large-scale folders, and more.

Then came version 0.28.0 and the Inference Providers ecosystem. Instead of a single inference backend, we partnered with multiple serverless providers (Together AI, SambaNova, Replicate, Cerebras, Groq, and more) to serve one API with transparent routing. We adopted a pay-per-request inference architecture that matched how people actually wanted to work.

Version 0.30.0 introduced Xet, a groundbreaking upcoming protocol for storing large objects in Git repositories. Unlike Git LFS, which deduplicates at the file level, Xet operates at the chunk level (64KB chunks). When you update a large file in a dataset or a model, only the changed chunks are uploaded or downloaded, not the entire file.

In a recent development, the migration was massive, starting with 20 petabytes across over 500,000 repositories. Yet it happened transparently, with full backward compatibility. One year later, all 77PB+ over 6,000,000 repositories have been migrated to the Xet backend, allowing for much faster (and smarter!) uploads and downloads. This happened with no user intervention, and no disruption to existing workflows 🔥.

Sources indicate that measuring the growth and impact of an open-source library is a tricky task. Numbers tell a story of their own:.

But the real scale becomes clear when you look at the ecosystem. huggingface_hub is a dependency for over 200,000 repositories on GitHub and 3,000 packages on PyPI, powering everything from major third-party frameworks like Keras, LangChain, PaddleOCR, ChatTTS, YOLO, Google Generative AI, Moshi, NVIDIA NeMo, and Open Sora, to countless smaller libraries and tools across the ML landscape. Our own ecosystem (transformers, diffusers, datasets, sentence-transformers, lighteval, gradio, peft, trl, smolagents, timm, lerobot, etc.) benefits from this foundation as well.

The remarkable part? Most of the third-party integrations happened organically, and we played no role in them. The Hugging Face Hub empowers the ML community in countless ways, yet we're continually humbled by how far it has gone and how widely it's used.

It has been revealed that version 1.0 isn't just about reaching a milestone. It's about building the foundation for the next decade of open machine learning. The breaking changes we've made aren't arbitrary; they're strategic decisions that position huggingface_hub to scale with the explosive growth of AI while maintaining the reliability that millions of developers depend on.

In a recent development, the most significant architectural change in v1.0 is our migration from requests to httpx. This isn't just dependency churn. It's a fundamental upgrade that brings the library into the modern era of HTTP.

Why httpx? The benefits are substantial: native HTTP/2 support for better connection efficiency and true thread safety that enables safe connection reuse across multiple threads. Most importantly, httpx provides a unified API for both synchronous and asynchronous operations, eliminating the subtle behavioral differences that existed between our sync and async inference clients.

It has been revealed that the migration was designed to be as transparent as possible. Most owners won't need to change anything. For those with custom HTTP backends, we've provided clear migration paths from configure_http_backend() to set_client_factory() and set_async_client_factory().

Additionally, hf_xet is now the default package for uploading and downloading files to and from the Hub, replacing the previously optional hf_transfer, which has now been fully removed.

Version 0.32.0 introduced Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration and tiny-agents, fundamentally changing how developers build AI agents. What once required complex framework integration now takes approximately 70 lines of Python.

The MCPClient provides a standardized way for AI agents to interact with tools, while the tiny-agents CLI lets you run agents directly from the Hub. Connect to local or remote MCP servers, use any Gradio Space as a tool, and build conversational agents that feel natural and responsive.

In a recent development, all of this is built on top of our existing InferenceClient and the dozens of Inference Providers it supports. We do believe Agents are the future, and huggingface_hub is there to provide the building blocks that enable AI builders to play with them.

The CLI has evolved from a simple command-line tool into a comprehensive interface for ML operations. The streamlined hf command replaces the legacy huggingface-cli with a modern resource-action pattern:.

The CLI comes with a sandboxed installer, making it easy to upgrade without breaking existing dev environments:.

With autocompletion support and an installer that works across platforms, the CLI now feels as polished as any modern developer tool.

Version 1.0 removes legacy patterns that were holding us back. The Git-based Repository class is gone. HTTP-based methods like upload_file() and create_commit() are simpler, more reliable, and better suited for modern workflows. The HfFolder token management has been replaced with explicit login(), logout(), and get_token() functions. The old InferenceApi class has been superseded by the more feature-complete InferenceClient. hf_transfer has been fully replaced by hf_xet binary package.

Sources indicate that these changes weren't made lightly. Most deprecations were confirmed months in advance with clear warnings and migration guidance. The result is a cleaner, more maintainable codebase that can focus on forward-looking features rather than supporting deprecated patterns.

Industry observers note that we understand that breaking changes are disruptive. That's why we've invested heavily in making the migration as smooth as possible. Our comprehensive migration guide provides step-by-step instructions for every change with explanations of why each change was necessary.

According to recent reports, most importantly, we've maintained backward compatibility wherever possible. HfHubHttpError, for example, inherits from both the old requests and latest httpx base HTTPError classes, ensuring that error handling continues to work across versions. With this release, we're fully committing to the future and we will focus exclusively on v1.0 and beyond, ensuring we can deliver the performance, features, and tools the community needs to interact with the Hugging Face Hub. Previous v0.* versions will remain available on PyPI, but they will only receive vulnerability updates.

We’ve worked hard to ensure that huggingface_hub v1.0.0 remains backward compatible. In practice, most ML libraries should work seamlessly with both v0.x and v1.x versions. The main exception is transformers, which explicitly requires huggingface_hub v0.x in its v4 releases and v1.x in its upcoming v5 release. For a detailed compatibility overview across libraries, refer to the table in this concern.

To our 280+ contributors who built this library through code, documentation, translations, and community support, thank you!

We’re also deeply grateful to the entire Hugging Face community for their feedback, bug reports, and suggestions that have shaped this library.

Finally, a huge thank you to our users -from individual developers to large enterprises- for trusting huggingface_hub to power your workflows. Your support drives us to keep improving and innovating.

Sources indicate that please star us on GitHub ⭐ to show your support and help us continue building the foundation of open machine learning. It has been five years, but it is still only the beginning!

Microsoft recommended Classic or the web client while two rounds of fixes restored normal service.

A recent enhancement broke attachment handling for some Fresh Outlook users, prompting Microsoft to recommend switching to the web or Classic version of its email client.

Recent findings suggest that things are going swimmingly for New Outlook, the email client that Microsoft would very much like users to migrate to. A code change meant that for some users, opening or uploading email attachments failed. It took the manufacturer two attempts to fix the problem.

It has been revealed that microsoft confirmed there were complications on November 20, as reports that customers were having problems with attachments began rolling in. By the end of the day, the company had added inline images in email to the litany of woe and "paused the rollout of a recent client patch that may be contributing to attachment failures.".

The advice for affected owners was to switch to the web version, or use Outlook Classic to open or upload attachments and view inline images.

It has been revealed that the good news was that Microsoft produced a fix. The bad news was that this fix only resolved problems with Office attachments and inline images, leaving other attachment types affected, according to incident notice EX1561765.

The Windows behemoth tried again with a "supplemental fix" and reported the remaining problems resolved on November 21.

Users needed to close and reopen Upcoming Outlook for the fix to take effect.

Microsoft mentioned it had tested the fixes before deployment. Administrators might reasonably wish the original upgrade had received the same attention. The preliminary root cause was a "recent update to the code which supports embedded web content unexpectedly caused impact.".

The clock is ticking for Outlook Classic. Microsoft is clear that Fresh Outlook is the future, though Classic Outlook will remain available until at least 2029. The fact that the manufacturer had to suggest that affected owners fall back on the old warhorse to perform that rarely used email activity – attachment handling – is less than confidence-inspiring.

Still, by the time Outlook Classic is finally put out to pasture, we're sure Microsoft's habit of sending out broken updates will also be a thing of the past. Right? ®.

Loading data, especially at the terabyte scale, is a major pain in any machine learning workflow. We suffered this while training SmolLM3, at one point we had to wait 3 hours before each run to download enough data.

Streaming has always been possible in the datasets library, but large scale training with massive datasets remained a challenge. That changes today 🔥. We spent a few months improving the backend, focusing on streaming datasets to make it faster and more efficient.

First things first: our changes are backwards compatible. You can still stream any dataset from the Hub with the same simple streaming=True flag. It's as easy as ever. 🚀.

Thousands of AI developers around the world use datasets daily; they should just get improved performance with zero extra work.

In a recent development, streaming was a lifesaver to promptly understand a dataset, but to train models, people were usually downloading the data locally, or using a cloud storage service such as S3. That's what we were doing for training SmolVLM, we had all of our data on S3 and were streaming directly from it.

We wanted to change that, so we decided to use streaming from the Hub when we were developing nanoVLM. Soon we found a significant issue: our test run generated over 100,000 requests in under a minute, which got our IP blocked by the Hub! 😅 This happened because every DataLoader worker was initializing the dataset independently. As we dug deeper, we found that this creates a storm of redundant requests, many of which are unnecessary. Our changes ultimately reduced startup requests by a factor of 100. According to recent reports, so, what changed? We focused on two phases: startup and streaming.

Together, these improvements can double your data throughput, allowing you to train faster and more efficiently.

It has been revealed that hugging Face uses Xet: a dedupe-based storage which enables fast deduped uploads and downloads. Unlike traditional remote storage, data transfers are faster on Xet because duplicated data is only transferred once. For example: uploading a large scale dataset to Hugging Face leverages Xet which accelerates uploads. Once the dataset is uploaded, it can be streamed right away.

Deduplication for Parquet is enabled through Parquet Content Defined Chunking (CDC). Thanks to Parquet CDC and Xet deduplication, uploading datasets on Hugging Face is faster than on any traditional remote storage.

It has been revealed that this is supported by our pyspark_huggingface package, a Spark Data Source to read/write HF datasets. It includes Parquet CDC and Xet support, accelerating data transfers on HF dramatically.

Some data file formats are not supported in datasets, and sometimes there is a need for more control, so we made it easy to build custom streaming pipelines. This has been battle-tested in the LeRobot library to sample video frames, and in the WebDataset library to stream TAR archives.

We improved the HfFileSystem in the huggingface_hub library to efficiently read files from remote Hugging Face dataset repositories and stream data:.

Passing a HfFileSystem to a torch DataLoader reuses the cached results from .ls() and .glob() which eliminates the need for additional requests when listing data files.

Sources indicate that we're now using these streaming enhancements in nanoVLM to train the next generation of SmolVLMs. With these tweaks, we achieve better performance from streaming than from training on our cluster's hierarchical hard disk setup. In fact, streaming is now as fast as reading the data from local SSDs! Previously, transferring data to local SSDs was the process that used to delay our trainings by three-hours. For more details, check out our GitHub.
