📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Braiin Limited confirmed on November 23, 2026 that it had entered a non-binding term sheet to acquire Hyderabad-based Marut Drones in phases, beginning with a majority stake. The proposed transaction is valued at approximately US$40 million, including upfront consideration, performance-linked earn-outs and growth capital.

According to recent reports, if completed, Marut would join Braiin’s Robotics and AI division and be integrated with Raptor300, its autonomous crop-spraying drone platform. Braiin intends to combine autonomous flight, computer vision, predictive maintenance and agricultural-data analytics with Marut’s certified drone platforms. Founder and CEO Natraj Balasubramanian stated the goal was to build “a leading AI-led aerial intelligence business,” initially in India and then across the company’s international markets.

The upfront portion is payable at completion, while the earn-outs depend on Marut’s subsequent performance. Braiin would also fund growth under a mutually agreed annual operating plan, with the remaining shares acquired in later performance-linked phases. The total therefore covers both the share purchase and investment in Marut’s operations.

Only confidentiality, exclusivity, costs and governing-law provisions are binding at this stage. Closing requires satisfactory due diligence, definitive agreements, an audit of Marut’s financial statements under US auditing standards, and Indian regulatory and third-party approvals, including foreign-investment and DGCA-related clearances. The final terms, timing and completion remain conditional.

Recent findings suggest that founded in 2019 by Indian Institute of Technology Guwahati alumni, Marut designs and manufactures agricultural, surveillance, tethered and multi-utility drones. Its in-house work spans airframes and payloads as well as Swift, its ground-control and fleet-management software, giving Braiin an established manufacturing and software base rather than requiring it to build those functions after entering India.

Industry observers note that braiin states Marut holds eight type certificates from India’s civil aviation regulator, the DGCA. They include the AG365, described as India’s first DGCA type-certified multi-utility agricultural drone, and a heavier drone with 30-litre capacity for agriculture, aquaculture and industrial applications.

Braiin reports that Marut has more than 100 dealers, seven DGCA-approved pilot-training schools and over 500 customers spanning farmers, dealers, cooperatives and institutions. Karnataka Police, the Indian Army and Indian Railways are among the named customers. Marut has also supplied drones to Fiji and Myanmar.

Recent findings suggest that raptor300 already gives Braiin an operating drone business in Sri Lanka. Braiin reports binding contracts there valued at US$35.93 million and approximately US$112 million under non-binding memoranda of understanding, with no assurance that any MOU will become a binding contract.

Industry observers note that marut’s manufacturing capacity, wider aircraft range and trained-pilot pipeline would provide additional fleet depth for those deployments. On the technology side, Raptor300 contributes patented vectorized spraying and autonomous tank-refilling systems, while Swift provides ground control and fleet management across Marut’s fleet. Joint product development and hybrid Raptor300–Marut deployments are intended to cover seeding, spraying, crop monitoring, analytics and fleet services.

Recent findings suggest that within India, Marut’s operations are concentrated in Telangana, Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra and Odisha. Braiin’s post-completion roadmap calls for national expansion, heavier-payload and lower-cost platforms, in-house batteries and flight electronics, and exports to Sri Lanka, Australia, the GCC, Southeast Asia, Africa and North America.

The proposed deal would give Braiin a faster route into India through assets that are difficult to replicate quickly: regulatory certifications, manufacturing, dealers and pilot training. Its wider significance depends on execution: converting the term sheet into a completed acquisition, then turning the combined aircraft, autonomy software and Sri Lankan pipeline into scaled AI-led services.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

President threatens 'tremendous tax' on overseas builds, but analysts question how restrictions would work.

US President Donald Trump has threatened a "tremendous tax" on American companies building datacenters overseas, arguing that the infrastructure should stay at home to preserve the country's AI lead over China.

Speaking at a White House press conference after returning from the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen, Trump portrayed AI leadership as a contest America could not afford to lose.

Trump went on to say that "we're not going to allow our companies to build datacenters outside of our country," adding that "they allowed that to happen with chips and everything else and it was very destructive to our country.".

The threat appeared to catch even his own administration unbriefed. "I haven't even said that to my people, but I'm telling them now," Trump said.

The Official White House Rapid Response account posted a video clip on X.

We asked the White House if the president intends to follow through, and we will let you know if we get an answer.

Trump remarked: "We're not going to allow companies to build datacenters in other countries. If they do that, they can, but we're going to put a tremendous tax on them. We want them to do it here.".

Omdia chief analyst Roy Illsley.

According to recent reports, the threat comes amid concerns that Chinese entities were able to use Nvidia's cutting-edge GPUs for training AI models by accessing cloud services hosted in third countries. The US Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) issued new rules to try and crack down on this practice last week.

Sources indicate that "We're not allowing datacenters to go into other countries, as China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen," Trump repeated. "We're going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try and do it. They want to build that one in Finland, and we're not allowing that to happen," he added.

Google is expanding its facilities in Finland, including one recently in the news because the developer had reportedly illegally felled 250,000 trees to make way for it.

Such a policy seems unlikely to be allowed by Congress, where both houses will be under the control of the Democrats when the new term begins in January.

Amazon, Google, and Microsoft already operate global datacenter networks to serve customers in different regions. Restrictions on further overseas construction would complicate those businesses.

Omdia chief analyst Roy Illsley expressed doubt that this is a serious threat.

"There will be ways around that if he does impose some executive order, and the ability to build datacenters is not just an American skill, many countries can build them, it is the equipment in them that is mostly US," he told The Register.

Industry observers note that "So I do not take this seriously as it would not work, there is no such thing as a US datacenter, they are made up of thousands of components from all over the globe. He could stop US capital from being invested in those countries, but that could have trade consequences.".

Mike Kharchenko of European hosting firm HostZealot remarked there are good reasons why the cloud giants operate datacenters outside the US, such as latency and regulatory compliance.

"A buyer in Frankfurt won't wait for a page to load from Virginia. Some countries require certain data to stay inside their borders, and big European clients write it into contracts anyway," he stated.

Trump claimed that communities in America that host datacenters are "making so much money that they don't know what to do with it.".

According to recent reports, those claimed benefits come alongside substantial public subsidies. Nonprofit organization Good Jobs First reported earlier this year that some states are losing billions in revenue because of the tax abatement schemes offered to companies to entice them to set up shop there. ®.

Voice Cloning with Consent

📅 28 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1441 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in this blog post, we introduce the idea of a 'voice consent gate' to support voice cloning with consent.
  • In a recent development, realistic voice generation technology has gotten uncannily good in the past few years.
  • Sources indicate that voice generation, and in particular the subtask of voice cloning, has notable risks and benefits.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in this blog post, we introduce the idea of a 'voice consent gate' to support voice cloning with consent. We provide an example Space and accompanying code to start the ball rolling on the idea.

In a recent development, realistic voice generation technology has gotten uncannily good in the past few years. In some situations, it’s possible to generate a synthetic voice that sounds almost exactly like the voice of a real person. And today, what once felt like science fiction is reality: Voice cloning. With just a few seconds of recorded speech, anyone’s voice can be made to say almost anything.

Sources indicate that voice generation, and in particular the subtask of voice cloning, has notable risks and benefits. The risks of “deepfakes”, such as the cloned voice of former President Biden used in robocalls, can mislead people into thinking that people have stated things that they haven’t said. On the other hand, voice cloning can be a powerful beneficial tool, helping people who’ve lost the ability to speak communicate in their own voice again, or assisting people in learning new languages and dialects.

In a recent development, so how do we create meaningful use without malicious use? We’re exploring one possible answer: a voice consent gate. That’s a system where a voice can be cloned only when the speaker explicitly says they consent. In other words, the model won’t speak in your voice unless you say it’s okay.

We provide a basic demo of this idea below:.

It has been revealed that the voice consent gate is a piece of infrastructure we're exploring that provides methods for ethical principles like consent to be embedded directly into AI system workflows. In our demo, this means the model only starts once the speaker’s consent phrase has been both spoken and recognized, effectively making consent a prerequisite for action. This turns an abstract principle into a concrete system condition, creating a traceable, auditable interaction: an AI model can only run after an unambiguous act of consent.

Recent findings suggest that such design choices matter beyond voice cloning. They illustrate how AI systems can be built to respect autonomy by default, and how transparency and consent can be made functional, not just declarative.

To create a basic voice cloning system with a voice consent gate, you need three parts:.

Our observation: Since some voice-cloning systems can now generate speech similar to a speaker’s voice using just one sentence, a sentence used for consent can also be used for voice cloning.

The consent bit: To create a voice consent gate in an English voice cloning system, generate a short, natural-sounding English utterance (~20 words) for a person to read aloud that clearly states their informed consent in the current context. We recommend explicitly including a consent phrase and the model name, such as “I give my consent to use the < MODEL > voice cloning model with my voice”. We also recommend using an audio recording that cannot be uploaded, but that instead comes directly from a microphone, to make sure that the sentence isn’t part of an earlier recording that’s been manipulated. Pairing this with a novel (previously unsaid) sentence further helps to directly index the current consent context - supporting explicit, active, context-specific, informed consent. While this design reduces risks of reusing prior recordings, it’s not foolproof; a person could still generate a matching phrase using another TTS system. Future iterations could explore lightweight audio provenance checks, speaker-embedding similarity, or metadata from real-time capture to help verify that the consent audio originates from the intended speaker.

The suitable-for-voice-cloning bit: Previous work on voice cloning has shown that the phrases provided by the speaker must have phonetic variety, covering diverse vowels and consonants; have a “neutral” or polite tone, without background noise and with the speaker in a comfortable position; and have a clear start and end (i.e., don’t trim the clip mid-word).

It has been revealed that to enact both of these aspects within the demo, we prompt a language model to create pairs of sentences: one expressing explicit consent, and another neutral sentence that adds phonetic diversity (covering different vowels, consonants, and tones). Each prompt utilizes a randomly-chosen everyday topic (like the weather, food, or music) to keep the sentences varied and comfortable to say, aiding in creating recordings that are clear, natural, and phonetically rich, while also containing an unambiguous statement of consent. This generation step is automated rather than pre-written so that each user receives a unique sentence pair, preventing reuse of the same text and ensuring that consent recordings are specific to the current session. In other words, the language model generates two fresh sentences per consent instance: one for explicit consent and one for phonetic variety. For example, the language model might generate: “I give my consent to use my voice for generating audio with the model EchoVoice. The weather is bright and calm this morning.” This approach ensures that every sample used for cloning contains verifiable, explicit consent, while remaining suitable as technical input for high-quality voice synthesis. (Note: It's not required that the language model be a "large" language model, which brings its own consent issues.).

Once the speaker’s input matches the generated text, the voice cloning system can start, using the speaker’s consent audio as the input.

There are a few options for doing this, and we’d love to hear further ideas. For now, there’s:.

You can copy the code to suit your own use.

Industry observers note that the code is modular so it can be sliced and diced in different ways to incorporate into your own projects. We’ll be working on making this more robust and secure over time, and we’re curious to hear your ideas on how to improve.

Handled responsibly, this technology doesn’t have to haunt us. It can instead become a respectful collaboration between humans and machines — no ghosts in the machine, just good practice. 🎃.

Not a big fan of trying to legislate every problem away but if malicious deep fakes are already illegal in most jurisdictions it seems that malicious voice cloning ought to be too.

Industry observers note that I think the problem with enforcement will be offshore usage (i.e. if a person from country X is illegally using a voice clone of a person from country Y, how will enforcement work?), as has already been shown with widespread global IP misuse. The second concern is going to be detection. Who is going to check that every single AI voice was or was not cloned with consent? Anything that would truly prevent misuse with robust checks would probably stifle the ability to iterate and develop swiftly and anything that didn't stifle the ability to iterate and develop quickly probably wouldn't truly prevent misuse. The classic regulatory Catch-22.

It's problems like these that kind of necessitate a global response and whilst I'm usually not one to advocate for supranational law-making, it would be nice to see the so-called international community create a joint response or at least initiative on this topic because it's going to be a brutal wake-up call one day.

In a recent development, at this point even just outreach and education on this topic would be helpful. In my time working with random developers and others in the OSS community, I've come across several suspicious requests from people I hardly know asking me for seemingly random recordings of my voice. Someone who doesn't understand the potential for misuse might provide such a recording and inadvertently have their voice used in scam campaigns.

AI Biology in 2027: Genome Models Become Tools for Designing Experiments

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1558 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Biology is full of plausible ideas that do not survive an experiment.
  • The opportunity for 2027 is a better conversation between prediction and experiment: choosing what to build, learning from what failed and deciding which uncertainty is worth resolving next.
  • The starting point is already substantial.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Biology is full of plausible ideas that do not survive an experiment. A sequence can look promising, a model can give it a high score, and a cell can respond in a way nobody expected. That friction is where AI biology becomes scientifically interesting.

The opportunity for 2027 is a better conversation between prediction and experiment: choosing what to build, learning from what failed and deciding which uncertainty is worth resolving next. More computational possibility will matter only if it helps a laboratory ask better questions.

The starting point is already substantial. The published Evo 2 study describes genome modelling across domains of life, while AlphaGenome predicts multiple molecular consequences of DNA variation. Neither establishes that a plausible sequence will be safe or useful in a patient. These forecasts concern experimental research, where that gap can be measured directly.

It has been revealed that A laboratory has room to test a few dozen candidates and a model can propose thousands. The useful intelligence lies in the choice between them. In 2027, prospective studies will show genome models improving experimental hit rates against stated baselines. That would make the model a better guide to scarce laboratory effort, rather than simply a prolific source of sequences.

According to recent reports, sequence plausibility is an inadequate endpoint for engineering. A promoter can look biologically familiar yet fail in the target cell; a successful design can become unhelpful when moved to another cellular environment. The meaningful comparison starts before the assay, with a fixed budget and a documented choice of controls.

It has been revealed that the October 2026 Evo 2 in-context learning work reports enhancer-design experiments, including testing in mouse brain. It is an early research result, not evidence of a human treatment. My forecast is that the next competitive distinction will be repeatable enrichment of useful sequences under a constrained experimental budget. The model must improve which candidates are built, rather than receive credit for finding one interesting sequence among thousands.

In a recent development, this is more attainable than accurate prediction of every regulatory interaction. It can succeed for a narrow assay even while broader biological generalization remains unreliable. Publication bias is a serious limitation: successful screens may be more visible than failures, which makes disclosure of the full candidate denominator essential.

Industry observers note that look for selection rules fixed before measurements, matched numbers of tested candidates, and negative controls. Replication in another laboratory would strengthen the forecast. Retrospective rankings, cherry-picked sequences, or comparisons with unusually weak baselines would weaken the apparent progress.

Biotech buyers should price these systems against experiments avoided and validated candidates gained. A contract should specify the relevant cell type, assay and baseline. A cheaper sequence-generation service can be economically inferior if it shifts more failures into expensive downstream validation.

A model can appear to understand a cell when it mostly recognizes the experimental setting. Move to another cell type or donor and the apparent understanding may unravel. In 2027, perturbation studies will make those unfamiliar conditions a more visible test, revealing which biological relationships travel and which predictions depended on staying close to home.

Sources indicate that predicting a cell's response is difficult because training data encode both biology and experimental practice. Batch effects, cell-state composition and measurement depth can masquerade as a response to treatment. Randomly dividing measurements from the same experimental setting can therefore produce an encouraging score without testing the intended scientific use.

The 2026 Virtual Cell Challenge explicitly places unfamiliar cellular settings at the center of evaluation. A 2026 perturbation-proteomics study also illustrates the growing effort to connect computational representations with measured cellular responses. Those efforts establish a research direction, not a universal simulator of living systems.

The next useful question is whether a model preserves the ordering of candidate interventions when the cellular context changes. Perfect reconstruction of every measured feature may matter less than correctly separating promising and harmful experimental directions. Conversely, good average reconstruction can conceal failure on the rare state the researcher actually needs.

Industry observers note that the strongest studies will identify what was held out, compare against simple population-average baselines, and publish errors for different cell states. Claims of generalization based only on random train-test splits should carry less weight than genuinely unfamiliar experimental conditions.

Treat a virtual-cell platform as a decision-support instrument with a defined operating range. Before buying a broad license, fund a blinded evaluation on the tech giant's own biological setting. Data generated outside that range may require new experiments and retraining rather than a larger subscription.

It has been revealed that A predicted molecular effect is a clue, and an crucial one. It can also tempt an interpreter to close the case too early. In 2027, variant-prioritization workflows will more clearly expose uncertainty and conflicting evidence. The scientific value will lie in helping researchers see what the score leaves unresolved, especially when molecular plausibility and clinical context point in different directions.

It has been revealed that the AlphaGenome Atlas offers predictions at extraordinary scale. Scale changes the search process: it allows researchers to ask which variants deserve attention across a large region. It does not remove the distinction between a predicted molecular effect and a demonstrated cause of disease.

A variant can change a molecular readout without explaining the patient's condition. Relevant evidence also includes inheritance, phenotype, tissue specificity and population frequency. When these disagree, hiding the disagreement behind a single score makes interpretation look easier than it is. My expectation is that useful products will show their reasoning ingredients separately, so researchers can decide which uncertainty to resolve next.

It has been revealed that the commercial incentive runs in both directions. A clean ranking is easy to sell, while an uncertainty-aware report can appear indecisive. That tension is why the prediction concerns documented workflows rather than an assumption that the whole market will suddenly adopt a common interpretation standard.

It has been revealed that look for reports that distinguish predicted regulatory effects from pathogenicity, identify the tissue being modelled, and preserve conflicting evidence. Better calibration on rare or previously unseen variants would strengthen confidence; an unexplained composite score would offer much less assurance.

In a recent development, diagnostic and research suppliers should preserve the evidence trail behind a recommendation. Laboratories need to know when an AI score can prioritize follow-up and when an established clinical interpretation process must decide the result. Marketing language should reflect that boundary.

The failed experiment is easy to leave out of the story and expensive to lose from the learning process. In 2027, published design-test cycles will bring unsuccessful candidates back into the next selection round. That creates a more demanding form of progress: the model must improve after biology disagrees with it, without learning the laboratory's measurement mistakes as if they were natural laws.

Industry observers note that public sequence collections contain the outcomes of biological selection. Engineering laboratories also need to learn from sequences that did not produce the intended result. If only successful designs enter the feedback process, a model can learn what looks publishable while remaining poorly informed about the boundaries of the assay.

Both the Evo 2 research and AlphaGenome's multi-output approach make it easier to generate hypotheses. The bottleneck then moves toward experiment design, measurement quality and the decision about which observation would be most informative. My forecast is about closing that loop in published experiments, rather than merely connecting software to laboratory equipment.

There is an important constraint: an apparent failed design may actually be a failed measurement or an incorrect experimental context. Learning automatically from every low signal can reinforce laboratory artifacts. A productive feedback loop therefore needs information about assay reliability alongside the biological result.

Sources indicate that look for full round-by-round candidate lists, documented failures and a fixed assay objective. Improvement should survive comparison with simply running more experiments. A later round that changes both the model and the biological target would be harder to interpret.

Invest in experiment metadata and usable negative results as deliberately as in model access. The strongest advantage may come from a trustworthy private learning cycle, provided the organization can separate a biological failure from a measurement problem and retain rights to reuse the resulting data.

The cell remains an exacting partner. It does not reward an elegant explanation merely for sounding plausible. The most valuable AI biology in 2027 will use that resistance productively, turning mismatches between expectation and measurement into better experiments and a clearer understanding of what the model still cannot know.

Some of these devices have no way of being updated; the software's burned in ROMs that are not visible to the operating system that's running. This could keep crumbling away.

I once was a significant fan of a website called LoperOS.org by Stanislav Datskovskiy. He was a Lisp evangelist. He's gone very quiet in recent years, but he compared building software out of C to building a model of a bridge or the Eiffel Tower out of toothpicks or matchsticks. The end structure is not very strong because it's mostly weak wood and glue. You build it out of this poor structural material because loads of people can work together on it. And C and tools like C are good at this; you can farm out development to whole teams of people. They're working with tweezers and toothpicks instead of bricks and cement because it's easier to do this over a team.

According to recent reports, somebody said, "If we built houses the way that we build software, then the first termite colony to come along would destroy civilization," because we built it out of bad materials. I'm not personally Christian, but I read the Bible and there's that line about building your house on sand. It doesn't matter how tough you make the house: if you built it on sand and the sand shifts, you've got a massive problem.

Industry observers note that this problem goes all the way down. Maybe we're going to have to replace the whole thing.

According to recent reports, god, I hope not. One of the things I think about happening is how in past generations of software we slapped new things on top of old things to protect the old things from the new things.

In a recent development, and it makes me wonder if the next version of slapping something on top of our entire infrastructure is AI. We put AI on top of it. We make AI handle bug hunting, vulnerability remediation, and security. It creates a situation where the stuff is safe for now, but software always abstracts layers as you get further up the stack. I wonder if AI is going to be the next level of abstraction to the point where we don't really understand what the code's doing anymore at all.

Right. Over time. So I think it's likely that is going to be one of the ways we try to solve this problem.

I don't see another way out of it because of the sheer volume of flaws that are being found. Like Liam stated, there's low-level stuff getting discovered now that no human would have found, but the fact that an AI found it means someone's going to exploit it at some point.

According to recent reports, I think for management this is going to look like a very tempting option, but it will accelerate the problem. We're in an iterative race at the moment – the Red Queen's race. You have to run as  fast as you can to stay where you are. We've got upcoming tools that are finding problems faster than ever, so it's tempting to try and use similar tools to fix them faster than ever, but that means nobody understands the fix. Then if another hole is found deeper down, the whole layer of fixes collapses.

In a recent development, one of the predominant development tools on the PC platform used to be Turbo Pascal. DOS wasn't written in C. Way back when, people accused Microsoft of plagiarizing CP/M. Microsoft didn't write DOS; Tim Paterson of Seattle Computer Products wrote the original. CP/M was written in a high-level language, PL/M, whereas DOS was hand-coded in Assembler. It wasn't plagiarism because they went a level down. In the early days people wrote this stuff in Pascal. I remember Unix catching on and C becoming trendy because it was so fast. For a little while a company called TopSpeed sold a Modula-2 compiler because not only was the code faster than C, but it compiled faster than C compilers back then. Ultimately the sheer inertia of C and C-related languages caught on and all that stuff got sidelined. Borland went through various transitions and Turbo Pascal became Delphi, which went to Embarcadero and is still around, though I'm not sure anybody cares anymore. I worked through one industry shift where Assembler and Pascal-related languages were replaced by C. It could happen again. It wasn't all that bad last time. I know it seems unimaginable now, but I'm not that old. Working in this field for less than four decades, I've watched an entire software industry get swept away and replaced. And we all kept our jobs, and we all kept working on pretty much the same hardware. Maybe that's going to happen again. I know it sounds unimaginable, but it honestly wasn't that bad.

Speaking of hardware, given these outages, connected services going offline are causing chaos. Setting aside the FAA – that's a public service that stranded travelers – banks, Apple, and Microsoft are business problems. We're seeing with AI where everyone is weighing the cost-benefit between hosted services where you pay for tokens versus turning the server closet back into a server closet. Is it time to come back on-premises with a lot of these things? Is it time to run your own Exchange server again or host your own file shares on your own network? It makes me wonder if the solution to some of these outage concerns going forward is going to be a return to on-premises.

Personally I think that's an excellent idea.

I agree, but so many of these companies are entrenched in every other firm – Microsoft, for example. It's going to be pretty hard to completely swing to the opposite end of the spectrum here.

In a recent development, sure. Maybe they need to start offering more self-hosted services again. But if everything you do is in Google or Microsoft 365, it's going to be hard to get yourself out of that, and probably very expensive, at least at first. Especially with the cost of hardware right now not going down given the AI push. So maybe we're all just trapped.

According to recent reports, you know what? I actually disagree there because, to take a different example: I used to be a motorcyclist. Early in my career I switched from tech support to IT manager to designing and building networks, and I turned up to work on a motorbike. Then I had a really bad crash, switched to three-wheelers, and discovered how bad London traffic had gotten. My injuries prevented me from going back on a solo bike most of the time, but years later I switched to bicycling. You can still cut through traffic very well on a bicycle in a lot of Europe. Car drivers got used to the delays; it gets ten minutes longer to get to work every year, but you don't notice ten minutes over a year, so you put up with it. My next-door neighbor didn't know what underground line he lived on because he drove everywhere. People got used to it taking two or three hours to drive to work and just put up with it. I've seen photos of massive West Coast freeways with eight lanes of stationary traffic. People will put up with amazing levels of delay and non-functionality if it happens gradually enough.

Right. No matter what happens, if there are more outages, we will be here to talk about them on The Kettle. If there are fewer, we probably won't, but one can hope.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NOTICE: Sneakernet is a work in progress. The documentation makes some promises that are not reflected in the current state of affairs. Links to to-be-written parts of the documentation are indicated in red.

Sneakernet is a system for securely1 sending digital messages to other people without using the Internet. Instead, messages are automatically passed on to other Sneakernet users on your local network – at your hackerspace, an event or conference, your local cafe, etc — and then physically carried to their destination on your “sneakers”, where they will be automatically delivered to any recipients on the same network (or handed over to be carried further on by someone else).

Sneakernet encourages slow, thoughtful participation in community and face-to-face meetings with the consumers who will carry your messages onwards to their destination, and entrust their own messages to you.

⇒ Head to Getting started to set up Sneakernet on your device.

Many applications can be built on top of sneakernet’s general-purpose messaging system, provided that they are tolerant of high latency and out-of-order messages. Some examples include:.

Building your own sneakernet applications is easy, too, in any programming language – see Building applications for more details.

Industry observers note that all messages are authenticated and all private messages are also encrypted. People who carry your messages along cannot tamper with them and cannot read your private messages. See Security for more details.
